Afghanistan.d:
Afghanistan's governments have long been run in part by people that foreign powers paid, trained or protected, and Pakistan's military intelligence service, the ISI, has reached furthest. Since the Taliban took Kabul in 2021, much of the leadership has come out of one Pakistani religious school, Darul Uloom Haqqania: its graduates include the interior and foreign ministers, and its late chancellor wrote that about nine in ten of the religiously educated people in the Taliban government were graduates or the sons of graduates. The interior minister also leads the Haqqani network, a militant group inside the Taliban that the top US military officer once called an arm of the ISI, and it was handed Kabul's security; the ISI's chief was in Kabul as the Taliban chose their prime minister. Pakistan denies interfering. UN sanctions monitors also find al-Qaeda-affiliated figures among senior Taliban officials.

Before 2021 the reach came through cash and agents. For more than a decade the CIA delivered bags of money to President Hamid Karzai's office, tens of millions of dollars that went on to relatives, politicians and warlords, and Iran's government paid his chief of staff in the same way; Karzai confirmed both. In 2012 the Afghan intelligence service told parliament it had arrested 15 government employees, including senior officials and a general, for spying for the ISI or Iran.

For people living there, the police in the capital answer to a faction accused of serving a neighbouring spy service, and for twenty years the men around the president were kept loyal with foreign money rather than by voters. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Afghanistan 9 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and 1.5 for courts, police and watchdogs, so residents have almost nowhere to take a complaint.

Angola.d:
Angola's state runs mainly on oil, and the state oil company, Sonangol, which awards offshore contracts, is where foreign firms have reached in most often. Oil traders, suppliers of oil platforms and construction groups have paid Angolan officials through local agents and bank accounts in Switzerland and Monaco to win business. The Dutch platform builder SBM Offshore admitted that from 1997 to 2012 the 'commissions' it paid its Angolan agents were passed on to at least nine Sonangol officials, and a Swiss court in 2025 convicted the oil trader Trafigura of paying a Sonangol-linked official, which it is appealing. A Brazilian construction group has also admitted paying about $50 million to unnamed Angolan officials for public works contracts.

The same pattern ran through the rebuilding of the country after its civil war. China International Fund, a Hong Kong company, ran Chinese-financed reconstruction in partnership with generals close to the former president José Eduardo dos Santos, and in 2022 Angolan prosecutors indicted two of those generals and the company, alleging that money meant for public housing went to private ends and that about $1.5 billion in Chinese payments for Angolan oil never reached Angola. The generals went on trial in 2024.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Angola 8 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 4 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For Angolans, this means the oil revenue and foreign loans that should pay for housing, schools, hospitals and wages have repeatedly been split with foreign companies and well-placed officers, and most of the officials paid have never been named at home.

Australia.d:
In Australia, outsiders reach in through three routes: criminal businesses buying police protection, foreign governments buying access to politicians, and private firms and gangs getting people into the bodies that write rules or spend public money.

The police route is the oldest and best documented. Two public inquiries, in Queensland in the late 1980s and in New South Wales in the mid-1990s, found corruption in the police entrenched rather than occasional: brothel, illegal casino and bookmaking operators in one state and drug dealers in the other paid officers regularly to leave them alone. In Queensland the police commissioner himself was jailed for taking about $700,000 in such bribes. Both led to standing anti-corruption commissions, but the pattern has continued at the border, where drug importers have recruited Border Force and state police officers in Sydney and Melbourne; Australia pays some of the world's highest wholesale drug prices, which makes an insider worth buying.

The foreign route runs mainly through China's United Front, the Chinese Communist Party office that organises influence abroad through community and business groups. Donors tied to it have given millions to both major parties, and community leaders linked to it have been prosecuted under the foreign-interference law. India's foreign intelligence service has also cultivated politicians and a state police force.

Closer to home, members of outlaw motorcycle gangs held union posts on state-funded building sites in Victoria, and a PwC partner hired by the Treasury to advise on laws against multinational tax avoidance passed its plans to colleagues advising the companies those laws targeted. For people here, that means the officers checking cargo or policing a neighbourhood may be paid by the trade they are meant to stop, and tax laws meant to make large companies pay can be weakened before they are written.

Bahrain.d:
Bahrain is a small Gulf kingdom whose largest industry outside oil is aluminium, and its documented case of outsiders reaching in runs through the state-controlled smelter, Aluminium Bahrain, known as Alba. To keep long-term contracts to supply Alba with alumina, the raw material for aluminium, the US company Alcoa placed a London-based middleman with close ties to senior members of the royal family between itself and the smelter. Sales went through his offshore companies, which marked up prices by about $188 million between 2005 and 2009, and he used that margin to pay tens of millions of dollars in kickbacks to the Bahraini officials who controlled the tenders. Alcoa's subsidiary pleaded guilty to bribery in the United States in 2014.

Bahrain's politics are also shaped by the rivalry between Sunni-led Gulf states and Shia Iran. The Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement active across the Arab world, has a documented presence; groups allied with Iran's Revolutionary Guards are thought to be present but are not documented inside the state. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Bahrain 4.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 5.3 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, both in the middle of the range.

For Bahrainis, this means a state company that belongs to the public paid inflated prices for its raw material for years, and the difference went to the officials running its tenders and the middleman connected to the royal family. The case was brought by a foreign court, and the officials who took the money have not been named at home.

Belgium.d:
Belgium is where outsiders reach into Europe and the Western alliance as a whole. Brussels hosts the main EU institutions and NATO's headquarters, and Antwerp is the port through which more cocaine reaches Europe than any other, so foreign governments, arms makers, companies and drug networks all have reasons to get people inside.

During the Cold War, Soviet and East German intelligence had long-term agents on NATO's own staff, and the same work goes on today: China's, Hungary's and Morocco's intelligence services have each been found paying a Belgian politician, trying to recruit EU officials, or placing their members on the staff of a mosque the state was asked to recognise. Gulf money reaches the people who negotiate and vote. Belgian prosecutors say Qatar and Morocco paid cash to members of the European Parliament, partly through a human-rights charity, in a case known as Qatargate; the accused deny it. Qatar also paid flights and holidays for the head of the European Commission's transport department while he negotiated the air agreement that opened Europe's skies to its state airline, and the Commission dismissed him in 2026.

In Antwerp, cocaine networks pay port workers, terminal staff, customs officers and police to pull containers out and pass on access codes, and moving a single container can earn a port worker more than €100,000. An Antwerp investigating judge wrote in 2025 that their inquiries had led to the arrest of port employees, customs and police officers, municipal counter staff, and justice staff in prisons and the courthouse. For people in Belgium and across the EU, this means decisions on trade, aviation and human rights may have been shaped by foreign payments, and the clerks, guards and officers handling their cases may work for the networks they are meant to stop.

Bolivia.d:
Bolivia is one of the world's main producers of coca, the plant cocaine is made from, and for more than forty years traffickers have bought the part of the state meant to stop them: the interior ministry and the anti-drug police. The pattern took shape in the 1980 'Cocaine Coup', when the country's leading trafficker, Roberto Suárez, helped pay for a military takeover, parts of the army protected traffickers for bribes, and his cousin became interior minister, in charge of the police. It has carried on since. Twice in recent years a former head of the anti-narcotics police, the FELCN, has been convicted in the United States of working for traffickers, by protecting cocaine loads, steering investigations away from allied gangs and assigning armed officers to guard shipments.

Foreign intelligence and secret officers' groups have reached the same offices. In the 1960s an interior minister said the CIA had recruited him, and in 1943 a secret faction of army officers helped overthrow the president and put one of its members in his place. One writer's account also says the Unification Church, the Korean-founded movement of Sun Myung Moon, backed the 1980 regime.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Bolivia 6.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 4.6 for its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, the police unit they would turn to about a trafficking gang has repeatedly been run by someone on a gang's payroll, and investigations have been pointed away from favoured traffickers and towards their rivals. Both recent convictions came from US courts, so Bolivians learned how their own anti-drug force was run from a foreign trial rather than from their own institutions.

Brunei.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Brunei, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows a foreign intelligence service, company, crime group, church or lodge paying or placing people inside its government.

Brunei is a small, oil-rich sultanate on Borneo where the sultan holds executive power and there is no elected parliament, so there are few public channels through which outside influence would come to light. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Brunei 3 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests, low by world standards, and about 4.6 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs.

For people living there, this means there is no documented case of an official acting for an outside interest, and the low score suggests the risk is small. With few public channels and middling oversight, though, such a case would be hard to bring to light, and a documented case would change this estimate.

Cabo Verde.d:
Little is documented for Cabo Verde, so this is an estimate. No case found so far shows a foreign state, company, criminal group or lodge paying or placing people inside its government. The Global Organized Crime Index rates the country low for officials working for criminal interests and comparatively strong in its courts, police and watchdogs, which suggests fewer officials act for outside interests here than in most of West Africa. The islands sit on Atlantic shipping lanes between South America, West Africa and Europe, so the ports are the place most exposed to outside money.

The lack of cases may also reflect how little investigative reporting covers the islands. If outside money does reach officials, it would most likely show up in the ports, in shipping and in public contracts, and residents would pay for it through lost public revenue rather than through anything they could see directly. For now there is no named official, company or group for Cabo Verdeans to hold to account.

Central African Republic.d:
In the Central African Republic a foreign armed group works from inside the state. Wagner, the Russian private military company tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, arrived in 2018 and placed its own people in the presidency: one of its men, Valery Zakharov, served as President Touadéra's national security adviser and was sanctioned by the United States for his Wagner ties. A US-sponsored research centre, the Africa Center for Strategic Studies, assesses that the old Wagner organisation has in effect taken over the state.

The arrangement has spread into the drug trade. Reporting from Bangui in 2026 describes Wagner's remnants supplying tramadol, an opioid painkiller, to members of the presidential guard and to a youth militia, with senior security officials alleged to control the market and payments flowing to Wagner and allied armed groups along the smuggling route. No one has been charged.

For people in the country, the president's security advice has come from a Wagner man answerable to Moscow rather than to Central African voters or courts, and some of the armed men around them are supplied with opioids by the same network. The Global Organized Crime Index rates the country among the very worst in the world for officials working for criminal interests, with almost no capacity in its courts, police or watchdogs to resist. Under the previous president, press reports said he had joined Freemasonry under the sponsorship of the Republic of Congo's president.

Colombia.d:
In Colombia the drug trade and the armed groups built on it have reached into every level of the state for more than forty years. The cocaine cartels and the AUC, right-wing paramilitaries who were also major traffickers, got their own people elected, paid into presidential campaigns and bought the officials meant to hunt them. Pablo Escobar, the Medellín Cartel's leader, won a seat in Congress in 1982, and in the 'parapolítica' scandal about 30 per cent of Congress was investigated, charged or convicted over collusion with the paramilitaries. Two directors of the national intelligence agency, the DAS, were later convicted of serving the cartels or paramilitaries, one for taking part in the murder of a presidential frontrunner, and a city chief prosecutor was jailed for shielding a drug gang.

What traffickers have wanted most from the state is protection from extradition to the United States, and they have paid police, legislators and lawyers to get it. Politicians under investigation have also bought the courts: two former Supreme Court presidents and the national anti-corruption prosecutor were convicted of taking money to bury cases. Allegations of drug money in presidential campaigns have followed elections from 1994 to 2022.

The reach continues locally. The Gulf Clan, the country's largest trafficking group, funds mayoral candidates in the towns along its routes and has hidden property in the names of people inside the justice system. For Colombians, this has meant voting for legislators and mayors whose campaigns traffickers helped fund, and taking cases before judges paid to bury files. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Colombia high for officials working for criminal interests, but its courts have shown they can reach their own members, which is how most of this became known.

Costa Rica.d:
Costa Rica lies on the route that carries Colombian cocaine north to the United States and across to Europe, and traffickers keep that route open by recruiting people inside the police and the security ministry to tell them what investigators know. The clearest case reaches near the top: the US Treasury found that a former vice-minister of public security, who later sat as a judge, helped move cocaine through the country and used his government contacts to learn about open drug investigations. He was arrested on a US extradition request in 2025 and has not been convicted.

The same method runs through the ranks of the national police. On the Caribbean side, trafficking groups have recruited local officers as lookouts to warn them of raids and checkpoints; in Guanacaste on the Pacific side, local officers have passed information to groups flying drugs out from clandestine airstrips. In 2026 the government said 116 officers of the public security ministry were under investigation after an internal intelligence report found some escorting criminals and coordinating secret drug flights, and that the report had sat with the previous government for months without an inquiry. Foreign companies seeking state contracts have also been accused of paying at the highest level, though the one such case against a president ended in acquittal on appeal.

For people living along the cocaine routes, the officers they would call for help may be the ones telling traffickers when the police are coming. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Costa Rica's officials as relatively unlikely to work for criminal interests, with institutions of middling strength.

Cyprus.d:
The deepest outside reach into the Cypriot state came from Greece, and its result is still the shape of the island. In the early 1970s Greece's military government had about 650 of its own officers serving in Cyprus's army, the National Guard, and it funded and controlled an armed group that wanted Cyprus joined to Greece. In July 1974, on the junta's orders, the National Guard attacked the presidential palace and overthrew President Makarios; Turkey invaded five days later and came to hold 37 per cent of the island, which remains divided.

Today the question is money. Cyprus is a small European Union member with a large financial and company-registration sector serving foreign clients, including Russian ones. In January 2026 a secretly filmed video appeared to show the president's chief of staff, his brother-in-law and a former energy minister discussing ways round the cap on campaign donations, cash for access to the presidency and help for businessmen avoiding EU sanctions on Russia. The chief of staff resigned, saying his words were taken out of context, the government called the video a maliciously edited attack, and a former Supreme Court judge is investigating; nothing has been proven.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Cyprus low to middling for officials working for criminal interests, but its courts, police and watchdogs score weak for an EU member. For Cypriots, this means a foreign government once used officers inside their own army to remove their elected president, and they still live with the partition that followed. Now the open question is whether wealthy outsiders can pay for a hearing at the top of government, and the bodies meant to answer it are weaker than in most of the EU.

Dominica.d:
The one documented case of outside money reaching Dominica's government involves a campaign donation. Al Jazeera reported that an Iranian businessman gave hundreds of thousands of dollars to Prime Minister Roosevelt Skerrit's election campaign and received an ambassador's post and a diplomatic passport in return; the businessman was later jailed in Iran for stealing oil revenue. Skerrit denies any trade, and no court has ruled on the claim.

If the report is right, a post that speaks for Dominica abroad went to a campaign donor, and a diplomatic passport, which carries legal protections overseas, went to a man later jailed for theft. Dominicans have no public record of what campaign donors receive.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Dominica low for officials working for criminal interests, with institutions of middling strength.

El Salvador.d:
In El Salvador criminal groups have reached the state both through local office and through the government itself. The country's two largest gangs, MS-13 and Barrio 18, grew out of Salvadoran communities in Los Angeles and now run neighbourhoods across the country. According to the US government, officials of President Nayib Bukele's administration negotiated with gang leaders inside the prison system: the US Treasury says the prisons director and the head of a programme for violence-hit neighbourhoods gave them money and privileges, in return for keeping the number of killings down and supporting the government at elections. A US indictment of 13 MS-13 leaders adds that a leader wanted in the United States was released and that the gang backed Bukele's party, Nuevas Ideas, in the 2021 election. The government denies any pact, and no court has tried the claims.

Drug trafficking has reached local office in the same way. The news site El Faro reported in 2011 that a network moving drugs along the northern border was led by a sitting mayor, with police, soldiers, judges and prosecutors paid to let shipments through; a court acquitted all nine defendants in 2021.

If these accounts are right, criminal organisations have bargained with the state over how many Salvadorans would be killed and how people would vote, and have used town halls to move drugs. Salvadorans cannot check how much of the fall in killings came from such a deal, because the evidence has never been heard by a court at home. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7.5 out of 10 and the strength of courts and watchdogs at 3.25.

Eswatini.d:
This is an estimate: no case on the map shows a foreign state, company, criminal group or religious body placing or paying people inside Eswatini's government. Eswatini is a small kingdom between South Africa and Mozambique where the king holds executive power and political parties cannot compete for government, so there are few independent sources inside the country that report on officials.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 6.5 out of 10, in its high band, and the courts, police and watchdogs that would resist them at about 3.2. A country with that profile, on the trade routes between South Africa and Mozambique, is one where traffickers and businesses seeking contracts would find officials open to payment and little chance of a case reaching court.

If that is happening, people in Eswatini would pay for it through public contracts that cost more than they should and policing that does not reach those who pay. With no named case, there is no official, company or group they can point to or hold to account.

France.d:
In France outside interests reach government mostly through the people who run it and the money behind their campaigns. One channel is the move from private banking into the offices that set economic policy. Two French presidents worked at the Rothschild investment bank before entering government, among them Emmanuel Macron, a partner there until he joined the president's office in 2012. No inquiry has found that the bank directed policy, and the claim that the Rothschild family runs France is an antisemitic conspiracy theory. As economy minister he helped Uber against his own cabinet colleagues, leaked documents show.

Campaign money is the second channel, much of it from abroad or the arms and oil trade: since the 1990s courts have traced secret funds of the state oil company Elf to political parties, and commissions on a submarine sale to Pakistan to a prime minister's presidential bid. In 2025 Nicolas Sarkozy became the first former president sentenced to prison, for conspiring with Muammar Gaddafi's intelligence chief to seek Libyan money for his 2007 campaign; he is appealing. Foreign spy services have placed people inside too: a Soviet agent held posts in French ministries and at NATO for nearly two decades. Freemasonry, a society of private lodges whose members pledge mutual help, has long had members in cabinets and senior posts, and the government now says the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist movement founded in Egypt, is working its way into local councils.

For people in France, decisions about banking, taxis or arms sales may already have been shaped by a firm, a network or a foreign government before ministers present them. The Global Organized Crime Index rates officials acting for criminal interests low and the courts strong, so the influence that matters comes through who holds office and who pays their campaigns.

Germany.d:
Germany has been a main target for foreign intelligence services since the Cold War, and they work by placing or recruiting people inside its institutions. East Germany's Stasi had a personal aide to Chancellor Willy Brandt, whose exposure in 1974 brought Brandt down, and agents in parliament and in the foreign intelligence service, the BND, whose counter-espionage against Moscow was for years headed by a KGB agent. The pattern continues: a BND officer is on trial for selling documents to Russia's FSB, and the spy services of Russia, China and Egypt have each recently had someone inside the management of a large payments company, an MEP's office and the government press office. Foreign governments also use money: several conservative MPs have resigned or been investigated over payments from Azerbaijan, and a subsidiary of Russia's state gas company paid for a state government's foundation set up to finish its pipeline to Russia.

Companies and banks reach in through people and paperwork. Chancellor Friedrich Merz chaired the German arm of BlackRock, the largest asset manager, until 2020, and a recent finance minister came from Goldman Sachs. Germany's risk agency copied large parts of the glyphosate makers' own application into the safety review the EU used to renew the weedkiller. At Hamburg and Bremerhaven, cocaine importers recruit customs officers and terminal staff to clear containers.

For people in Germany, critics of Moscow and Beijing live alongside people those governments have recruited inside parliament, the spy services and business, and a safety decision about a chemical used on farms rested partly on text its makers wrote. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 2 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs above 7, so most of these cases are investigated and many reach court.

Guatemala.d:
Guatemala's state has been reached from outside for seventy years, first by a foreign intelligence service and now by drug traffickers. In 1954 the CIA chose an exiled army officer, Carlos Castillo Armas, kept him on its payroll, and sent him in with CIA-trained fighters to overthrow the elected president, whose land reform had taken land from the US-based United Fruit Company; he then ran the country until he was killed in 1957. The agency kept paid sources inside the army afterwards, including a colonel linked to two killings in the early 1990s.

Today the country lies on the land route that carries South American cocaine north to Mexico and the United States, and the trafficking groups that use it buy officials at every level the drugs pass through. Since 2005 the people charged, convicted or sanctioned in the United States for working with traffickers have included the head of the anti-narcotics police, border-town mayors, members of Congress and the Central American Parliament, and a vice-president and interior minister. One presidential candidate, Mario Estrada, was jailed in the US in 2020 for seeking cartel money in return for promising the cartel open access to the country's ports and airports and seats in government. Corruption rings inside customs have reached the presidency itself, and CICIG, a UN-backed commission that helped expose them, was later shut down by the government.

For Guatemalans this means the police officer, mayor or legislator they would turn to may be working for traffickers, and import duties that should reach the treasury have gone to officials instead. Most cases against powerful figures are now heard in US courts rather than at home. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 8 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at 4.

Haiti.d:
In Haiti armed gangs control much of the capital, Port-au-Prince, and large areas of the Artibonite valley, and the line between the gangs and the state has worn thin from both sides. Politicians have funded and armed gangs to control territory and voters. Canada and the United States have sanctioned a former president, sitting and former senators and other political figures for financing gangs, and a UN panel of experts says former legislators have armed groups and used them to drive violence before elections. Those named deny it.

The gangs in turn reach into the state. The UN panel reported in October 2026 that some police officers supply gangs with weapons and information, and that at least one member of the new municipal commission in Cité Soleil, one of the capital's poorest districts, is an active gang member. Cocaine traffickers have bought protection at the top of the police for three decades, from the police chief of the 1990s military regime, indicted in the US over Colombian bribes, to a former commander who admitted taking millions to protect shipments, and the US Treasury says Michel Martelly worked with traffickers as president, which he denies.

Outside control of the state is old here: from 1915 a New York bank, the forerunner of Citigroup, owned Haiti's national bank and, under US occupation, ran its finances for decades. For people in Haiti today, the gangs that kill, kidnap and drive them from their homes are paid for by some of the politicians asking for their votes and supplied by some of the police meant to protect them. With courts and watchdogs scoring 2.2 out of 10 on the Global Organized Crime Index and officials acting for criminal interests at 8.5, none of the sanctioned politicians has faced a Haitian court.

India.d:
India's government is run largely by members of one organisation. The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) is a Hindu nationalist volunteer body founded in 1925; it trains full-time organisers and lends them to the governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), where by convention one of them always holds the party's general secretary post for organisation and reports back to the RSS chief. Prime Minister Narendra Modi was one of those organisers, and by the press's count about seven in ten BJP ministers have RSS roots. The reach goes beyond the cabinet into the bodies that shape what people learn and how disputes are judged: RSS-linked figures have been placed on the central bank's board, at the head of the national history research council and on the state-formed Ram temple trust, most new military feeder schools went to RSS-linked or BJP-linked bodies, and in Gujarat members of an RSS-family group were made public prosecutors in trials over riots in which their own members were accused.

Crime reaches the state from below. An official report in 1993 found crime syndicates 'virtually running a parallel government', protected by politicians and officials of all parties, and gang leaders in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar have held assembly and parliamentary seats for years. Companies that depend on state contracts are accused of paying officials, and Pakistan's intelligence service has repeatedly recruited people inside India's state, from diplomats and naval sailors to the director of a defence research laboratory.

For people in India this means their laws are drafted by a cabinet drawn mostly from an organisation that publishes no membership list, their children's textbooks and military schools are increasingly handed to the same network, and victims of communal violence have faced prosecutors from the movement on trial.

Ireland.d:
For much of the twentieth century, the outsiders inside Irish government were organised bodies of men from Ireland itself, working in private: a secret republican brotherhood and then Catholic organisations. The Irish Republican Brotherhood, an oath-bound society, recruited the leaders of the Irish Volunteers militia and used it to launch the rising that led to independence; afterwards an IRB faction inside the new national army backed its own minister, until a mutiny in 1924 led to its members being dismissed and the society dissolving.

After independence the Catholic Church reached further. The Knights of Saint Columbanus, a secretive Catholic men's order, counted the head of the 1948 government and other members of his cabinet among its members according to biographers. In 1951 that cabinet dropped the Mother and Child Scheme, a plan for free health care for mothers and children, after the Catholic bishops privately objected; the health minister resigned, and the published letters showed how far the bishops had decided government policy.

In recent decades the documented reach has come from money: an official tribunal found in 2011 that the businessman Denis O'Brien made payments to the minister who 'delivered' him the country's second mobile phone licence, findings O'Brien rejects. Recent heads of government have also joined the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders network while in office; membership is lawful and no finding shows it directed a decision.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Ireland 4 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and above 7 for its courts and watchdogs. For people in Ireland, that history meant decisions on their families' health care were made in private letters between bishops and ministers, and it means a valuable public licence can be decided by a minister acting for a businessman.

Japan.d:
In Japan, outside interests reach the governing Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) by supplying what a party in power needs: money, organised votes and campaign workers. The pattern goes back to the party's early years, when the CIA secretly funded it and recruited informers inside it in the 1950s and 1960s. Since then companies have repeatedly paid the men at the top: in the clearest case, the US aircraft maker Lockheed paid about ¥500 million to Prime Minister Kakuei Tanaka's office to sell jets to a Japanese airline,. Yakuza groups and the racketeers tied to them drew billions in loans from leading banks and brokers.

Religious movements and nationalist lobbies now supply votes and volunteers. After the 2022 killing of former prime minister Shinzo Abe, the LDP's own survey found that 179 of its 379 members of parliament had ties to the Unification Church, a Korean-founded movement; Tokyo courts have since ordered its Japanese branch dissolved. Komeito, the party of the Buddhist lay movement Soka Gakkai, governed alongside the LDP for most of 1999 to 2025. Nippon Kaigi, a lobby that wants to rewrite the post-war constitution, and the political arm of the Shinto shrines each run a league of MPs that has counted most cabinet ministers under recent prime ministers. North Korea has reached into Japanese firms too, with police alleging in 2024 that a small Japanese company passed its clients' software work to North Korean engineers.

For voters in Japan, this means the people they elect may owe their campaigns to a church a court has ordered dissolved, ministers belong to lobbies whose membership the government does not disclose, and, as a parliamentary inquiry found after the Fukushima meltdown, a regulator can end up serving the power companies it is meant to police.

Kiribati.d:
No case on this map documents a foreign state, criminal group or company paying or placing officials inside Kiribati's government, so this account rests on general conditions.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Kiribati low, 1.5 out of 10, for officials working for criminal interests, but below 5 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. A weak oversight score means there are few institutions in a position to notice outside influence if it came.

For people in Kiribati this means the risk that officials are serving criminal interests appears low, but the means of checking are thin. If outside influence did reach their government, it would most likely show in fishing licences, aid-funded contracts or policing, and with limited courts and press it could go unexamined.

Kuwait.d:
Outside interests reach into Kuwait's government by three routes on the record: an Islamist movement working openly in politics, foreign businesses paying the officials who control visas and arms purchases, and Iran recruiting inside the army.

The Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt that aims to bring its members into power, has a Kuwaiti branch that broke with the international organisation after Iraq invaded in 1990. Its party, the Islamic Constitutional Movement, regularly won seats in parliament through the 1990s and 2000s and at times sent members into the cabinet.

Foreign suppliers have paid officials directly. A Bangladeshi member of parliament whose companies supplied cleaners for government contracts was convicted in 2021, alongside a senior Interior Ministry general, of paying ministry officials to issue visas for more than 20,000 workers, some on fake papers. A parliamentary inquiry in 2024 found that a European helicopter maker paid commissions on a defence contract and named eight senior officials, though parliament was dissolved before any prosecution. In 2011 a Kuwaiti court convicted soldiers serving in the army of passing military information to Iran's Revolutionary Guards.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Kuwait 6 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and just over 5 for its courts and watchdogs. For Kuwaitis this means the officials who decide who may live and work in the country, and those who spend the defence budget, have been paid by foreign suppliers, while migrant workers brought in on bought visas carry the cost. The inquiry into the helicopter deal put the public money wasted at €349 million.

Lebanon.d:
In Lebanon, foreign states have reached into the government for most of the past seventy years, and today it is an armed party aligned with Iran that sits inside it. In the 1950s CIA officers carried cash to the president's chosen candidates. From 1982 Syria's military intelligence chief in Lebanon vetoed candidates, drew electoral districts and shaped security and judicial appointments, until Syrian troops left in 2005.

Hezbollah, a Shia party with its own armed wing, has held a place inside the government since. In 2008 its fighters took over west Beirut, and the settlement gave it and its allies a cabinet veto. It now holds about 14 of the 128 seats in parliament, and in the government formed in 2025 its nominees run the health and labour ministries; with its ally Amal it controls six of the 24 portfolios. At least 28 countries list it as a terrorist organisation.

Finance has its own version of the pattern. For 30 years the central bank was run by a former Merrill Lynch banker who had managed the prime minister's personal portfolio, and after the currency peg he defended broke down in 2019, he was charged with embezzling public funds.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Lebanon 9.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 3 for its courts and watchdogs, close to the worst in the world. For people in Lebanon this means a party with its own army sits in the cabinet that is supposed to decide when the country goes to war, and the central bank that set the value of their wages and savings was run for decades by a political patron's personal banker.

Liechtenstein.d:
Liechtenstein is a small principality between Switzerland and Austria whose banks and trust companies hold money for foreign clients, and the one recorded claim of outsiders reaching inside its institutions came from that business. In 1999 a report by Germany's foreign intelligence service, published by Der Spiegel, accused unnamed Liechtenstein banks, politicians and judges of helping the Russian mafia and drug cartels launder money. The government called the report dubious and unfair; a member of parliament was arrested in 2000 and acquitted in 2002, and an investigator hired by the government rejected the allegations while finding weaknesses in legal cooperation. The claim that officials worked for criminals was never proven, but the country was briefly blacklisted by the international anti-money-laundering body and ended anonymous accounts opened by trustees.

No case since then shows a foreign government, crime group or company paying Liechtenstein's officials. The Global Organized Crime Index places it among the countries where officials are least likely to work for criminal or outside interests and rates its courts, police and watchdogs as strong.

For people who live in Liechtenstein, this means the officials they deal with are rated as rarely acting for someone else, and the one serious accusation was tested and not upheld. The risk, if it returns, sits where the 1999 report looked: in the banks and trustees that manage foreign money and the officials who supervise them.

Malawi.d:
In Malawi, the documented outside reach is through the procurement of the country's security forces, where a single foreign supplier is alleged to have bought his way into contracts with the police and the army. Malawi's anti-corruption bureau reported in 2022 that companies linked to Zuneth Sattar, a UK-based businessman, won contracts worth more than 150 million dollars from both forces over four years, and that he paid officials to secure them. The bureau's report named dozens of people, and arrests reached a former police chief, a cabinet minister and the vice president, who denied wrongdoing and died in a plane crash in 2024. These are findings and arrests, not convictions.

The mechanism is common where security spending is large and kept away from public scrutiny: the buyer is the state, the details are confidential on security grounds, and one well-connected supplier can win repeated contracts if the officials signing them are paid. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Malawi's institutions as weak and finds a moderate level of officials serving outside interests.

For Malawians this means that tax money meant to equip the police and army went, through contracts the bureau says were bought, to the companies of one outside supplier, with the alleged payments reaching as far as the vice president's office. The cases have not been decided, so people still do not know who in their government took part or what the public received for the money.

Malta.d:
In Malta, outside interests have reached the state in two ways: through private companies that win large state contracts with help from the people closest to the prime minister, and through the licences Malta grants to firms that then operate across the European Union.

The clearest example of the first is the gas power station built under a state contract. One of the builder's directors secretly owned a company in Dubai that leaked papers listed as expected to pay into secret Panama companies set up for the energy minister and the prime minister's chief of staff; the journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia was investigating that company when a car bomb killed her in 2017, and the director now faces trial over her murder while all three men face corruption charges. A public inquiry found that the Maltese state had created an 'atmosphere of impunity'.

The second channel runs through Malta's online gambling industry. Because a Maltese licence lets a betting firm operate across the EU, Italian mafia groups, including the 'Ndrangheta from Calabria and Cosa Nostra from Sicily, have secretly owned or run Malta-licensed betting companies to collect bets and launder money, according to Italian investigations over the past decade. Malta's regulator suspended licences once the investigations surfaced.

For people in Malta this means they pay for electricity from a plant whose contract prosecutors say was tied to payments meant for the two men around the prime minister, and the reporter who tried to expose it was killed. It also means their country's licences have served as cover for mafias, and the Global Organized Crime Index finds officials there often serving criminal or outside interests.

Mexico.d:
In Mexico, drug cartels have put officials on their payroll at every level of government for more than forty years, from town police to the federal cabinet. Where a cartel controls a route or a town, it pays the local police, the prosecutors who decide which cases go forward and, in several states, the governor. The officials hired to fight the cartels have been bought most often: the national anti-drug chief, generals, dozens of agents in the federal organised-crime prosecution unit, prison directors who let a cartel leader walk out twice, and a federal security minister. In 2025 the Sinaloa Cartel's co-founder admitted in a US court that his people had paid Mexican police and military commanders for decades so the cartel could operate freely.

The same buying goes on in town halls today. Whole municipal police forces in Michoacán, Guerrero, Tamaulipas and elsewhere have been disbanded or taken over because they worked for cartels, and a federal operation begun in 2024 had detained more than 85 officials, including at least 19 mayors, across nine states by mid-2026. In Iguala in 2014 the mayor and police acted for a local gang and took 43 students who then disappeared.

Others have reached in too. During the Cold War the CIA counted two future presidents among its contacts inside the government, foreign companies seeking business have paid officials at Pemex, the state oil company, and in 2020 financial investigators examined a former first lady's ties to a Catholic order over public money given to charities; nothing has been found.

For Mexicans this means the police officer, prosecutor or governor they depend on may be working for the people they should be stopping, and a crime reported to them may go straight to the cartel.

Mongolia.d:
Nothing is documented of a foreign state, company, crime group or religious body paying or placing people inside Mongolia's government, so this is an estimate based on conditions.

Mongolia sits between Russia and China, its two large neighbours and main trading routes. The Global Organized Crime Index finds a moderate level of officials serving criminal or outside interests and rates its courts, police and watchdogs in the middle range. A country with that profile is one where outside money could reach some officials, most likely through licences and public contracts, but where institutions have some capacity to notice and respond.

For people in Mongolia this means there is no named official, company or group acting for an outside interest that they can point to or hold to account. The estimate rests on the index's assessment rather than on any inquiry or court ruling, and a documented case would change it.

Myanmar.d:
In Myanmar the army has for decades drawn drug lords and armed crime groups into the state itself, trading protection and business for their loyalty. In the 1990s ceasefire deals gave heroin warlords protection from extradition and business openings, and one became among the junta's main builders, winning road and port contracts while new refineries opened in his home region. The same arrangement continues along the borders with China and Thailand. Militias the army has formally placed under its command, and armed groups allied with it, control the parts of Shan and Karen states that produce much of Asia's methamphetamine and host compounds where trafficked workers are forced to defraud strangers online. Their leaders hold military rank, seats in parliament and state honours while partnering with Chinese-run crime groups; the commander of the Karen Border Guard Force helped build the scam city of Shwe Kokko and received a top state honour, and the UK and US have since sanctioned him.

A Buddhist nationalist monks' group, Ma Ba Tha, reached into lawmaking. The religious affairs ministry drafted four 'race and religion' laws from texts its members proposed, and parliament passed them in 2015. They restrict religious conversion and marriage between Buddhist women and non-Buddhist men.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds Myanmar's officials serving criminal interests to one of the highest degrees in the world, with almost no court or police capacity to check them. For people in Shan and Karen states this means living beside drug labs and guarded compounds run by forces the army counts as its own, and roads and ports built by firms that grew from drug money. Muslim residents and Buddhist women live under marriage and conversion rules drawn from a monks' movement's drafts.

Netherlands.d:
In the Netherlands, outsiders reach in at three points: cocaine gangs work through the people who move goods and handle information, foreign intelligence services target the international courts in The Hague and the country's high-technology firms, and large companies reach into government policy.

At Rotterdam, Europe's largest port, they have paid terminal workers and IT contractors for the PIN codes that release containers, private security guards to keep searches away, and a customs officer whose job was choosing which containers get scanned. At Schiphol airport they recruit staff whose passes let them move freight past controls. They also buy information from inside the state: police officers and trainees have searched police systems for gangs at a set price per name, and court staff with access to personal records have sold them to suspects. Courts have convicted such insiders many times, and gangs that rely on them have killed people connected to trials against them.

The Hague hosts the International Criminal Court, which tries war crimes, and foreign services have tried to get inside it. In 2022 a Russian military intelligence officer with a false Brazilian identity flew in to take up a post there while it was investigating war crimes in Ukraine; Dutch intelligence turned him back. In 1975 a Pakistani metallurgist working inside the Dutch side of a uranium-enrichment consortium took its centrifuge designs home, and they later reached Iran, Libya and North Korea. Large multinationals reach policy through their access to ministers and coalition negotiators, enough to put into a coalition plan a tax cut for shareholders that no party had campaigned for.

For people in the Netherlands this means their personal details can be sold from a police terminal or a court desk, and violence follows the gangs that have bought insiders.

Nigeria.d:
In Nigeria the people reaching into government are mostly after oil and gas. Foreign oil companies, engineering firms and commodity traders have paid officials for licences, cargoes, construction contracts and favourable legal outcomes, and many have admitted it, or been found to have done it, in foreign courts; one engineering consortium admitted paying about $180 million to officials, from the top of government down to the state oil company, to build a gas plant. A US diplomatic cable records a Shell executive saying in 2009 that the company had seconded its own staff to every ministry dealing with oil, which Shell denies.

The cost falls on the public treasury: money lost to a bribed contract, an oil block sold through a former minister's company, or an arbitration award obtained by fraud is money that does not reach schools, clinics or roads. A London judge found that one company had bribed a government lawyer to win an arbitration award of over $11 billion.

Pressure also comes from inside the country. Confraternities, secretive brotherhoods that began at universities, are hired by politicians for election work, and some have been rewarded with government posts; police in several countries treat the best known, Black Axe, as an organised crime group, even though the constitution bars members of secret societies from elected office. A man wanted in the US on drug charges has sat in the Senate, and in 2012 the president himself said the jihadist group Boko Haram had sympathisers in the army, police and government, naming no one. Voters where confraternities work face intimidation at the polls, and people in the north-east cannot be sure the forces protecting them are not compromised. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Nigeria high for officials working for criminal interests, with middling courts and watchdogs.

Pakistan.d:
In Pakistan, outsiders reach into the state through three channels: international lenders and banks, religious and militant movements, and the country's own military intelligence acting outside the law.

The lender channel runs through the economic offices that a bailout depends on. Three times Pakistan has handed its economy to someone from the lenders' side: a former World Bank finance chief made caretaker prime minister in 1993, a Citibank executive of about 30 years who became finance minister and then prime minister, and, during the 2019 IMF talks, an IMF staff member made governor of the central bank, the official who sets interest rates and manages the currency.

Religious movements reach into the army and the courts. Under General Zia, members of Jamaat-e-Islami, the main Islamist movement, were given jobs across the judiciary; in 1992 a member of Tablighi Jamaat, a worldwide missionary movement, was put in charge of the ISI, the military's spy agency; and Islamist officers have repeatedly been caught organising from inside, from a 1995 plot with a militant group to kill the prime minister and army chief and declare a caliphate to Hizb ut-Tahrir's recruitment of a brigadier. The ISI in turn reaches into elected politics: its officers tried to buy defections to bring down Benazir Bhutto in 1989, and Pakistan's Supreme Court found in 2012 that it had passed bank money to politicians in the 1990 election to stop her winning.

For Pakistanis this means the price of food and borrowing has more than once been set by officials whose careers were made at the institutions lending to the country, that the army and spy service charged with protecting them have held officers working for movements of their own, and that at least one election was bought by the state's own spies.

Paraguay.d:
Paraguay's record shows criminal and foreign-linked money reaching the top of government, the Congress, town halls and the middle of the justice system. The Global Organized Crime Index gives it one of the highest scores in the world for officials working for criminal interests.

At the top, the reach runs through the Tri-Border Area around Ciudad del Este, where free-zone trade lets goods and money move with little checking and where Hezbollah, the Lebanese armed movement and party, has long had finance networks. The US Treasury sanctioned a former president and a sitting vice-president in 2023, saying their representatives collected bribes at private Hezbollah events in Paraguay; the sanctions on the former president were lifted in 2025 without any court ruling either way.

Below that, cocaine networks moving drugs along the Hidrovía river route and across the Brazilian border keep legislators, prosecutors, police, court staff and prison guards on their side. Prosecutors have charged sitting members of the Chamber of Deputies, mostly from the governing Colorado Party, with getting traffickers released, taking their money for campaigns or laundering it, and Brazil's largest prison gang, the PCC, has paid prison staff on the border to let its members out. In Ypejhú, a border town, the mayor came from a trafficking clan, and in 2017 a court found he had ordered the killing of a journalist who reported on it.

For people in Paraguay this means the police who should investigate traffickers, the prosecutors who should charge them, the courts that should try them and the deputies who write the laws have all had members on the traffickers' side, and a reporter who names a local boss may be dealing with the town hall itself.

Portugal.d:
In Portugal outside interests have reached government mainly through finance: a banking family that stayed close to power from the dictatorship onward, and international bankers placed in charge of the state's own sell-offs.

Banco Espírito Santo, run by the Espírito Santo family, had been close to power since the Salazar dictatorship, and its last head was nicknamed 'owner of all this'. Its collapse in 2014 wiped out the savings and shares of people who had trusted it. Prosecutors say money from the group reached a former prime minister, José Sócrates, while he was in office; the trial began in 2025 and all defendants are presumed innocent.

During the 2011 bailout the route ran through the lenders. A former vice chairman of Goldman Sachs International moved from heading the IMF's European department, as it lent to Portugal, to overseeing the government's privatisations and the restructuring of state firms and banks that the bailout required. The World Economic Forum also picked a future prime minister and European Commission president for its leadership network while he was foreign minister, though selection is not a finding of influence.

Outside these cases the record shows little organised crime inside Portuguese offices; the Global Organized Crime Index scores Portugal in the middle range for officials working for criminal interests and fairly well for its courts and watchdogs. For Portuguese people, the state assets sold in the bailout years were sold under a banker who had come from the lender, and voters are still waiting to learn whether a prime minister they elected was being paid by the country's most politically connected bank.

Rwanda.d:
In Rwanda the documented outside presence inside government is not hidden: a foreign-funded institute places its own advisers in the offices that plan and track what the state does. The Tony Blair Institute for Global Change, a London-based non-profit founded by the former UK prime minister, has supported units in the offices of the president and prime minister that set government priorities and check whether ministries deliver them, and has worked on Rwanda's system of performance contracts for officials. The institute reports work with governments in more than 45 countries, and its largest donor is the foundation of the American billionaire Larry Ellison.

The advisers are employed by the institute, not by the Rwandan state, and answer to their employer in London rather than to anyone Rwandans elect. Residents can read the programme descriptions the institute chooses to publish, but have no public way to see what advice was given or how its donors' priorities shaped it.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Rwanda in the middle range both for officials working for criminal or outside interests and for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs.

Saudi Arabia.d:
In Saudi Arabia most of the documented reach runs two ways: foreign arms and aircraft suppliers paying the Saudi officials who buy from them, and Saudi intelligence money going out into foreign banks.

The kingdom is one of the world's largest buyers of weapons and aircraft, and suppliers have paid officials in the state bodies that place the orders. The clearest case is the communications contract for the Saudi Arabian National Guard, the force that protects the royal family: a British company then owned by Airbus held it from 1994, and British prosecutors said about 12 per cent of its revenue went to Saudi officials, including the Guard's then deputy head, to keep contracts worth at least £1.6 billion. The company pleaded guilty, though two executives were acquitted in 2024 after arguing the British government required the payments. A Brazilian aircraft maker also admitted paying an official of a Saudi state company $1.65 million to secure an aircraft purchase.

Outward, Saudi intelligence has gone into foreign finance: Kamal Adham, head of Saudi intelligence until 1979, fronted the secret takeover of a Washington bank by BCCI, a bank later closed worldwide for fraud, and paid a $105 million fine in the United States.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives Saudi Arabia one of the highest scores in the world for officials working for criminal interests. For Saudis, this means a share of the public money spent on defence has gone to the officials and princes who chose the suppliers, the cases have been brought only abroad, and residents have no domestic route to check how state money is spent at home or overseas.

Sierra Leone.d:
Sierra Leone sits on the route that carries South American cocaine to Europe through West Africa, and traffickers using it look for protection inside the state rather than ways around it. They need the people who control an airport, an immigration desk or a landing clearance, and the record here shows them reaching each of those, up to the cabinet and, by press reports, the president's own family.

In 2008 a plane carrying about 700 kilograms of cocaine and painted with Red Cross markings landed at Lungi, the international airport, with help from airport and security staff who were later convicted; proceedings indicated that the aviation minister had cleared the landing, and he was dismissed but never tried. In 2025 Reuters reported that a Dutch cocaine trafficker on Europe's most-wanted lists had 'high-level protection' in the country and was married to the president's daughter; the government said it was investigating, dismissed the head of immigration, and denies knowing where he is.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 8 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 4. For people in Sierra Leone that means the convictions have reached baggage handlers and guards while the allegations against ministers and the presidential household stay untried, and police and immigration officers have little reason to act against a man said to be protected by the people they answer to.

Solomon Islands.d:
In the Solomon Islands foreign governments compete for the loyalty of members of parliament, and the money goes to MPs directly. Taiwan used to pay into a discretionary fund run by the prime minister's office, from which payments go to MPs, and when the country switched recognition from Taiwan to China in 2019, MPs told reporters that both Beijing and Taipei had offered them hundreds of thousands of dollars for their votes. China then took over the fund. In 2022 the prime minister's secretary told a parliamentary committee that Chinese money had gone to 39 of the 50 MPs in late 2021, weeks before Prime Minister Manasseh Sogavare survived a no-confidence vote; the opposition said the money kept him in office, which his office denied.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 7.5 out of 10. For voters this means they cannot tell whether their MP's vote was cast for them or for the government paying into the fund.

Spain.d:
In Spain, outsiders reach the state mainly through party finance and planning permission, along the drug routes on its southern coast, and through religious and foreign ties at the very top.

Construction and property money is the most widespread channel. Businesses seeking public contracts or building permits have paid the officials who grant them, and the courts found that the governing People's Party itself took part in one such kickback scheme from 1989; the ruling, in the Gürtel case, was followed within a week by the removal of Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy in a vote of no confidence. On the Costa del Sol a town council was dissolved in 2006 after its mayor, planning chief and many councillors were arrested for taking developers' money.

Along the Strait of Gibraltar, hashish and cocaine groups pay municipal police, customs officers, dockworkers and airport ground staff around the port of Algeciras to wave loads through At the top, in 2008 Saudi Arabia's king sent $100 million to a Swiss account whose sole beneficiary was Spain's own king, Juan Carlos, while Spanish firms were building a Saudi high-speed railway; Swiss prosecutors could not establish a link to the contract, and Spanish prosecutors closed their inquiry because the head of state was immune.

Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation of priests and lay members, ran Franco's finance, trade and planning ministries from 1957, and members have since served as interior minister and on the Constitutional Court, where one sat for seven years on the challenge to the abortion law without producing a draft ruling. For people in Spain, this means public contracts and building permits have been decided by who paid, and around Algeciras the police and port staff may be on a trafficker's payroll.

St. Vincent and the Grenadines.d:
Nothing is documented here, so this is an estimate. No case has been found of foreign governments, companies or criminal groups paying or placing officials in St Vincent and the Grenadines.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 2 out of 10, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 5.4, near the middle of the scale. The pressure that exists nearby is the cocaine route north from South America through the eastern Caribbean.

For residents, this means there is no known case of an official here acting for an outside paymaster, and the low score suggests the risk is small. The estimate rests on the index's assessment rather than on any inquiry or court ruling in the country, so it describes what conditions suggest, not what has been checked, and a case that has not yet come to light would change it.

Switzerland.d:
Switzerland is where much of the world's governance sits, and much of the infiltration recorded here is aimed at those bodies rather than at the Swiss state. Geneva hosts the World Health Organization, the UN Human Rights Council and the ISO, which sets world technical standards; Zurich hosts FIFA, Lausanne most Olympic sports federations, and Basel the Bank for International Settlements. Outsiders have worked to get inside each. Tobacco companies spent years working through consultants and other UN agencies to weaken the WHO's tobacco work, according to a WHO expert inquiry, and private funders pay for WHO programmes they choose. Bid committees have allegedly paid FIFA and Olympic voters for hosting rights, and a man the US Treasury lists as a member of a Eurasian criminal group was elected head of the world amateur boxing body, which then lost its Olympic role. When Microsoft wanted its document format approved by the ISO, partner companies joined national committees to vote yes, and Sweden's vote was annulled.

The country's banks and commodity traders are also a channel for reaching other governments. Swiss-based traders have been convicted of bribing officials who hand out oil contracts in Africa and Latin America.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 1.5 out of 10. For Swiss residents, this means paying for prosecutors who keep finding the country's banks and traders moving bribes. For people elsewhere, it means that decisions taken in Geneva, Zurich and Lausanne on health spending, technical standards and which country hosts which games can be shaped by whoever got people or money inside first.

Tanzania.d:
In Tanzania the documented reach-in comes mainly from foreign companies selling power, weapons and finance to the state, which have won or kept contracts by paying officials or people close to them. The pattern has repeatedly reached cabinet level. In 2008 a little-known US firm's emergency electricity contract, which a parliamentary committee found fraudulently concluded and which the Prime Minister's office had pushed, led the prime minister and two energy ministers to leave office. A British arms maker paid its local agent about $12 million, roughly 30 per cent of the price of a $40 million military radar sold in 1999, and the attorney general at the time later resigned as a minister after British investigators found $1 million in his offshore account, though Tanzania's anti-corruption bureau cleared him. A South African bank's local arm paid $6 million to a 'partner' firm with a government official among its directors while raising $600 million for the state, and $122 million from a power-company escrow account was moved to a private power producer whose associate had paid a minister.

Other outside ties sit closer to the ruling party. Since 2022 a leadership school in Kibaha, paid for by China's Communist Party, has trained officials from Tanzania's ruling party and five others in southern Africa, openly and with government agreement.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials working for criminal interests here at 6 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 4.2. For Tanzanians, this means electricity, defence and borrowing have repeatedly cost them more because officials took a share, foreign donors held back almost $500 million in budget support over one scandal, and in most cases no one in Tanzania has been convicted of taking the money.

Tonga.d:
No case is documented of a foreign state, company or criminal group paying or placing officials inside Tonga's government, so this is an estimate based on conditions.

Tonga is a small kingdom where, until reforms in 2008, the monarch held most day-to-day power, and decisions about the country's money could be made by the king and a few advisers. The Global Organized Crime Index places Tonga in its Moderate band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 6 out of 10. That score suggests outside money could reach some officials, most likely through public contracts, licences or decisions made by a small circle around the government.

For people in Tonga this means there is no named official, company or group acting for an outside interest that they can point to or hold to account. The estimate rests on the index's assessment rather than on any inquiry or court ruling, and a documented case would change it.

Turkmenistan.d:
Turkmenistan is one of the most closed states on Earth: there is no independent press, no opposition party and no court that rules against the government, and almost nothing about how the state works is made public. The one documented case of outsiders reaching in comes from a foreign court record about companies selling to the government. To keep its vehicle sales to the Turkmen state, the German carmaker Daimler gave a high-level official an armoured Mercedes worth about $300,000 as a birthday present in 2000, paid about $250,000 to translate and print 10,000 German copies of the Ruhnama, the spiritual guide written by President Saparmurat Niyazov, and made other payments to officials. Daimler settled the US case in 2010.

No case shows a foreign state or criminal group placing people inside the government. The Global Organized Crime Index puts Turkmenistan in its severe band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 9 out of 10, among the highest in the world, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at 2.2, among the lowest.

For people in Turkmenistan this means that foreign companies seeking state orders have learned to pay officials and flatter the president's personality cult, and the cost is carried in public spending they cannot see. No journalist, judge or auditor in the country can find out whether officials act for outside interests, and the only account of this case came from prosecutors abroad.

United Arab Emirates.d:
The United Arab Emirates uses its wealth to place its own people at the head of international bodies and to bring foreign institutions into its orbit. It gave Interpol's foundation about $54 million, reported to equal the regular dues of all other member countries combined, and in 2021 a senior UAE interior ministry official was elected Interpol's president despite complaints from detainees that he was responsible for their torture. In 2023 the chief executive of ADNOC, the state oil company, presided over the UN's COP28 climate talks, and leaked briefing papers showed his team preparing to raise oil and gas business in meetings with foreign governments.

The UAE is also a place where outside crime reaches others' governments. Dubai's free-zone companies, whose owners can stay hidden behind a required local sponsor, have been used by foreign drug organisations to employ the men who work for them, including one that prosecutors say paid politicians and a security chief in Bosnia.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in the UAE at 6.5 out of 10. For residents and visitors, this means the officials responsible for policing and detention in the UAE have also run the world's police cooperation body, so a complaint against them can reach the institution they lead.

Uzbekistan.d:
In Uzbekistan, foreign companies entered one of the country's most valuable markets by paying the president's family. Three foreign telecom groups, VimpelCom, Telia and MTS, paid companies controlled by Gulnara Karimova, elder daughter of then-President Islam Karimov, to obtain mobile licences and radio frequencies; Uzbek prosecutors put her kickbacks at $869 million, and the three firms later paid about $2.6 billion between them to settle foreign bribery cases. Karimova has been convicted twice in Uzbekistan and remains in prison.

The pattern shows how access to a closed economy worked: under Karimov, a foreign investor did not compete in an open tender but paid a gatekeeper close to the ruler. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in Uzbekistan at 7 out of 10 and the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs at 3.8, so the conditions that made such deals possible have not gone away.

For people in Uzbekistan, this meant paying for a mobile service whose licences were sold privately to the president's daughter instead of to the operator offering the best terms. Most of the settlement money went to the governments of the United States, the Netherlands and Sweden, not to Uzbekistan, and weak courts leave citizens with little means to find out whether officials are making similar arrangements today.

Vietnam.d:
In Vietnam, the documented pattern is businesses and criminal networks buying the officials who are meant to regulate or police them, up to the level of ministers and the central bank.

The largest case is in banking. A property tycoon secretly controlled one of the country's commercial banks for a decade through more than two dozen nominee shareholders, used it to take about US$12.5 billion in loans for her own companies, and paid the head of the central bank's inspection department $5.2 million to keep it off the watch list; she was sentenced to death in 2024. In 2021 a company bribed health officials across the country to buy its overpriced Covid tests, and the scandal led to the dismissal of the health minister and Hanoi's mayor, after which the president resigned. Crime groups have done the same with the police: a Saigon gang boss who ran gambling and extortion for about 15 years had senior police officers and a deputy national chief prosecutor on his side, and police drug teams have been charged with shielding a Laos–Vietnam trafficking network.

The Global Organized Crime Index places Vietnam in its High band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 7 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at 4.8.

For people in Vietnam this means bank savings, public health budgets and police protection have all been for sale to whoever paid the official in charge. Savers ran on the bank when its condition came out, and an ordinary courier caught with drugs can be executed while the officers who protected the network are tried in the same courts.

Albania.d:
Albania sits on one of the main routes by which cannabis and other drugs move from the Balkans across the Adriatic into Italy and the rest of the EU, and the trafficking groups on that route often work across both countries. The risk this creates is that family and political ties reach from those groups into the police and the ministries meant to stop the trade.

The clearest illustration reached the top of the police. Italian police arrested a cousin of the interior minister, the minister in charge of Albania's police, in a probe into an Albanian-Italian group moving cannabis, and wiretaps in that probe mentioned the minister. He was later convicted only of abuse of office; the trafficking charges did not end in a conviction, so no court has said whether the group had the minister working for it.

Albania is a candidate to join the EU, and how its courts handle ties between ministers and crime groups is one of the tests it is judged on. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Albania 6.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 5 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, the middle of the range. For people living there, this means the officials who decide which smuggling cases are pursued may be related to, or answerable to, the smugglers, and a verdict that leaves the trafficking question open does not tell them which it is.

Antigua and Barbuda.d:
Antigua and Barbuda is a small state with a small civil service, and the documented cases show outsiders with far more money than its government reaching the one official whose signature they needed.

Agents working for Colombia's Medellín Cartel ordered Israeli military weapons in Antigua's name, with forged papers, to arm the forces of a cartel leader. An Israeli diplomatic note said the guns were shipped at the apparent instruction of the minister Vere Bird Jr, son of the prime minister, and after Colombia complained an official inquiry recommended he be barred from public office for life. The island's business as an offshore financial centre, where foreign-run banks take deposits from around the world under Antiguan licences, created the second opening. R. Allen Stanford ran Stanford International Bank from Antigua and was later convicted in the United States of a $7 billion fraud; the head of the Antiguan regulator meant to supervise his bank took cash, private-jet flights and sports tickets from him, left the bank's real assets unexamined and told US investigators his office had no power to help them.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores the country 3 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 4.7 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, both cases meant outsiders used the state's name and licences for their own business: Antigua's name went on a cartel's arms order, and thousands of savers, on the island and abroad, lost their money in a bank that the regulator had been paid not to look at. In both cases the facts came out through pressure from abroad, from Colombia and from US prosecutors, rather than from Antigua's own institutions.

Austria.d:
Austria sits between east and west, and Vienna has long been a base for foreign spy services.
