The documented reach-in now runs mostly from Russia, both into Austria's own security state and into the international bodies that have their headquarters here. The clearest illustration is a former officer of Austria's domestic intelligence agency, convicted in 2026 of working for Russia through Jan Marsalek, the fugitive former Wirecard executive: he used police databases to find people Moscow was looking for, including a journalist, and handed over work phones from the interior minister's office. He plans to appeal.

The same approach has been used on sport. The International Biathlon Union, which runs the Olympic sport of skiing and shooting from Salzburg, was led for 25 years by a president whom an independent inquiry found took Russian cash, hunting trips and favours, and in return shielded Russian athletes and blocked work against Russian doping; Austrian and Norwegian prosecutors opened investigations.

A quieter route runs through international networks of future leaders. Sebastian Kurz, chancellor in 2017–19 and 2020–21, is listed as a member of the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders network for people under 40. Being selected is not wrongdoing, and no inquiry has found that the network directed his government's decisions.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Austria 4 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 7.5 for its courts, police and watchdogs. For exiles, journalists and others Russia's government wants to find, the risk is that an official with access to state databases may be working for a foreign service, which turns the state's own records into a way of locating them; for athletes, it has meant competing under a governing body that one country had paid to take its side.

Bangladesh.d:
In Bangladesh outsiders have reached public institutions from several directions: drug traffickers buying protection in the border district where most methamphetamine pills enter, a business group taking control of banks that hold ordinary people's savings, religious movements reaching the army and the schools, and a neighbouring spy service reaching an election.

Almost all yaba, a cheap methamphetamine pill made in Myanmar, enters through Cox's Bazar district, and the trade has paid local politicians and police there. The government's own list of yaba traffickers named the district's member of parliament, but the trafficking claims never went to trial. From 2017 the S. Alam Group, a Chittagong conglomerate, took over Islami Bank Bangladesh, remade its board and management, and came to control several other Islamic banks, in one case through 19 subsidiaries to get round the legal limit on ownership; the bank needed emergency central bank money in 2023.

Religious movements reach in through the army and through policy. The 2012 coup attempt the military says it stopped was linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir, a banned international movement that seeks a single Islamic state, and Hefazat-e-Islam, a coalition of madrasa clerics, said the government made all 29 changes it had demanded to the 2017 school textbooks. A former head of Pakistan's spy agency told Pakistan's Supreme Court in 2012 that it had funded the party that won Bangladesh's 1991 election, which that party denies.

For people in Cox's Bazar, a complaint about dealers may go to the people protecting them. For depositors across the country, the bank holding their savings may be run for the group that owns it, and parents have seen their children's textbooks rewritten to a clerical movement's demands.

Belize.d:
No case of an outside party placing people or money inside Belize's government or companies remains on this map after checking. That is a statement about the documented record, not proof that none exists.

Belize sits between Mexico and Guatemala on the Caribbean coast, on routes used to move cocaine north from South America, and it offers offshore company registration. Those are the conditions under which outside money tends to look for officials willing to help. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Belize 5.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests, in the middle of the range, but only about 3.6 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, which is weak.

For people living there, this means there is no documented case in which they can name an official acting for an outside party. The weak resilience score matters more: if traffickers or foreign buyers did reach officials, the courts, police and regulators that should catch it are rated as poorly placed to do so. The records that would show it first are the ownership of registered companies and how drug cases on the coast and the border are handled.

Bosnia and Herzegovina.d:
Bosnia and Herzegovina sits on the Balkan route by which cocaine and other drugs reach western Europe, and Balkan cocaine networks with bosses abroad use the country to move and clean their money. The documented pattern today is those networks paying Bosnian officials to help: in 2024 police in Sarajevo arrested 23 people for trafficking and laundering money for the inner circle of a cocaine boss already sentenced in the Netherlands, and Europol, the EU police agency, said those detained included corrupt officials who had worked for the group. The case is at the charging stage.

Outsiders have found a way into the security services before. During and just after the 1992–95 war, Iran, one of Bosnia's few wartime allies, built a presence inside the Interior Ministry; in 1996 NATO-led troops raided a training site where Iranians worked alongside Bosnian ministry staff, and the United States made shutting down the intelligence agency close to Iran a condition of its military aid.

The divided government left by the 1995 peace deal gives outsiders room. Power is split between the Federation and the Serb-run Republika Srpska, each with its own police and ministries, and between ethnic parties within them, so there are many separate offices to approach. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Bosnia 8 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests, among the highest in Europe, and about 3.9 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, among the lowest.

For people living there, this means an official handling their permit, case or complaint may also be working for a criminal network whose leaders live abroad, and the bodies that should catch that are rated among the weakest on the continent.

Bulgaria.d:
Bulgaria sits on the Balkan route, the main land route by which drugs and smuggled goods enter the European Union, and smugglers get through it by paying the customs officers and border police who are supposed to stop them. When the United States sanctioned Bulgarian officials and business figures for shielding smuggling networks in 2021, it was the largest anti-corruption action of its kind Washington had taken against any single country, and several of those named held customs and border posts.

The same sanctions reached the top of the state. The US Treasury said Delyan Peevski, a member of parliament whose family's media group owned half of the country's largest newspapers, used bribes and influence to control key institutions; in 2013 parliament had made him head of the national security agency, the body meant to catch this kind of capture, and he quit a day later only because thousands protested. That agency has also taken on as an adviser a businessman police later accused of leading an extortion gang, though he was acquitted. The courts are a third target: a man known as 'the Notary' is alleged to have gathered compromising files on judges and prosecutors to steer their decisions, claims still under investigation.

For people living here, this means goods crossing the border without the checks the law requires, a security service whose leadership has been open to the people it should watch, and possibly judges who answer to whoever holds material on them. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Bulgaria high for officials working for criminal interests and its institutions only middling. Few of those named abroad have been charged at home, so residents have little evidence that a paid official ever loses the job.

Cambodia.d:
In Cambodia the people who run scam compounds have been brought inside the circle of power. The compounds are fenced sites where trafficked workers are held in debt bondage and forced to run online fraud against people abroad. Their owners have been given honorary titles, made advisers to the country's leaders and seated in its parliament, and successive US and British sanctions have named political protection as the reason the compounds operate in the open. Chen Zhi, founder of the Prince Group conglomerate, is the clearest example: he served as an official adviser to two prime ministers while, according to US prosecutors, his group ran such compounds, and in 2026 Cambodia stripped his citizenship and sent him to China. A sitting senator has also been sanctioned over the same trade.

Cambodian courts have prosecuted none of the people sanctioned abroad. That leaves the workers held in the compounds without any Cambodian court acting for them, and it means the people defrauded overseas, whose losses the US Treasury puts in the billions of dollars a year across Southeast Asia, are paying an industry whose owners sit beside the country's lawmakers.

Foreign religious movements have also courted the same leadership: the Unification Church's political arm gave Hun Sen awards while he was prime minister. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Cambodia among the worst countries in the world for officials working for criminal interests, with weak courts, police and watchdogs to push back.

Chad.d:
In Chad outside money reaches in at two levels: foreign companies seeking oil rights go to the presidency, and drug traffickers go to the security services. At the top, the clearest case is a Chinese energy company: an envoy working for CEFC China Energy, which promoted China's Belt and Road programme, offered President Idriss Déby a $2 million bribe, dressed up as a donation, to win oil rights, and was convicted for it in New York in 2018. The company's chairman denied authorising him.

Lower down, tramadol, a prescription painkiller, is trafficked illegally across the Sahel, and the network moving it through Chad counted high-ranking army and intelligence officials among its members. Analysts who read the court papers when ten members were convicted in 2020 described large sums circulating among them, some used in attempts to bribe judges and the security services.

When army and intelligence officers are inside a trafficking network, Chadians depend for protection on police and courts that the same network has tried to buy, and when oil rights are offered to the president for cash, decisions about the country's main resource are made for the payer. The 2020 conviction shows Chad's courts can act, but the Global Organized Crime Index rates Chad among the countries where officials most often work for criminal interests, and its courts, police and watchdogs among the weakest.

Déby, president from 1990 to 2021, was also named as a Freemason in press reports, alongside several other presidents of former French colonies in Central Africa. Freemasonry is a fraternal society whose members meet privately in lodges and swear oaths of mutual support. No lodge was named for him, and no decision of his is tied to it.

Comoros.d:
Comoros, a small island state off East Africa, has been reached by outsiders through the men around its president and through its officials. For about eleven years from 1978, its presidential guard was commanded by Bob Denard, a French mercenary who worked for France's secret services: he led the coup that returned President Ahmed Abdallah to power, then ran the force meant to protect him while building up business interests and Comorian citizenship. When Abdallah ordered the guard disarmed in 1989 he was shot dead shortly afterwards, and Denard led another coup in 1995 that French troops ended; the court that later tried him recognised the secret services' role.

The more recent documented reach comes from a tobacco company. Leaked records from British American Tobacco (BAT) show the company arranging bribes for Comorian officials, part of a run of payments in several African countries that included efforts to block tobacco-control laws based on the World Health Organization's tobacco treaty. A British fraud inquiry closed without charges and BAT denies wrongdoing.

For Comorians, this means that for a decade the armed men around their head of state answered to a foreigner tied to another country's spy service, and if the tobacco payments worked as reported, they now live under weaker limits on tobacco sales and advertising than the treaty sets. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Comoros high for officials working for criminal interests, with very weak courts, police and watchdogs.

Cote d'Ivoire.d:
Two kinds of outside reach are documented in Côte d'Ivoire: an international lender placing its own official at the head of the economy, and Freemasonry among the officials who run security and justice.

In 1990 the International Monetary Fund pressed President Félix Houphouët-Boigny to put Alassane Ouattara, who had directed the IMF's African Department, in charge of economic policy; he became prime minister that November while the IMF's programme was still running, later returned to the IMF as its deputy head, and has been president since 2011. For Ivorians this meant that the man running their economy during an IMF programme came from the lender setting its conditions.

Freemasonry is a fraternal society whose members meet privately in lodges under a national grand lodge. Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that the prime minister and the interior minister, who was responsible for the police, were Freemasons, and that the state prosecutor had been received by the Grande Loge de Côte d'Ivoire. The reporting does not show that the tie decided who was appointed or prosecuted, and membership is lawful, but if it did there would be no public record of it.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Côte d'Ivoire high for officials working for criminal interests, with courts, police and watchdogs of middling strength. No documented case on the map shows a criminal group paying Ivorian officials.

Czech Republic.d:
Outside reach into the Czech state has come from China and from the prime minister's own company. China has worked through business and the presidency: a former president took as his economic adviser the chairman of a Chinese energy company that was buying Czech assets, a man who had served in a Beijing body that builds contacts with foreigners on China's behalf.

The most direct case is at home. Prime Minister Andrej Babiš owns Agrofert, a farming, food and chemicals group that receives EU farm subsidies, and a European Commission audit found he still controlled it while in office and was in a conflict of interest. He returned as prime minister in 2025 and has moved the shares into a new trust, saying the conflict is resolved.

For Czechs, this means a head of government whose ministers set the rules and grants that reach his own company. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Czech officials low to middling for working with criminal interests, with relatively strong institutions.

Dominican Republic.d:
In the Dominican Republic outside money has reached officials through public works contracts and, far more often, through the drug trade. Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction company, admitted paying $92 million in bribes in the country to win public works, and a former public works minister was convicted over it.

The Dominican Republic is a transit point for cocaine bound for Puerto Rico, the United States and Europe, and traffickers buy protection at every level that can touch a shipment. They have recruited officers of the National Drug Control Agency to guard loads, navy officers in charge of port security, army colonels who leaked arrest warrants and raid plans, and intelligence and interior officials who gave a fugitive trafficker a state identity card and gun permits. The reach goes into Congress: a deputy elected for Santiago in 2020 was arrested in Miami while still in office and admitted sending about 5,000 kilograms of cocaine to Florida, and other deputies and a state programme director have been named in trafficking inquiries. A convicted trafficker says his money paid for a presidential campaign, a claim never tested in court. Since 2009 the drug agency has removed hundreds of staff and the national police has expelled well over a thousand officers.

For Dominicans, public works were paid for under contracts that carried tens of millions of dollars in bribes, and the officers, legislators and officials meant to stop the drug trade have included people working for it, so a raid can be known to the target before it happens. The Global Organized Crime Index rates the country in the middle range for officials working for criminal interests, with weak courts, police and watchdogs.

Equatorial Guinea.d:
Equatorial Guinea is a small oil and gas producer on the Gulf of Guinea, ruled by Teodoro Obiang since 1979, and the record of outsiders reaching into its government runs almost entirely through oil. The foreign companies that produce and trade its oil have paid the president, his family and the officials who award contracts. A 2004 US Senate inquiry found that American oil companies producing most of the country's offshore oil made payments to Obiang, his relatives and officials for land, office leases, security and scholarships for officials' children, and that Obiang and his family held secret shares in their joint ventures with the government. Later, the Dutch company SBM Offshore admitted that between 2008 and 2012 its local agents passed money on to at least nine officials of the oil ministry and the state oil company, and a Swiss-based commodity trader has pleaded guilty in Britain to bribing officials in five African oil states, this one among them.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 9 out of 10, among the highest anywhere, and the courts, police and watchdogs that would resist them at just over 2. That combination describes a state where the people in office control the main source of money and no independent body can question how contracts are given out.

For Equatoguineans, this means oil revenue that could pay for services has been shared between foreign companies and the ruling family, with officials' children educated abroad on company money. With one president in power for more than four decades and weak courts, they have no domestic route to find out who was paid; every documented case was brought by investigators abroad.

Ethiopia.d:
Very little is documented of outside forces getting inside Ethiopia's government. The one case on the map is about religion rather than money. Abiy Ahmed, prime minister since 2018, belongs to the Ethiopian Full Gospel Believers' Church, a Pentecostal church, and sometimes preaches there. He converted after the 1998–2000 war with Eritrea, and in 2019 he formed the Prosperity Party, which governs today. Pentecostal churches are a fast-growing Protestant movement in Ethiopia, which has long been mostly Orthodox Christian and Muslim. Religious belief is lawful, and no record shows the church directing government decisions.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 6 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at 4.5, which suggests more is going on than has been documented. Ethiopia has been through civil war in Tigray and continuing conflict in Amhara and Oromia, which makes reporting on officials harder.

For Ethiopians, the documented picture is of a head of government whose faith ties him to a particular religious community in a country with several large faiths. Whether that shapes who is appointed or which policies are chosen has not been shown, and the weak watchdogs mean there is little official scrutiny of how decisions are made.

Gabon.d:
In Gabon, two connected networks tied to France have been part of how the country is ruled. The first is Freemasonry, a society of private lodges whose members swear oaths of mutual support. Gabon's two main lodges were founded by Omar Bongo, president from 1967 to 2009, and are tied to two French Masonic bodies, the Grand Orient de France and the Grande Loge Nationale Française. Bongo led them until he died, and his son Ali Bongo was installed as grand master by the French lodge's leader in the year he became president. For most of the half-century to 2023, the head of state was also the head of the country's lodges, with ministers, the head of the National Security Council and a police chief among the members.

The second is the system known as Françafrique. From 1960 the French presidency's Africa office, run by Jacques Foccart, built personal networks tying French officials, business and intelligence to the leaders of former colonies such as Bongo, negotiated defence agreements with secret clauses allowing French intervention, and oversaw elections; France intervened militarily in Gabon in 1964. Those decisions escaped scrutiny by France's parliament.

The links survived the 2023 coup. The grand mastership went to a provincial governor after the coup leader, Brice Oligui Nguema, reportedly declined it, and the leader of the Grand Orient de France met him in secret in Libreville to offer support. For people in Gabon this means the president, ministers and security chiefs have met as lodge brothers in private meetings connected to bodies in the former colonial power, and voters have no way to know what is agreed there. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for outside or criminal interests at 7.5 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at 3.5.

Ghana.d:
In Ghana the documented networks inside government are private loyalties: lodges and churches whose leaders sit close to power. Freemasonry, a society of private lodges whose members pledge mutual support, runs through the political class of both main parties: a former president has said he joined in 1967, ministers of the previous and current governments have confirmed membership when questioned in parliament, and the Asantehene, the country's most powerful traditional ruler, was honoured in 2024 for 25 years in the order. Church leaders have also been given places in state projects: a Pentecostal pastor sat as secretary of the board of the National Cathedral, a $97 million church project run from the presidency, and an audit in 2025 found project money used to repay a loan with no agreement to a company linked to him; the board was dissolved.

The second pattern is drugs moving through West Africa on their way to Europe and the United States, and the officials drawn into that trade. In 2006 a large cocaine load landed from a ship and then disappeared, and a senior police officer recorded meeting suspects at his home returned to duty after an inquiry found the police account unsatisfactory; a year earlier a sitting MP was jailed in the United States for smuggling heroin.

For Ghanaians this means ministers, the security chief and the leading traditional ruler share private loyalties residents cannot see into, and public money for a state church project went to a firm tied to a pastor on its board. Traffickers have reached both the police and the legislature, and the officer involved in the lost cocaine kept his job. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7.5 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 5.3.

Guinea.d:
Guinea holds one of the world's largest untapped iron ore deposits, at Simandou, and the documented case of outside interests getting inside its government is about mining rights. In 2008 the government took two blocks of it from the mining company Rio Tinto and gave them to a company controlled by Israeli businessman Beny Steinmetz. A Swiss court later found that he got them by bribing a wife of President Lansana Conté; he denies wrongdoing. The deal shows how a foreign investor could win national resources by paying someone in the president's household rather than through open bidding.

The country's lodges are another channel to the top. In 2012 the magazine Jeune Afrique reported that President Alpha Condé oversaw the Grand Lodge of Guinea, the national body of Freemasonry, a society of private lodges whose membership is not made public.

For Guineans, the Simandou case meant that control of one of the world's largest untapped iron deposits was decided by a bribe, and years of potential state revenue were lost while the rights were contested. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 8 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at under 3, so cases like this tend to be pursued abroad, if at all.

Honduras.d:
Honduras is one of the main stopping points for cocaine flown and shipped from South America towards Mexico and the United States, and over the past two decades trafficking groups bought protection at the very top of the state. According to US courts, traffickers paid a president, his brother in Congress and a national police chief to let cocaine through, and trial evidence said drug money paid for the governing National Party's election campaigns. The clearest single case is Juan Orlando Hernández, president from 2014 to 2022, who was convicted in New York of protecting cocaine shipments and pardoned by the US in 2025.

The arrangement worked from the bottom up as well as the top down. On the Guatemalan border, a cocaine trafficker became mayor of his own town and paid into the ruling party's presidential campaign in return for national protection. Nor was it confined to one party: a secretly recorded video from 2013, published in 2024, shows the Cachiros, a Honduran trafficking clan, offering campaign money to the brother-in-law of Xiomara Castro, later president for the rival Libre party; he denies taking it and resigned. The Cachiros also laundered money through a bank owned by one of the country's most powerful political families, which regulators closed after the US sanctioned it.

For Hondurans, this means mayors, police, Congress and the presidency have all been used to move cocaine, and campaigns across the main parties have been offered or paid drug money, according to US trial evidence. The main cases were tried abroad, and the former president was released, so Hondurans have not seen these officials tried at home. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 8.5 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at under 4.

Indonesia.d:
In Indonesia outside forces have reached the state mainly through money, training and religious organisations. For most of Suharto's rule, which began in 1966, the planning agency and finance ministry were run by economists the Ford Foundation, a US charity, had paid to train at Berkeley; this 'Berkeley Mafia' opened the country to foreign investors, and the tie to international lenders continues: in 2016 a World Bank managing director went straight back to the finance ministry. Islamic organisations reach the top by an open route: a chairman of Nahdlatul Ulama, the largest Muslim organisation, became president in 1999, and its leader was vice-president from 2019 to 2024.

Money buys officials at every level. Foreign aircraft makers paid the head of the state airline while he was buying from them, and a US seed company paid an official assessing its genetically modified cotton; facts like these have mostly come out through foreign prosecutors. At home, contractors on the national electronic ID-card project paid the Speaker of the House of Representatives, who was jailed for 15 years. Courts and police have been bought too. A fugitive tycoon paid two police generals to lift his Interpol alert and a prosecutor to seek a Supreme Court ruling clearing him, and an executed trafficker claimed, untested in court, that police, narcotics and customs officers had brought drugs in for him.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Indonesia 8 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and below 5 for its courts and watchdogs. For Indonesians this means what their state buys, which crops reach their farms and whether a wealthy suspect is caught can depend on who has paid, and they have often relied on other countries' courts to find out.

Israel.d:
In Israel the outside party with the deepest reach into the state is the settler movement, which builds Israeli communities in the occupied West Bank. An official report in 2005 found that the defence, housing, education and energy ministries had paid for and supplied unauthorised settlement outposts against the government's own rules. Since the 2022 coalition deal the movement's leaders hold the offices themselves: a settler who co-founded a group litigating against Palestinian building now runs the civil administration that decides on land and building in the West Bank, and a leader of the Kahanist movement, convicted in 2007 of supporting the banned anti-Arab Kach group, controls the police. Several governments have sanctioned both men for inciting settler violence.

Money reaches the same circles. Developers bribed two Jerusalem mayors, one later prime minister, for planning approvals, and prosecutors say Benjamin Netanyahu, as communications minister, gave valuable decisions to the owner of the largest telecoms company in return for favourable coverage, which he denies at trial. Police are investigating two of his aides over money, routed through a US lobbying firm, to promote Qatar. Foreign spy services have recruited insiders as senior as the deputy head of the secret biological weapons institute, for the Soviet Union, and a former energy minister, for Iran. Courts have convicted police officers of passing case files to crime families.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Israel 5.5 out of 10 both for officials working for outside interests and for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. For Palestinians in the West Bank, the officials deciding whether their homes stand or their attackers are pursued now come from the movement that wants their land. For Israelis, news may be shaped by deals with regulators, and a statement to police about a crime family may leak.

Jordan.d:
In Jordan, outside forces have reached the state through its rulers, its border guards and its parliament. For about twenty years, until 1977, the CIA made secret yearly payments of millions of dollars to King Hussein; President Carter stopped them just before The Washington Post reported them. Today's pressure comes from drug smugglers on the Syrian border. Smugglers moving captagon, an amphetamine pill made in Syria, need the border to stay open to them, so they recruit the people guarding it, and serving and former soldiers have been convicted of carrying pills and weapons across.

The Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement that works to bring its members into power, competed openly through its own party, the Islamic Action Front, which became the largest party in parliament in the 2024 election. In 2025 the government banned all of the Brotherhood's activities and said it would seize its assets, after arrests over an alleged weapons plot that the group said it knew nothing about.

Jordan is also a headquarters of UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees. UN investigators concluded in 2024 that nine of its staff in Gaza may have taken part in the Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023, and they were dismissed; a separate review found Israel had not shown evidence for its wider claims.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Jordan 6 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and above 5 for its courts and watchdogs. For families in northern Jordan this means living on a smuggling route where some of the soldiers paid to stop the drugs have been caught moving them. For the voters who made the Islamic Action Front the largest party, it means their party's parent movement is now banned and its members face arrest.

Korea, DPR.d:
In North Korea the state itself is the organisation that crosses borders, and the one documented case on this map runs the other way: the government reaching into an international body rather than an outside force reaching into it. In the Pyongyang office of the UN Development Programme, the UN's main aid agency, most local staff were nominees chosen by the government against UN policy, their salaries were paid to the state in hard currency, officials had to be present at project visits, and the government moved its own funds abroad through a UN account. A 2008 US Senate inquiry set this out, and the UN suspended its programme there in 2007 after the government refused new controls.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives North Korea the worst possible score, 10 out of 10, for officials taking part in criminal activity, and one of the lowest anywhere for its courts and watchdogs. The US Justice Department has charged networks that placed thousands of North Korean IT workers, using stolen or fake identities, in remote jobs at foreign companies, with their wages paid into accounts controlled by the state.

For people in North Korea this means that aid meant for them passes through staff picked by the government, and money from work done abroad in their name goes to the state rather than to them. With no independent courts, press or watchdogs, they have no means of learning how the aid or the earnings are spent, or of challenging it at home.

Kyrgyzstan.d:
In Kyrgyzstan criminal networks have reached into the state through the customs service, the office that decides what crosses the border and what duty is paid on it, and through seats in parliament. A smuggling operation with people inside customs controls both what comes in unchecked and how much revenue the state loses. The clearest case is Raiymbek Matraimov, a deputy head of customs whom journalists tied to a scheme that moved hundreds of millions of dollars out of the country, and whom the US sanctioned in 2020; at home he settled by repaying money and served no prison term at the time.

Men accused of leading crime groups have also stood for parliament. In 2006, in the turmoil after President Akayev's fall, a man described as a criminal leader, who had faced charges including murder, won a seat and used it to lead protests demanding the prime minister's resignation, before he was shot dead weeks later. The state has been harder on those who expose these links than on the officials named: journalists from the organised-crime reporting network OCCRP and the Kyrgyz outlet Kloop, who documented the customs scheme, were prosecuted or forced out, while the official they wrote about stayed free.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Kyrgyzstan 8.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 4 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. For people in Kyrgyzstan this means customs revenue that should have paid for schools, roads and hospitals has left the country, the officials at the centre of it face little at home, and the reporters who tell them about it pay a higher price than the officials do.

Lesotho.d:
Lesotho's largest public project is the Lesotho Highlands Water Project, a World Bank-backed scheme of dams and tunnels that sells the country's water to South Africa, and it is where foreign companies reached in. Engineering and construction firms from abroad working on the scheme paid Masupha Sole, chief executive of the state authority that ran it, through intermediaries, and Swiss bank records later showed millions of maloti he could not explain. In 2002 Lesotho's own High Court convicted him of bribery and jailed him for 15 years after appeal, and it went on to convict a Canadian engineering firm and a German consultancy; the World Bank barred the Canadian firm from its contracts for three years.

That case is unusual because a small, poor country prosecuted the foreign companies itself. No later case of a foreign state, company, crime group or lodge placing people inside the government remains on this map. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, has a documented presence, but nothing ties it to any decision. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Lesotho 7 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 4 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, which suggests the thin record reflects thin reporting more than an absence of influence.

For people in Lesotho this means the scheme that sells their main natural resource was run for years by an official taking money from the firms building it, and they pay for that kind of arrangement through inflated contracts and lost public money. Today the risk is greatest in contracts, licences and policing that ordinary residents cannot easily question.

Lithuania.d:
Lithuania has faced two kinds of reach-in: Russia's intelligence services recruiting people inside its armed forces and security units, and money from business reaching politicians and their parties. In both, its own courts have done the catching.

Russia's military intelligence, the GRU, and its security service, the FSB, have repeatedly tried to buy people with access. A GRU agent working as a surgeon at a military hospital recruited an air force officer at the base that hosts NATO's Baltic air patrols, paying him a few hundred euros at a time for defence documents and officers' files, and an FSB officer was caught in 2015 trying to recruit members of the unit that guards the president so that listening devices could be planted in her office and home. Both Russian agents were jailed and later released in a 2019 spy swap.

On the money side, the clearest case is the president removed in 2004: a Russian helicopter businessman who had funded his campaign was then granted citizenship by presidential decree, and the constitutional court and parliament impeached him, the first European head of state removed that way. Domestic business has bought in too. In 2024 the Supreme Court made final the convictions of the Liberal Movement's leader, a Labour MP and an executive of one of the country's largest business groups for bribes paid to get decisions through parliament, and fined both parties.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Lithuania's institutions as fairly strong and finds a moderate level of officials serving criminal interests. For Lithuanians this means the soldiers and guards protecting them and the members of parliament voting on their laws have each been targets for payment, but when it has come to light, their own courts have convicted those involved.

Malaysia.d:
In Malaysia outside money and movements have reached the state at the top and on the street. At the top, the route ran through 1MDB, a state investment fund set up to finance development. Goldman Sachs bankers paid bribes to officials in Malaysia and Abu Dhabi to win the fund's bond business, sold about $6.5 billion of bonds at roughly ten times the normal fees, and billions were then stolen; Najib Razak, prime minister until 2018, was convicted over more than $1 billion found in his own accounts.

Religious movements have reached government by a more open route. Anwar Ibrahim, a founder of the Islamic youth movement ABIM, brought its aims into cabinet in the 1980s as education minister, and analysts link the Islamisation of schooling under him to the rise of religious conservatism among Malays; he became prime minister in 2022.

At street level, traffickers moving methamphetamine from the Golden Triangle pay narcotics officers to release suspects and put seized drugs back on sale; the anti-corruption commission has prosecuted such officers repeatedly, mostly in Johor and the Klang Valley around Kuala Lumpur. Outsiders have also used Malaysian companies as cover: a former triad boss sanctioned by the United States became chairman of a listed firm in 2020, and a UN sanctions panel reported that North Korea's intelligence agency controlled Kuala Lumpur firms, with a member of the ruling party as a director, that fronted for a seller of military radios.

For Malaysians, a public fund meant to pay for development filled a prime minister's accounts and left the country with the debt, and people in Johor and the Klang Valley live where some of the officers paid to stop drugs have sold them back onto the street.

Marshall Islands.d:
The documented outside reach into the Marshall Islands is an attempt by foreign businesspeople to buy a law that would have given them their own territory. Two China-born businesspeople paid members of parliament and other officials over several years to pass a law creating a semi-autonomous 'special administrative region' on Rongelap Atoll. Both pleaded guilty in the United States, and the US government later barred a former Marshallese president and an MP from entering the country for taking the bribes; the former president denies it.

The scheme shows how a small Pacific state can be approached. A parliament of a few dozen members meant that paying a handful of lawmakers could move a law. The Global Organized Crime Index finds a relatively low level of officials serving outside interests in the Marshall Islands, which fits a country where this was a single scheme rather than a settled arrangement.

For the people of Rongelap this means lawmakers were paid to put their home under a separate set of rules written for the buyers. No one has been charged in the Marshall Islands, so the case was settled in a foreign court, and Marshallese have no ruling of their own on which officials took money.

Micronesia.d:
What is documented for the Federated States of Micronesia is an accusation made by its own head of state. In 2023, shortly before leaving office, President David Panuelo wrote a long letter saying China was using bribery and threats against Micronesian officials as 'political warfare', with the aim of keeping the Pacific country on Beijing's side, or neutral, if war broke out over Taiwan. He wrote that he had considered switching diplomatic recognition from China to Taiwan. China rejected the claims, no court or inquiry has tested them, and no official has been named as taking money.

The method described is one suited to a small state: a government of a few dozen senior officials decides which of China or Taiwan it recognises and how it votes abroad, so paying or pressing a handful of them can move the whole country's foreign policy. What China would gain, if the account is true, is a Pacific government that stays friendly or neutral in a war over Taiwan. The Global Organized Crime Index finds a relatively low level of officials serving outside interests in Micronesia.

For Micronesians, if the president's account is true, some of their officials have made decisions on foreign policy and security after taking money or giving way to threats from abroad. Because nothing has been investigated, they cannot tell which officials, if any, were involved, or whether later choices about Taiwan and defence were made freely.

Montenegro.d:
In Montenegro, organised crime has had protectors at the top of the state for three decades. In the 1990s, when cigarettes were smuggled from Montenegro across the Adriatic to Italy, Italian anti-mafia prosecutors charged that the state itself protected the trade and indicted the country's leader, Milo Djukanovic, in 2008; immunity kept him from trial, and he went on to lead Montenegro until 2023.

Today the trade is cocaine, and the protection has reached the justice system. Montenegrin clans such as the Kavac clan have needed judges, prosecutors and police chiefs who will look away or tip them off, and messages from Sky ECC, a cracked encrypted phone service used by criminals, have exposed how far this went. Since Europol, the EU's police agency, passed those messages to Montenegro, former heads of the Supreme Court, the special prosecution office and the police have been charged with protecting crime groups. The clearest case is the former Supreme Court president convicted in 2026 of using her position to shield a smuggling network run by her son.

Foreign governments have tried to reach in too. Prosecutors accused two Russian military intelligence officers of plotting with pro-Russian opposition MPs to seize parliament in 2016 and stop Montenegro joining NATO; a first court convicted them, but a retrial acquitted everyone.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials in Montenegro widely serving criminal interests. For people there this means that the judges, prosecutors and police chiefs they would turn to were, in several cases, working for the groups they were meant to pursue, and anyone whose case reached the Supreme Court in those years cannot be sure it was heard fairly. Most of these charges are still unproven, and the evidence came from foreign police and prosecutors rather than from Montenegro's own institutions.

Namibia.d:
In Namibia, the documented outside reach is through the country's natural resources, where a foreign company is alleged to have bought access from the ministers who control it. Namibia's fish belong to the public, and the government hands out quotas, licences to catch a set amount. In the case known as 'Fishrot', leaked files published in 2019 showed that Samherji, one of Iceland's largest fishing companies, had paid people close to the government to obtain horse-mackerel quotas. The fisheries and justice ministers resigned and were arrested with several associates, and they face racketeering, corruption and money-laundering charges under Namibia's organised crime law. Samherji denies paying bribes, and no one has yet been convicted.

The mechanism is one seen wherever a few ministers control who may take a public resource such as fish, timber or minerals: a foreign company that pays those ministers or their associates can be given a share that would otherwise go to local firms or be sold for the public's benefit. The Global Organized Crime Index finds a moderate-to-high level of officials serving outside interests in Namibia and rates its institutions as fairly weak.

For Namibians, if the charges are proved, two ministers sold a public resource to a foreign company. Local fishing firms and their workers lost quota they would otherwise have had, and the state lost income that would have gone to the public budget. The trial has run for years, so people still wait for a court to say who took part.

New Zealand.d:
In New Zealand the documented reach into government comes from two directions. The Chinese state has had people in Parliament whose ties to it were known to the intelligence services but not to voters, and international free-market and business networks have counted finance ministers, prime ministers and deputy prime ministers among their members.

The parliamentary side shows in how such cases end. When the intelligence agencies raised concerns about MPs' relationships with the Chinese government, the matter was settled quietly between party leaders and the MPs retired at an election; the clearest example is Jian Yang, a National MP who had been a Communist Party member and had taught at Chinese army schools that trained intelligence linguists. Voters learned the reason for his departure only from the press afterwards. Money has also reached the parties in ways voters could not see: three businessmen split $200,000 in donations to the National Party in 2017 and 2018 into smaller gifts under other names so they would not be declared, though their fraud convictions were overturned on appeal because the law requires a personal gain.

The network side works through training and contacts rather than money. The Mont Pelerin Society, a club founded to spread free-market ideas into policy, the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme, and the Atlas Network, a US-based body that funds and trains free-market think tanks, have each had a member in one of New Zealand's top offices over the past three decades. No inquiry has found that any of them directed a decision, but residents have no public record of what is discussed inside them.

Organised crime has little hold on officials here: the Global Organized Crime Index gives New Zealand one of the world's lowest scores for officials working for criminal interests.

North Macedonia.d:
In North Macedonia outsiders have reached into politics and the justice system by paying or directing individual office-holders, most visibly around the 2018 agreement that renamed the country so it could join NATO, which Russia opposed. Interior ministry documents seen by investigative reporters say Ivan Savvidis, a Russian-Greek billionaire and former member of Russia's parliament for the ruling party, paid at least €300,000, some carried across the Greek border in cash, to more than a dozen politicians from several parties, nationalist groups and football hooligans ahead of protests in which a petrol bomb was thrown at parliament; he denied funding the protests. Leaked counter-intelligence files from 2017 say a Serbian intelligence officer at Serbia's embassy gave instructions to an MP in the ruling coalition and that Russian intelligence officers tried to recruit army and interior ministry staff.

The justice system has been bought from inside as well. The Special Prosecution Office, set up to pursue high-level crime after a wiretapping scandal, was compromised when a television personality close to its head sold the country's richest man milder treatment in his case; in 2020 a court jailed him for bribing her and jailed her for misuse of office. Separately, the foreign minister joined the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders network in 2025, which is lawful and shows no decision taken for it.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives North Macedonia a fairly high score for officials working for criminal or outside interests and middling strength in its courts and watchdogs. For people in North Macedonia this means a decision about their country's name and alliances was contested with foreign money paid to their own politicians, and the office created to prosecute the powerful was itself for sale.

Palau.d:
Palau's documented case shows how a criminal group can reach a small state's government through the front door of business and goodwill. In Pacific island states, organised crime groups from Macau and Hong Kong arrive as investors and cultural associations, ask local officials to sit on their boards, and propose casinos or special economic zones that would sit partly outside national law.

The clearest example is Wan Kuok-koi, known as 'Broken Tooth', a former head of Macau's 14K triad whom the US Treasury sanctioned in 2020. Immigration records reported by OCCRP, a network of investigative journalists, show he was listed as a 'guest of the government' on a visit in 2018–19, and a serving postmaster general and a state governor became directors of his Palau association, which planned a casino zone on Angaur island where he would control customs, ports and an airport. It stopped in 2019 when the president, warned by Taiwan of Wan's record, came out against it, and the association applied to dissolve. OCCRP did not establish that the Chinese state directed the effort, and no one in Palau has been charged.

For a country of about 18,000 people, two serving officials lending their names gave a sanctioned gang leader local standing, and one island came close to hosting a casino zone under his control. What stopped it was a presidential decision on a foreign government's warning, not a law that blocked it.

Peru.d:
In Peru, foreign money has reached the head of state more than once, and criminal networks have bought people inside the offices that keep the country's records, grant its pardons and guard its ports.

At the top, the money has come from abroad. Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction group that admitted paying bribes in a dozen countries to win public contracts, reached presidents and their campaigns, and two former presidents have been sentenced over it, one for taking about $35 million for the contract to build the Interoceanic Highway. In the 1990s the CIA paid at least $10 million to the head of the national intelligence service. Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members carry their faith into public life, has had members serving as ministers and as mayor of Lima; membership is lawful and no finding links it to a specific decision.

Lower down, criminals buy the officials who handle paperwork, sentences and inspections. Senior staff of the national property registry rewrote the recorded owners of disputed land for a Lima lawyer's network, the board that advised the president on pardons sold early release to convicted drug traffickers, and cocaine groups pay security staff, dockworkers and customs contacts at Callao, the main seaport, where by one investigation's account less than a fifth of the cocaine passing through is detected. Judges and the council that appointed them have been recorded on wiretaps trading rulings and promotions. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Peru high for officials working for criminal interests.

For Peruvians this means they have paid for public works awarded in return for bribes, a land title can be changed by whoever paid the registrar, a trafficker can buy his way out of prison, and someone going before a court cannot be sure the outcome was not arranged.

Qatar.d:
Qatar's documented case runs outward, with Qatar's own money reported to have reached inside another country's government. Israeli prosecutors are investigating aides of the Israeli prime minister over money reported to have come from Qatar to promote its image from inside his office.

Qatar's residents have no elected body able to ask how state money is spent abroad. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Qatar fairly high for officials working for criminal or outside interests.

Samoa.d:
No case of outside groups paying or placing officials in Samoa is documented yet, so this account is an estimate based on general conditions. The only outside organisation recorded as present is Shincheonji Church of Jesus, a South Korean religious movement, and its presence is lawful and not evidence of wrongdoing.

The Global Organized Crime Index places Samoa in its low band, scoring it low for officials working for criminal or outside interests and in the middle range for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. Neighbouring Pacific states have seen bribes for business deals, and small island governments with few investigators are the kind of place where such pressures can go unnoticed.

For residents, the absence of cases means there is no specific harm to point to, not that none exists. The bodies that would bring such cases to light, the courts, police and audit office, are the ones whose middling scores leave that question open.

Senegal.d:
In Senegal the strongest outside force inside politics is a religious one that comes from within the country: the Sufi brotherhoods, above all the Mourides, whose leader, the Khalife général, commands the loyalty of millions of followers. Their holy city, Touba, has run its own affairs with wide autonomy since 1928, and presidents court the Khalife: a visit before the yearly Grand Magal pilgrimage has become customary, and newly elected presidents have gone to Touba within days, some putting Mourides in their governments. For Senegalese, this means decisions about spending in Touba, such as its water and sanitation, are agreed between the president and a religious leader no one elected.

Foreign religious movements have reached the presidency too. The Unification Church, a Korean-founded church, gave its $1 million Sunhak Peace Prize to President Macky Sall in 2020 while he was in office, and press reports have named past presidents as Freemasons, members of a fraternity whose members meet in private lodges, which one of them denied.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Senegal in the middle range both for officials working for criminal interests and for the strength of its courts and watchdogs.

Singapore.d:
Singapore's government treats foreign influence, most often linked to China, as something that works through ordinary community life: business chambers, clan and grassroots associations and universities. Its response is to name the people it believes are being used, and it does this by ministerial decision, not by trial. In 2017 it expelled a US-citizen professor at the state university's public-policy school as an 'agent of influence' working with an unnamed foreign intelligence service, which he denied. Since 2024 a foreign-interference law lets it designate residents, so far a business-chamber leader who had attended a Chinese Communist Party united front body, and make them report each year their political donations and foreign ties.

The city is also a base from which other governments are reached. For years a Singapore ship-supply firm run by Leonard Francis bribed US Navy officers with cash, travel and gifts for ship schedules and inside information, while a civilian Navy contracting officer in Singapore stopped an early inquiry; US prosecutors charged 33 people.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 1.5 out of 10, among the lowest in the world, and courts and watchdogs at about 7.8. For residents the trade-off is plain: people who lead community or business groups with ties to China can be publicly named and made to disclose their links, and a resident can lose the right to live here on a ministry's word without hearing the evidence in court.

Somalia.d:
In Somalia the outside force reaching furthest into the state is al-Shabaab, the al-Qaeda-linked armed Islamist group fighting the federal government, which places its own people inside the government it is trying to overthrow. Its members take public jobs, sometimes under false names, to collect information for taxing businesses and choosing targets, and defectors are often taken into the security forces without vetting. In 2019 a woman working under a false name in the Mogadishu mayor's office blew herself up at a meeting there, killing the mayor and other officials, and the government has dissolved a Chamber of Commerce board after finding the group's representatives on it.

Alongside the state's tax system the group runs its own. A UN panel of experts described 'mafia-style' taxation at Mogadishu's port and markets, and the Mogadishu-based Hiraal Institute estimated in 2020 that it raised close to as much as the government. Foreign states compete for influence at the top as well: from 2019 to 2021 the intelligence agency was run by a former reporter for Qatar's state-funded Al Jazeera, whom Somali media and analysts accuse of channelling Qatari money and interests into government, which Qatar denies.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 8 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 1.9, among the weakest anywhere. For people in Somalia that means paying tax twice, to the government and to the group fighting it, and working in offices where a colleague may be passing on who should be taxed or killed.

Sri Lanka.d:
In Sri Lanka, outsiders have reached the state mostly through the people its leaders chose to bring inside it, and Sinhala Buddhist monks are the clearest example. Under President Gotabaya Rajapaksa, from 2020, a council of senior monks met him every month with ministry secretaries present to advise on carrying out policy, from education to land deeds and national security, and the government reported acting on its proposals. Monks sat on a presidential task force allocating land around archaeological sites in the Eastern Province, with no Tamil or Muslim member at first although those communities are over 70% of the province's people. In 2021 the leader of Bodu Bala Sena ('Buddhist Power Force'), a monks' group accused of stirring violence against Muslims, was put in charge of a task force to draft a single legal code, which the Bar Association said was taking over the work of Parliament.

Money has reached the top through contracts and through the central bank. China Harbour Engineering, the Chinese state firm that built Hambantota port, is accused of funding Mahinda Rajapaksa's 2015 campaign, which it denies. In 2015 a central bank bond sale favoured a dealer owned by the governor's son-in-law, and a presidential commission held the governor responsible for the losses, though a special court later dismissed the charges.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 7 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 3.7. For Sri Lanka's Tamils and Muslims, this meant decisions on their land, their schools and the law that would govern them were shaped by clergy of another faith, through bodies that bypassed the elected parliament, and for all Sri Lankans it meant the central bank's bond sales handled for the benefit of insiders.

Sudan.d:
In Sudan armed and political movements have repeatedly taken over the state from inside, and two of them are now at war over it. Secret groups of army officers seized power in 1969 and 1989. The second was the work of the National Islamic Front, Hassan al-Turabi's movement derived from the Muslim Brotherhood, which had spent the decade after he became attorney general in 1979 placing members in high posts in government and the security services. Under Omar al-Bashir, the officer it brought to power, the movement filled state jobs with its own people, including judges and prosecutors.

Bashir's government also made the Janjaweed militias it had used in Darfur into a state force, the Rapid Support Forces, whose leader took over gold mines and, after Bashir fell in 2019, became deputy head of the ruling council. A committee set up by the transitional government began removing the people placed under Bashir, but the courts ordered some back to work, and the movement's leaders are under US, Canadian and EU sanctions for blocking civilian rule. Since the army and the Rapid Support Forces went to war in 2023, the US Treasury says Islamists tied to Iran hold posts in the army-backed government, including the finance minister, and that a militia of up to 20,000 fighters beside the army was trained by Iran's Revolutionary Guards; these are sanctions, not court rulings.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 8.5 out of 10 and courts, police and watchdogs at about 2.3. For people in Sudan the courts and ministries they deal with are still staffed by one movement's appointees, and the war fought through their towns is between two forces that both grew inside the state, one of them found by the US to have committed genocide.

Syria.d:
Under the Assad family, the people who held the Syrian state were themselves a closed group that had worked in secret inside it. The Military Committee was a secret body of army officers formed in 1958, kept secret even from its own party's leaders; it carried out the 1963 coup that brought the party to power and then held the real power behind it. One of its founders, Hafez al-Assad, seized power in 1970, and he and his son Bashar ruled until December 2024.

In the last decade of that rule the drug trade was not something that had bought its way into the state; it was run by the state. Captagon, an amphetamine pill smuggled across the Middle East and the Gulf, was made and moved by people at the centre of the government, and Syria produced about 80% of the world's supply, according to the British government. The UK, the US and the EU sanctioned the president's brother Maher al-Assad, whose army unit they said facilitated production and distribution and a sitting member of parliament was sanctioned over companies that produced and moved the pills. These are sanctions imposed by foreign governments, not court verdicts, and the former president and his brother live in Russia.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives Syria the highest possible score, 10 out of 10, for state-embedded crime, and about 2 for the strength of courts, police and watchdogs. For people in Syria this meant that the police and courts answered to the same people who ran the drug factories, so the trade could not be stopped from inside. Estimates cited by the British government put the trade at up to $57 billion, money that went to the ruling family and its army units rather than to the public.

Thailand.d:
In Thailand criminal businesses reach into the state through the police and the legislature, and the protection they buy is the same whether the money comes from drugs or from gambling. Thailand borders Myanmar's Shan State, one of the largest methamphetamine and heroin producing areas in the world, and networks linked to it move money into Thai property and politics.

In 2023 a sitting senator was indicted on drug trafficking and money-laundering charges tied to a Myanmar businessman whom the United States had sanctioned for supporting Myanmar's military government, and Thailand's narcotics board seized property worth over 400 million baht from homes connected to his family; the case has not reached a verdict. The same year Thailand's deputy national police chief was removed and investigated over alleged protection of an online gambling network, a case that split the police leadership in public.

Organised groups outside the elected system have also long decided who holds power. In 1932 the People's Party, founded by Siamese students in Paris and grown to about a hundred officers and civilians, ended absolute monarchy with army units, and its members then held the prime ministership for about two decades; the army's habit of taking power by coup dates from that event. Paetongtarn Shinawatra, the prime minister removed by the Constitutional Court in 2025, had also been named to the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme, which is not a finding of wrongdoing.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 7 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 5. For people in Thailand this means a senator charged over drug money helped vote on their laws, and when a deputy police chief is accused of protecting gambling operators, residents cannot be sure which complaints to the police will be followed up.

Trinidad and Tobago.d:
In Trinidad and Tobago the documented reach-in has come through people holding cabinet posts while serving outside interests, and through contractors on the country's largest public works. The clearest case is the new terminal at Piarco International Airport, built in the late 1990s: contractors, led by a Miami engineering firm, worked with the then finance minister to rig bids and charge inflated prices, hiding the scheme through offshore companies. Six of them pleaded guilty in US courts, and in 2023 a Miami jury found the former minister and two businessmen liable for racketeering and fraud, with a final judgment of US$131.3 million for Trinidad and Tobago.

The second case shows a private international body with its own senior figure inside the cabinet. Jack Warner was a vice-president of FIFA, world football's governing body, while he served as works minister and then national security minister until 2013. US prosecutors later charged him with taking bribes in his football roles; FIFA banned him for life, and in 2025 Trinidad's High Court blocked his extradition, so the charges have never been tried.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores both officials acting for criminal interests and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 5 out of 10. For people in Trinidad and Tobago this means the airport they paid for cost them far more than it should have because their finance minister was working with the contractors, and the minister responsible for their police was also an officer of an outside body later accused of selling votes. In both cases the account came from US courts, and the money recovered depends on collecting a foreign judgment.

Tuvalu.d:
No case of outside groups paying or placing officials in Tuvalu is documented, so this account is an estimate based on conditions. Tuvalu is a nation of about 11,000 people on low-lying atolls, and its government depends heavily on foreign aid and on agreements with larger partners. Elsewhere in the Pacific, payments for business deals have drawn smaller states into larger powers' rivalries; none of this is documented in Tuvalu.

The Global Organized Crime Index places Tuvalu in its Minimal band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 1.5 out of 10 and courts, police and watchdogs at 5.9. For Tuvaluans this means there is no known current harm from hidden outside influence. The risk is that a country this small has only a handful of officials, auditors and police, so if an outside interest did reach in, there would be few people in a position to notice it.

United Kingdom.d:
In Britain, outsiders have reached in through three channels: foreign intelligence services recruiting people inside the state, organised fraternities and societies placing members in office, and companies getting inside the departments that regulate them. From the 1930s to the 1960s Soviet intelligence had agents inside MI6, MI5, the Foreign Office and atomic research; the clearest case, Kim Philby, ran MI6's section against Soviet activity while working for Moscow. Czechoslovak intelligence later recruited MPs from both main parties. The same openings are still used. MI5 warned MPs in 2022 that a solicitor funding an MP's office worked covertly for China's United Front Work Department, a Communist Party body that builds influence abroad, and a former Welsh member of the European Parliament was jailed in 2025 for taking money to make pro-Russian speeches.

Fraternities sit inside the state too. In Northern Ireland every prime minister from 1921 to 1969 belonged to the Orange Order, a Protestant fraternity, and a 1973 army intelligence estimate put 5 to 15% of soldiers in a locally recruited regiment in loyalist paramilitary groups, some of whom took part in killings of Catholic civilians. In England, Freemasons have long held posts in the police and courts.

Companies use money and access: businessmen have paid MPs to table questions, the big accounting firms have lent tax staff to the Treasury to help draft law they then advise on, and suppliers backed by ministers and peers got a 'VIP lane' for pandemic contracts. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 3 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at 7.6. For people in Britain, this means rules drafted by those they apply to, and, in Northern Ireland, families still seeking inquiries into killings in which soldiers and police took part.

Vanuatu.d:
No case of outside groups placing people inside Vanuatu's government or paying its officials is documented, so this account is an estimate based on general conditions.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in Vanuatu at 3 out of 10, a low score, but scores its courts, police and watchdogs at only 4.9, in the middle of the range. That means experts judge that officials are not often working for criminal or outside interests, but that the bodies meant to catch it if they were are only moderately able to do so.

For ni-Vanuatu, as the country's people are called, the absence of cases means there is no named official or company to hold to account, not proof that none exists. With courts and watchdogs in the middle of the range, it would take time for any hidden outside influence on officials to come to light.

Yemen.d:
Yemen has been at war since 2014, and its government is now in large part a coalition of armed factions, several backed by a foreign power. In the north, the Houthi movement, a Zaydi Shia armed group, took over the capital Sanaa and its state institutions in 2014–15, dissolved parliament and since 2016 has governed through its own Supreme Political Council, which appoints the cabinet in Sanaa and still rules most of Yemen's population. The UN called that a clear violation of the constitution.

In the south, the clearest case of outside placement is the Southern Transitional Council (STC), a movement seeking a separate southern state that was formed in 2017 with help from the United Arab Emirates. In 2022 the STC joined the eight-member Presidential Leadership Council, the internationally recognised government's top body, and its leader became a vice-president, so the UAE's client sat at the head of the state. That arrangement broke down at the end of 2025, when the STC launched an offensive in the south and Saudi-backed forces struck back; its leader fled to the UAE in January 2026 and was removed from the council.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Yemen's courts, police and watchdogs at 1.9 out of 10, one of the lowest scores in the world, and officials acting for criminal interests at 8. For Yemenis, this means that decisions about who governs their region, who collects their taxes and who controls the ports are made by armed groups rather than by any elected body, some of them funded and directed from Abu Dhabi, Riyadh or Tehran. When those patrons fall out, as in late 2025, civilians are caught in the fighting, and there is no court or police force they can turn to when an armed group takes their land or money.

Algeria.d:
In Algeria the documented reach-in comes from two directions: foreign firms paying officials for state contracts, and the cocaine trade buying protection inside the security state. Contractors have worked on the public works ministry and Sonatrach, the state oil and gas company, through agents. The clearest example is the East-West motorway, begun in 2006 by Japanese and Chinese consortia: in 2015 an Algiers court jailed an adviser to the Chinese group, a former director of highways and other ministry staff over kickbacks on the project, whose cost rose from $6 billion to at least $13 billion. Bribery charges brought in Italy against a foreign oil-services firm over Sonatrach contracts ended in acquittal, but Algeria's energy minister from 1999 to 2010 was later sentenced in absentia to 20 years for corruption.

The cocaine trade reached into the police. When 701 kilograms of cocaine were found at the port of Oran in 2018, hidden in a cargo of imported meat, press reports tied the importer to judges, prosecutors, mayors and the children of senior politicians. The seizure brought down the head of the national police, and he and several generals were later convicted of corruption and illicit enrichment rather than drug offences; Algeria has published little about who protected the shipments.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Algeria 7.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 4 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For Algerians, this means public money for roads and energy has passed through officials who took a share, while the officials who let cocaine through a state port have not been named in court, and residents cannot tell whether they are still in post.

Argentina.d:
Argentina's state has more than once been run from inside by secret circles of officers and lodge members. Secret lodges of officers made and unmade the first governments after 1812 and, by most historians' account, organised the 1943 coup that began Juan Perón's rise. The clearest case is P2, a secret Masonic lodge run from Italy, whose membership lists seized in 1981 named an interim president, three ministers, the head of the joint chiefs of staff, a member of the military junta and ambassadors.

Since the 1990s the route has run more through economists and money. Twice a team trained in business-funded think tanks has moved into the economy ministry, the first time with a dollar peg that ended in frozen savings and the 2001 collapse, and since 2023 with partners of the Atlas Network, a US-based funder of free-market think tanks, which says they shaped the president's reforms. Companies have paid presidents and ministers for contracts.

Crime reaches the police and the courts, above all in Santa Fe province, around Rosario. Drug and gambling bosses there have had a former head of the provincial police, senior detectives who warned them of raids and steered murder inquiries toward rivals, and Rosario's own chief prosecutor, convicted in 2025 of taking a gambling financier's bribes; prosecutors charged a provincial senator as the network's political head, and his colleagues kept his immunity for years. Federal judges, who hear drug cases, have been convicted in the north and in Mendoza of selling traffickers release or house arrest.

For people around Rosario, the detective, prosecutor or judge who should stand between them and the gangs may be on the gangs' side, while nationally the rules on prices, wages and savings have been set by teams tied to think tanks and foreign banks.

Azerbaijan.d:
Azerbaijan's economy rests on oil and gas, and the state oil company, SOCAR, is closely bound up with the government. Outsiders have tried to get in by sharing the oil wealth with the officials who control it: in the late 1990s foreign investors trying to buy SOCAR in a privatisation they expected to be rigged made senior Azerbaijani officials their secret partners, promising them two-thirds of the profits and flying millions of dollars in cash into the country, and an American investor was convicted in New York in 2009 for his part.

The documented pattern since then runs outward, with the oil sector and Azerbaijani money reaching into the international bodies that set rules for it. When Azerbaijan hosted the UN climate summit, COP29, in 2024, its president had been a SOCAR vice-president, and its chief executive, a deputy energy minister, was secretly filmed by campaigners posing as investors discussing oil and gas deals; critics said this broke the rule that a host must act impartially. An independent inquiry for the Council of Europe's parliamentary assembly, Europe's human rights body, reported in 2018 a strong suspicion that some members had acted for Azerbaijan in return for money or gifts, a practice that became known as caviar diplomacy.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Azerbaijan 8.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 4 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, this means the oil wealth that belongs to the country has been treated as something officials could privately share with foreign buyers and the European bodies meant to report honestly on their rights have themselves been targets of their government's money.

Barbados.d:
Barbados has one documented case of an outside party reaching into its government, and it came from a company seeking state business rather than from organised crime or a foreign state. Senior executives of the Insurance Corporation of Barbados Limited paid the island's Minister of Industry, Donville Inniss, about $36,000 in 2015 and 2016 to help the company win two government insurance contracts covering more than $100 million of state property.
