The money went through a US bank account in the name of a friend's dental company in New York, which is why a US jury, not a Barbadian court, convicted him of money laundering in 2020; he was sentenced to two years in prison.

No other case of a foreign government, company, crime group or lodge placing people or money inside the state remains on this map. The Global Organized Crime Index gives Barbados 3 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests, low by world standards, and about 6.1 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, better than most of the Caribbean. Barbados is also an offshore financial centre that registers international companies, the kind of business that can draw outside money.

For Barbadians, this means a minister used his office to steer the insurance of public property to a company that paid him, and the case came to light only because the money passed through the United States. The likeliest places for outside money to reach in are the ones this case shows: who wins public contracts, who funds politicians and who owns the companies registered on the island.

Benin.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Benin, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows a foreign state, company, criminal group or lodge paying or placing people inside its government. Two French Masonic bodies, the Grand Orient de France and the Grande Loge Nationale Française, are thought to have members in Benin but are not documented.

Benin is a coastal West African state whose port at Cotonou handles goods for its larger neighbour, Nigeria, and for landlocked states to the north, so much of the trade that crosses it belongs to outsiders. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Benin 6 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 3.8 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. That combination describes officials under real pressure and weak checks on them.

For people living there, this means that if outside interests are paying or placing officials, it is likely to show up in port and customs work, public contracts and policing, and residents would pay through lost public revenue and weaker protection. With no named case, there is no official or company they can yet challenge.

Botswana.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Botswana, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows a foreign state, company, criminal group, church or lodge paying or placing people inside its government, and no outside organisation is recorded as present.

Botswana's economy rests on diamonds, mined mainly through a long-standing partnership between the government and the De Beers company, and on that kind of single, valuable export outside interests often seek influence. Against that, the Global Organized Crime Index scores Botswana 4.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 5.4 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. That puts it in the middle of the range and ahead of most of its neighbours. The lack of cases may also reflect limited investigative reporting.

For people living there, this means there is no named official or company to hold to account, and no evidence that public decisions are being bought. If a case exists, it would most likely surface through mining and other licences, public contracts or policing of the borders, and those are the records residents would need to see.

Burkina Faso.d:
What is documented for Burkina Faso is Freemasonry at the top of the government that ran the country until 2014. Freemasonry is a fraternal society whose members meet privately in lodges under a national grand lodge, led by an elected grand master. Under Blaise Compaoré, who ruled from 1987 to 2014, the presidency and the foreign ministry were linked through the Grande Loge du Burkina: the magazine Jeune Afrique reported that Compaoré had been its grand master and that his foreign minister, Djibrill Bassolé, succeeded him in that post.

In those years, the two men who set the country's foreign policy led, one after the other, a private body whose meetings and membership are closed to the public. Lodge membership is lawful, and the reporting does not show any decision taken for the lodge. What it shows is a tie between the people running the state and a network Burkinabè voters had no way to see into or question.

The record does not reach into the present military government. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Burkina Faso high for officials working for criminal interests and very weak in the courts, police and watchdogs that would check them, so outside influence on officials would meet little resistance at home, but no current case of it is documented here.

Cameroon.d:
The documented case in Cameroon reaches into the presidency itself, which Paul Biya has held since 1982. Le Monde reported that in his early years Biya passed tens of millions of French francs, some of it from the state oil company, to esoteric orders styled on the medieval Knights Templar and to the personal account of their French leader, Raymond Bernard. The presidency called Bernard an 'old friend' and declined to comment.

If that reporting is right, oil revenue that belongs to the public went to the head of a private spiritual order abroad rather than into the state budget, and the decision was made at the very top. Cameroonians have never had an official account of those payments, and the same man still holds office, so there is no route by which an inquiry would start from inside the government.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Cameroon among the countries where officials most often work for criminal interests, and its courts, police and watchdogs as weak. On those terms, money moved out of a state company by the presidency is unlikely to be traced or recovered by Cameroon's own institutions.

Chile.d:
In Chile, outsiders have reached the state through two routes: the people trained to run it, and money paid to the politicians who write its laws.

During the Cold War the reach came from Washington. Between 1963 and 1973 the CIA spent about $13 million on Chilean parties, candidates and a newspaper, including slightly more than half the cost of the winning 1964 presidential campaign. Under General Pinochet's military government, a US-funded exchange that had trained more than a hundred Chilean economists at the University of Chicago, the 'Chicago Boys', supplied the men who ran the economic ministries and the central bank, and the founder of a Catholic conservative student movement was the principal author of the 1980 constitution. That constitution is still in force after voters rejected two replacement drafts.

Since the return to democracy the money has come mostly from Chilean companies. The lithium miner SQM and a large holding group paid campaigns through fake invoices. A fishing company paid a senator while the 2012 fisheries law went through Congress, a law that handed a large share of the national catch to companies controlled by a few families with no end date; he was sentenced to prison for bribery. As Chile has become a drug transit route, officers of the Carabineros, the national police, have been charged with reselling seized drugs and protecting dealers.

For Chileans this means living under a constitution and an economic programme drawn up by people placed in power without a vote, and under fishing and mining rules shaped by companies that paid the legislators. In some neighbourhoods the police meant to stop the drug trade work for it. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Chile's officials and institutions in the middle of the global range.

Congo, Dem. Rep..d:
For nearly thirty years the armies of Congo's neighbours, and the armed groups they back, have placed their own people inside the Congolese state. After a Rwandan-backed rebellion brought Laurent-Désiré Kabila to power in 1997, a Rwandan officer served as chief of staff of Congo's army. When Uganda occupied the north-east, its army chief decreed the Ituri region a new province in 1999 and appointed its governor, and the UN's International Court of Justice later ordered Uganda to pay Congo $325 million for its occupation. Rebel groups have been folded into Congo's own army and then walked out again with their troops.

The clearest case today is M23, a rebel force that took the eastern cities of Goma and Bukavu in early 2025. UN sanctions monitors report that Rwanda's army commands it and that it has appointed provincial governors, put Rwandans in charge of mining, tax, banking and border control, and removed customary chiefs; Rwanda denies directing M23.

Outsiders choosing Congo's rulers is older still: from 1960 the CIA paid Joseph Mobutu and the governments it favoured, and Mobutu ruled until 1997. Across the country today the reach comes through mining, where foreign investors and commodity traders have won mining and oil rights by paying officials or through personal ties to the presidency, and one of the largest miners has paid the state $180 million to settle bribery claims it denies.

For people in the east, the governors, tax collectors and border officers over them have more than once been appointed by a foreign army or a group it backs. Across Congo, mining wealth that should have reached the state budget went to insiders, and the Global Organized Crime Index rates Congo among the worst in the world for officials working for criminal interests.

Croatia.d:
Croatia's documented cases show foreign companies and banks reaching the country's national assets through its head of government. The clearest is the national oil company, INA. MOL, a Hungarian oil company in which the Hungarian state has influence, wanted to run it, and Croatian courts found that Prime Minister Ivo Sanader took a 10 million euro bribe from MOL's chief executive to give it that control. MOL denies the bribe, and Hungary has not handed the executive over to Croatia. Sanader was also charged with taking a commission from an Austrian bank, Hypo Alpe-Adria, for arranging a state loan in the 1990s, but on retrial he was acquitted, and that acquittal was upheld in 2025.

For Croatians, the national oil company they part-own is still managed by the firm the courts found paid their prime minister for that control, and his conviction did not change who runs it. Croatian courts could punish the official who took the money but not the executive who paid it, because he lives in another EU country that will not send him back. The case shows a gap in how Europe deals with this kind of reach: the country that is harmed can try its own politicians, but the company and its managers stay out of reach.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Croatia in the middle range for officials working for criminal interests and for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. The courts have reached a former head of government, though it took most of a decade, and the Hypo charge shows how hard such payments are to prove once they are years old.

Denmark.d:
Very little outside reach into the Danish state or Danish companies is documented on the map, and what there is comes from two directions: a foreign spy service working through an insider, and a business-led network at the head of state.

Russian intelligence has paid people working inside Denmark to collect information. In the clearest case, a Russian man employed by a Danish fuel cell maker spent several years gathering information on energy technology from that company and from the Technical University of Denmark and passing it to Russian intelligence for money; a court in Aalborg sentenced him in 2021 to three years in prison and permanent expulsion. Russia called the case a witch hunt.

King Frederik X is listed among alumni of the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme, which he joined as crown prince. The Forum is the Swiss-based organisation behind the annual Davos meeting of business and political leaders, and its programme gathers people under about 40 into a five-year network of meetings and courses. The king's role is ceremonial, so the membership does not show the Forum deciding anything for Danes, only that its network reaches the office that formally heads the state.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Denmark among the very lowest countries in the world for officials working for criminal interests, and among the strongest for its courts, police and watchdogs. For Danes, this means the officials they deal with are unlikely to be working for criminal or foreign interests, and the documented risk sits with the research and energy firms that foreign intelligence wants to learn from.

Ecuador.d:
Ecuador sits between the two largest cocaine-producing countries, Colombia and Peru, and its Pacific ports have become one of the main exits for cocaine bound for Europe and the United States. The trafficking groups that run this trade pay the officials who could stop it. At the coast they recruit port workers and customs officers so that drugs hidden in banana shipments leaving Guayaquil pass inspection. Inland they buy judges, prosecutors, police commanders and prison staff, so that members are released, cases are delayed and sentences are cut; in 2024 the leader of Los Choneros, the gang that has run much of the prison system, walked out of Guayaquil's top-security prison with guards suspected of helping. Decrypted messages on one trafficker's phone led to the conviction of 20 people, among them the former head of the council that oversees Ecuador's judges.

Foreign companies reach in through the money. Oil traders and builders from abroad have paid officials at Petroecuador, the state oil company, and in the ministries above it for contracts, and the bribes have reached two vice-presidents: one now in prison, and another, later president, charged over a Chinese-built dam, which he denies. Reporting in 2023 also alleged that money from a man linked to traffickers reached the circle of the then president's family; that remains unproven.

For people in Ecuador a court ruling may have been bought, a gang leader may leave prison on a paid order, and the port and police staff around them may be on a gang's payroll, while the bribes came out of the oil money and loans that pay for schools, hospitals and power. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials working for criminal interests at 7.5 out of 10, with the courts and watchdogs meant to resist them at under 4.5.

Eritrea.d:
This is an estimate: no case on the map names a foreign government, company or criminal group placing or paying people inside Eritrea's government. Eritrea has been governed by one party, the People's Front for Democracy and Justice, since independence in 1993, has held no national election in that time and has no independent press, so very little can be checked from outside.

What reporting there is points to criminal business run from inside the state rather than reaching in from outside. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 9.5 out of 10, one of the highest scores in the world, and says military officers and ruling-party members dominate smuggling of people, gold, alcohol, tobacco and counterfeit goods, much of it across the border with Sudan, and that officials involved are rarely prosecuted. A 2013 report presented at the European Parliament said the army's border surveillance unit took part in smuggling Eritreans into Sudan, where thousands are reported to have died in captivity.

If that picture is right, Eritreans who try to leave the country pay the same officers who are meant to guard the border, and money from gold and trade ends up in private hands. The strength of courts and watchdogs scores 2.2 out of 10, and there is no independent body inside the country where a resident could take a complaint.

Fiji.d:
Fiji sits on the shipping and air routes that carry methamphetamine and cocaine across the Pacific to Australia and New Zealand, and traffickers moving those drugs have got inside its police and customs. The minister for policing told parliament in 2025 that 27 police officers had been involved in 33 drug cases since the start of 2023. In one of them, two officers of the police counter-narcotics unit and a senior customs manager were among seven people charged with helping methamphetamine through Nadi airport in air cargo, and the unit was later disbanded. Leaked chats published in late 2025 appeared to show senior officers, including the head of the organised crime department, discussing drug shipments and payments with traffickers; the police commissioner confirmed that seven senior officers were under investigation, and the claims have not been tested in court.

For people in Fiji, this means the officers responsible for stopping drugs at the airport and the border may be working for those bringing them in. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 4 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at about 5.4, a middle position in which cases are being investigated and charged rather than ignored.

Gambia.d:
Under Yahya Jammeh, president from 1994 to 2017, The Gambia's state businesses were handed to a small circle around him, and part of that circle was tied to a foreign armed movement. Lebanese businessmen whom the United States designates as financiers of Hezbollah, the Lebanese Shia party and armed group, received state monopolies, including the national fuel supply and half of the state telephone companies. OCCRP, a network of investigative reporters, estimated that more than $100 million from Gambian telecoms reached Hezbollah.

For Gambians, this meant they paid for fuel and telephone calls through monopolies given to the president's associates, and some of that money left the country to fund a foreign armed group rather than reaching the treasury. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at about 5.

Greece.d:
Greece's record shows two lasting ways in: organised groups inside the armed forces and police, and creditors and bankers inside the state's finances.

After the Second World War, IDEA, a secret society of officers who had served in units that worked with the German occupiers, grew inside the army, and its members led the 1967 coup and held key posts under the junta that ruled until 1974. More recently the neo-Nazi party Golden Dawn built support inside the police: after the May 2012 election, polling stations used by Attica police officers gave it just over 20 per cent of the vote against about 6 per cent at civilian stations nearby, and in 2020 its leaders were convicted of running a criminal organisation.

Control of the state's money has repeatedly passed to outsiders. From 1898 to 1936 a commission of six creditor powers collected Greek monopoly revenues and taxes to repay loans. In the late 1980s a banker who owned the Bank of Crete said he paid ministers in return for state deposits, and two former ministers were convicted. When the debt crisis began in 2010, a former Goldman Sachs and J.P. Morgan trader ran the agency that manages Greek borrowing, then returned to one of the banks holding Greek bonds. A Swiss drug company has settled US charges of bribing Greek public hospital staff and doctors.

For people in Greece, this means migrants and opponents were policed by officers many of whom backed a criminal organisation, and the state's borrowing during the crisis was run by people from the banks that lent to it. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7.5 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 5.1.

Guinea-Bissau.d:
Since the mid-2000s Guinea-Bissau, a small West African country of islands and mangrove creeks with weak central control, has been a transit point for South American cocaine headed to Europe. The trafficking networks did not need to buy junior officials one by one, because they reached the commanders of the armed forces themselves. In 2013 US prosecutors charged the heads of the navy, the air force and the army with offering their positions to help move cocaine. The army chief, who had led a coup the year before, was also charged with offering to store cocaine for the FARC, the Colombian guerrilla army, and sell it weapons. Only the navy chief was caught, in a sting at sea; the other two stayed in Bissau and were never handed over.

The armed forces have repeatedly overthrown or threatened elected governments, so the people traffickers paid are the same people who decide who governs. The navy chief, back home after his US sentence, was blamed by the president for a failed attack on the government palace in 2022.

For people in Guinea-Bissau, this means the officers commanding their army, navy and air force have been accused of working for foreign traffickers, and those accused have remained free and in some cases in power. With the courts and watchdogs scoring under 2.7 out of 10 on the Global Organized Crime Index and officials acting for criminal interests at 8.5, the cases against them have been brought abroad, and drug cases at home rarely reach trial.

Hungary.d:
Hungary's documented cases show foreign intelligence services working through Hungarians who hold European posts. Russia's services had a Hungarian member of the European Parliament working for them: Béla Kovács, elected for the nationalist party Jobbik, was convicted in Hungary in 2022 of spying on EU institutions for Russia and lives in Russia. Hungary's own intelligence service has used its position in Brussels in a similar way, with officers under diplomatic cover at Hungary's mission to the EU trying for years to recruit Hungarians employed at the European Commission, the EU's executive, a network the Commission has confirmed.

Both run through the same opening: Hungarians who hold seats or jobs in EU institutions have access to information and decisions that affect all 27 member states, which makes them worth recruiting for Moscow and for Budapest's own government. Hungary has also been on the receiving end of a foreign power placing its own people in charge. In October 1944 Nazi Germany detained the regent and installed the leader of the Arrow Cross, Hungary's fascist movement, as head of government; in under three months its death squads killed up to 38,000 Hungarian Jews.

Inside Hungary today, the Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 7.5 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at about 4.8, a weak position for an EU member. For people in Hungary, this means a representative they elected to the European Parliament was working for a foreign intelligence service, and Hungarians working in EU institutions have been targeted by their own country's spies, so decisions that affect their rights, funds and trade are taken with a foreign or partisan service listening in.

Iran.d:
In Iran the documented reach into the state has come from foreign intelligence services and from religious and fraternal networks. In 1953 the CIA, with British help, bribed members of parliament and organised the security forces to remove the elected prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh, after he nationalised Iran's oil; the CIA's own history says the coup was carried out under its direction. The Shah then ruled as a close US ally until the 1979 revolution, and the head of Iran's main Freemason lodge served twice as his prime minister.

Since the revolution, both real attacks from inside and accusations of spying have shaped who holds posts. In 1981 bombs planted by men who had taken jobs inside the ruling party's headquarters and the prime minister's office killed about 70 officials, then the president and prime minister; Iran blamed the People's Mojahedin, an armed opposition movement, though no group claimed the attacks. In 2023 Iran hanged a former deputy defence minister as a British spy, a charge he said was extracted under torture. Members of the Hojjatieh Society, a Shia religious association, sat in government bodies until they were purged in 1983, and former members are reported to have later held posts in the judiciary and security services.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Iran 9.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 3 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs, among the weakest results anywhere. For people in Iran this means there is no independent court or free press able to examine which networks hold posts inside the state, and an official accused of spying is tried in courts that are not independent of the government bringing the charge.

Italy.d:
Italy's mafias get inside the state mostly at the level of the town hall. They supply votes to local politicians and in return take a say over public jobs, building contracts, permits and health services, until a town's administration works for the clan. Since 1991 the national government has dissolved town councils and local health authorities 402 times after finding them under mafia control, mostly in Calabria, Campania and Sicily but also in Lombardy, Piedmont, Emilia-Romagna and Rome's own seaside district. In Palermo during the post-war building boom, a man close to the Corleone bosses ran the city's building permits, and in Campania a Camorra clan paid local officials for twenty years to accept toxic waste from northern industry. Mafia-delivered votes have put politicians into regional governments and the Interior Ministry, and a President of Sicily has been convicted of helping Cosa Nostra.

Companies and secret networks have reached even further. In the early 1990s the 'Mani pulite' inquiry found that firms paid the governing parties a cut of public works contracts, and at one point more than half of parliament was under indictment. In 1981 police seized the membership list of P2, a hidden Masonic lodge, and found it included dozens of members of parliament, serving ministers, nearly 200 senior military officers and the heads of all three intelligence services.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Italy 7 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and above 6 for its courts and watchdogs. For people in southern Italy especially, their elected council can be removed and replaced by commissioners for up to two years, public building and hospital supplies can go to firms a clan controls, and the land around their homes may hold waste the clan was paid to bury.

Kazakhstan.d:
Kazakhstan's state draws most of its money from oil and gas, and the documented cases of outsiders reaching in all run the same way: Western companies competing for the country's fields and pipelines paid consultants and agents, often through offshore accounts, knowing the money would reach the Kazakh officials who decided who got the work. Through the 1990s and 2000s, a US oilfield services company, a British engineering group and others admitted in US or British settlements to paying, or intending to pay, officials of the state oil company and of a pipeline venture owned by the Kazakh and Chinese governments; one of them also took on a local distributor secretly owned by a high-ranking official.

The case that reached highest was at the top of the state. US prosecutors charged in 2003 that an American adviser to President Nursultan Nazarbayev had moved about $20 million through Swiss accounts to the president and a former prime minister so that Western firms would win oil contracts, including in the Tengiz field. It ended in 2010 with the adviser pleading guilty only to a tax offence, so the bribery claims against Kazakh leaders were never proven in court.

No case on this map shows a foreign state, crime group or secret society placing officials in Kazakhstan. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Kazakhstan 6 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 5 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For people in Kazakhstan, this means the contracts for the oil and gas that fund their state have repeatedly been won by paying the officials who awarded them, and everything known about those payments comes from foreign prosecutors; no Kazakh court has tested it.

Korea, Rep..d:
In South Korea, three kinds of outside force have reached into politics: religious movements, through gifts, cash and mass sign-ups to a party; the large family-run business groups, through payments to presidents; and North Korea, through agents who try to recruit people inside parties and the army. The Unification Church, a Korean-founded movement, has worked closely with Seoul governments since the 1970s, when a US congressional inquiry found it acting as a secret envoy for the state. In 2026 its leader was jailed for arranging luxury gifts for the first lady and cash for a senior lawmaker of the governing People Power Party (PPP), and investigators found thousands of its followers had joined the party ahead of a leadership vote. Another movement, Shincheonji, signed up tens of thousands of its members to the same party.

The business groups depend on state decisions about mergers, licences and pardons, and Samsung, the largest, has been found by courts to have bribed two presidents' circles. North Korea's ruling party has run cells that placed members in the leadership of a party with seats in the National Assembly, worked as a politician's secretary, tried to recruit local politicians in a province, and paid a serving army captain in cryptocurrency for access to the military's command network.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores South Korea 4 out of 10 for officials working for outside interests and 8 for its courts and watchdogs, among the strongest in Asia. For South Korean voters this means churches have paid their way to a first lady and packed a party's membership, companies have bought presidential favours, and the North keeps trying to recruit inside their parties, but also that their courts have been able to expose and convict those involved.

Laos.d:
In northern Laos a foreign-run casino company administers part of the country. In 2007 the Lao government gave Kings Romans, a company headed by the Chinese businessman Zhao Wei, a concession to set up and run the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone in Bokeo province, where Laos, Thailand and Myanmar meet. The US has since sanctioned his network for trafficking heroin and methamphetamine and laundering money through the zone, which he denies, and the US State Department reports that the zone is controlled and administered in part by transnational criminal organisations. No Lao official has been investigated or prosecuted for complicity.

The arrangement is how criminal networks get inside the state in Laos: rather than bribing officials one by one, they are handed land and the power to run it, under a legal concession. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Laos 7.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 4 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs.

For people in Laos this means land in Bokeo has been handed for decades to a company the US says moves drugs and launders money, and residents there live partly under rules set by its operators.

Liberia.d:
In Liberia, outside bodies have shaped who governs and how state money is spent. For most of the country's history a fraternal order was part of the route to power: membership of the Masonic Order, Liberia's Freemason body, was widely seen as a requirement for leadership in the True Whig Party, which ruled for over a century, and by the 1970s most high officials were Masons, with President William Tolbert as the order's Grand Master. Samuel Doe, who killed Tolbert in 1980, banned the order and was later initiated into it himself.

After the civil wars, international lenders reached directly into the state firms. Under a 2005 programme designed and funded by the IMF, the World Bank and the US government, foreign financial controllers sat inside the port authority, the main airport, the state oil refiner and the forestry agency with power to co-sign their major transactions, until signing authority returned to Liberian hands in 2009.

Today the documented pressure comes from cocaine traffickers using Liberia as a stop on the route from South America to Europe. After the country's largest recorded seizure in 2026, nearly four tonnes bound for Europe, police charged the head of their own major crimes unit, named a senior airport security officer as a participant, and said senior government officials were involved; these are charges, not convictions.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Liberia 7.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 4 for its courts and watchdogs. For Liberians this means that, if the charges hold, the police unit meant to fight serious crime and the officer guarding the main airport were working with traffickers, and they cannot rely on those offices to stop drugs passing through their country.

Luxembourg.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Luxembourg, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows a foreign state, company, crime group or lodge paying officials or placing people inside its government.

The Global Organized Crime Index, which scores every country on how far its officials work for criminal or outside interests, rates Luxembourg among the lowest in the world on that measure. That means experts judge that officials there rarely act for criminal interests.

For people living there, this means no named official or company can be shown to be acting for an outside party, and the index suggests officials face less of this pressure than in most countries. If outside money did reach in, it would most likely show up in who funds politicians, who wins public contracts and who sits on the boards of companies the state regulates, and residents are best protected when those records are public.

Maldives.d:
The Maldives sits between India and China's shipping routes in the Indian Ocean, and the one recorded claim of an outside power reaching inside its politics comes from that rivalry. In December 2024 the Washington Post reported that Maldivian opposition politicians had planned to pay 40 members of parliament, including some from President Mohamed Muizzu's own party, to vote to impeach him, using about $6 million to be sought from India. Muizzu had won office promising to reduce India's influence. The paper said an officer of India's foreign intelligence agency explored ways to remove him through two intermediaries, who confirmed the plan existed. No money is reported to have been paid, Muizzu's coalition won a parliamentary majority in 2024, and a former president denied any Indian role.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates the Maldives in the middle range for how far officials work for criminal or outside interests, and rates its courts, police and watchdogs as fairly weak. Conditions like that usually mean some officials can be paid to serve business or criminal interests and the bodies meant to catch them have gaps.

For Maldivians, this means the members of parliament they elect have been treated, at least in planning, as votes a foreign-backed group could buy to remove their president. In daily life the weak institutions are more likely to show as bribes asked for ordinary services and state contracts going to favoured firms.

Mauritania.d:
No case has yet been documented of a foreign state, company or crime group paying Mauritanian officials or placing people inside the government, so this account is an estimate based on general conditions.

Mauritania lies on the route by which South American cocaine crosses the Sahara and the Sahel towards North Africa and Europe. The UN Office on Drugs and Crime reported in 2024 that across Mauritania and its Sahel neighbours, traffickers include members of the political elite and use their profits to get into state institutions and avoid prosecution, and Mauritania itself has made some of the largest cocaine seizures in the region. The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials there often serving criminal interests and rates its courts, police and watchdogs as weak.

If the estimate is right, the pressure would show most in policing and border control, and people in Mauritania would face traffickers who are protected by officials rather than stopped by them. Without a named case there is no official or company they can yet hold to account.

Moldova.d:
Moldova's courts, banks and elected offices have been used by outside money, most of it Russian, on a scale few countries match. The courts were used as a laundering machine: in the scheme known as the Global Laundromat, Russian companies signed fake debts that Moldovan judges ordered paid into a Moldovan bank, moving tens of billions of dollars out of Russia, and prosecutors later charged judges who approved them. The banks were taken from the inside with the help of the government: in 2014 about $1 billion, equal to roughly 12 percent of the country's economic output, vanished from three banks including the state savings bank, and a former prime minister was jailed for taking money to let a businessman's investors take control of it.

Russian money has also paid for political parties, candidates and paid protesters, reaching as high as the presidency. Igor Dodon, president from 2016 to 2020 and leader of the pro-Russian Socialist Party, was filmed saying his party received monthly funding from Russia, and has been charged with high treason and illegal party financing; his trial is still under way. Moldova's courts have banned a party for serving a foreign state's interests and jailed elected officials, including a regional governor, for funding their campaigns with undeclared Russian money.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials in Moldova widely serving criminal interests. For Moldovans this means a court ruling could be bought by a foreign client, the savings they and the state held in the banks were taken with the help of the people running the government, and some of the people they elected, including the governor of the autonomous region of Gagauzia and, if the charges hold, a president, owed their campaigns to a foreign government.

Morocco.d:
The documented reach into Morocco's state comes from two directions: drug traffickers who have recruited elected politicians into their networks, and a religious order whose follower holds the top post that shapes religion.

Morocco is one of the world's main producers of cannabis resin and lies on routes that carry cocaine across North Africa to Europe. Traffickers there need local officials and elected figures who can protect property, permits and shipments. The clearest case is the 'Escobar of the Sahara' network, named after a jailed Malian trafficker, in which a court in 2026 convicted a former regional council head and two former members of parliament from the governing party among dozens of defendants; appeals are open.

On the religious side, a follower of the Boutchichiya, Morocco's largest Sufi order (a Muslim brotherhood built around a spiritual teacher), has run the ministry that oversees the country's mosques since 2002, under five prime ministers. This is recorded as influence, not wrongdoing.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials in Morocco often serving criminal interests. For Moroccans this means that some of the people they elected to parliament and regional councils were working with a drug network rather than against it, and the ministry that shapes what is preached in their mosques has been led for more than two decades by a follower of one Sufi order.

Nauru.d:
In Nauru, a small Pacific island state whose main export is phosphate, outside money arrives mainly from Australia, and it has reached the island's politicians through the two things Australia buys there: phosphate and the hosting of asylum seekers.

Australian businesspeople seeking phosphate deals have been prosecuted in Australia for paying Nauruan politicians; one Sydney businessman was jailed in 2018 for paying an MP and a minister, and a Gold Coast phosphate trader is still awaiting trial on a charge of conspiring to bribe them. The second channel is the asylum detention centre that Australia pays contractors to run on the island. In 2023 the Sydney Morning Herald and The Age reported that subcontracts worth millions went to firms tied to Nauru's leaders, with banking records showing suspect payments to the justice minister and to a company of a man who later became president. The reporters said they were not claiming the payments were bribes, the minister denies wrongdoing, and Australia's Home Affairs department had been warned of bribery allegations for more than a decade.

In a country this small, a few contracts from one foreign government make up a large share of the money in circulation, and the politicians who decide on them can also benefit from them.

For people in Nauru this means that phosphate, one of the few sources of national income, has been sold through deals prosecutors say were bought, cutting what reaches the public. Ministers who benefit from Australian contracts have a private reason to keep the detention centre open whatever residents want.

Nicaragua.d:
In Nicaragua the documented reach into the state has come from the United States, first through its banks and later through its government's money for Nicaraguan politics. In 1911 and 1912 New York bankers, backed by Washington, lent Nicaragua money in return for its National Bank as collateral and a majority stake in the National Railway, while the US president appointed the collector of Nicaragua's customs. When the president they dealt with faced a revolt, US Marines landed, and they stayed, with one short break, until 1935. While the loans ran, the country's money, its main railway and the duties collected at its ports were managed for foreign creditors.

In the 1980s the reach came through politics. The National Endowment for Democracy, a foundation funded by the US Congress, paid for opposition groups and the newspaper La Prensa, and Congress added more for the opposition campaign before the 1990 election, which the opposition won. Nicaraguans who voted then were choosing between sides of which one was funded in part from Washington.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives Nicaragua one of the lowest scores in the world for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, and one of the highest for officials working for criminal or outside interests. No recent case on the map shows a foreign state, company or crime group placing people inside the Nicaraguan government. For people in Nicaragua today, this means that if officials are working for outside interests, there is no domestic body able to examine it.

Norway.d:
Norway is one of the countries where outside forces have the least documented hold on government. The Global Organized Crime Index puts it in its minimal band, with one of the world's lowest scores for officials working for criminal interests and strong courts, police and watchdogs.

The exceptions the record shows are a foreign spy service inside the foreign ministry and a drug importer working with the police. During the Cold War the KGB had an agent in Arne Treholt, a Labour Party official who sat in fishing and Law of the Sea talks with the Soviet Union and became head of the Foreign Ministry's press department before his arrest in 1984 and conviction for treason. For Norwegians it meant that a man passing information to the KGB took part in their country's fishing and sea-boundary talks with the Soviet Union.

Inside the police, drug enforcement depends on officers handling informants with little outside oversight. Eirik Jensen ran the Oslo police narcotics section for years while helping an informant he managed bring around fourteen tonnes of hashish into the country, and was jailed for twenty-one years, the most senior police conviction of its kind in Scandinavia. For people in Oslo it meant the unit meant to stop the drug trade was protecting one of its suppliers. Both cases also showed the courts holding senior officials to account.

Panama.d:
Panama's place in the record comes from its role as a corridor for ships, money and companies, and from the people who have paid their way into its government because of it. Its law firms set up companies for clients abroad, its free zone in Colón lets goods pass without entering customs, and its banks have held money for traffickers and rulers alike; each of these has drawn foreign buyers of influence.

Under military rule in the 1980s the state was rented out from the top. Manuel Noriega, the army commander who ran the country, took money from Colombia's Medellín cartel to make Panama a shipping platform for cocaine while also being paid as a CIA source, and the military's candidate installed as president in a rigged 1984 vote was a former World Bank vice-president who brought in IMF-required austerity. Cartel, spy service and lenders all dealt with the same small group of men in uniform.

The largest recent reach came from Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction group that admitted paying bribes across Latin America and Africa to win public contracts. It says it paid Panamanian officials during the 2009–2014 government, and the trial of more than 20 people, including a former president who joins by video from asylum abroad, opened in 2026.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Panama high for officials working for criminal interests. For residents, public contracts and protection from the law have been on offer to the corridor's biggest users, and Panamanians paid for the public works on which the bribes were earned.

Philippines.d:
In the Philippines, the groups that reach into government are the ones that can deliver votes or cash at election time: churches, illegal gambling operators and the businesses that live off public contracts. Iglesia ni Cristo, a Philippine church of about 2.6 million members, tells its members to vote as a bloc for the candidates it chooses, which can decide close Senate races; in return its leaders receive government posts, and the church puts its members on the streets to defend officials from its own ranks when they face charges.

Gambling money has bought protection at every level of office. Operators of jueteng, an illegal numbers game run across the country, were accused of paying President Joseph Estrada 5 million pesos a month, an accusation that led to his impeachment trial and fall in 2001. From 2016 the government licensed Chinese-run online gambling firms serving players in China, which Senate hearings tied to fraud, trafficking and the torture of workers; the firms secured local protection by placing allies in office, most clearly Alice Guo, elected mayor of Bamban in 2022 while such a hub ran in her town, later found by a court to be a Chinese citizen and sentenced to life for trafficking. Congress banned the industry in 2025.

Public money is reached the same way: lawmakers' development funds were routed to fake foundations that ran no projects, with losses put at about 10 billion pesos. The Global Organized Crime Index scores the Philippines high for officials working for criminal interests. For Filipinos this has meant public money meant for their towns going to connected firms, a president accused of taking gambling bosses' money, and towns run by officials whose loyalty was to a gambling compound.

Romania.d:
In Romania, the documented reach into the state has come from organised movements and foreign states trying to place their people in power, and from private lodges whose membership officials do not declare.

The most serious case is recent. In 2024 Romania's Constitutional Court annulled the presidential election after declassified intelligence documents said the first-round winner, Călin Georgescu, had risen through a campaign funded and coordinated by a foreign state, which the authorities identified as Russia; he was barred from the rerun and later charged with plotting a coup. Romania has seen a movement installed inside the state before: in 1940 the fascist Iron Guard was given the Interior Ministry, the Bucharest police and every county prefecture, and used them for killings until it was expelled after a failed coup.

Freemasonry, a fraternity whose members meet privately in lodges and swear mutual support, is lawful in Romania, and officials are required to list such memberships in their declarations of interests. A 2019 magazine report, based on unnamed Masonic sources, said the interim interior minister and the head of the Gendarmerie, the militarised police, belonged to lodges without declaring it; the claim rests on that one outlet.

For Romanians, this means a presidential vote had to be rerun because a foreign state was found to have backed a candidate, and they cannot check whether the people in charge of their police owe loyalty to a private society. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Romania in the middle range both for officials working for criminal interests and for the strength of its courts and watchdogs.

San Marino.d:
In San Marino, the documented reach into government comes from builders and bankers who paid politicians for the permits and licences they needed. In a state of about 34,000 people, a small number of politicians decide who may build and who may open a bank, and the courts have found that those decisions were bought.

In the case known as Conto Mazzini, named after an account held under the name 'Giuseppe Mazzini' at a Sammarinese bank, prosecutors showed that construction and banking entrepreneurs paid politicians, including former government ministers, with cash drawn from that account. About 200 million euros were seized, and an appeal court upheld most convictions in 2022.

For residents, it meant building permits and banking licences went to those who paid, while builders and bankers who did not pay competed against firms that had bought their approvals, and the buildings and banks approved that way are still part of daily life. It also shows the courts reaching former ministers.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores San Marino in the middle range both for officials working for criminal or outside interests and for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs.

Serbia.d:
In Serbia the reach into the state comes mostly from Belgrade's organised crime groups, and they work through the security services rather than around them. Gangs with a share of the Balkan heroin, cocaine and cannabis trade have recruited or merged with police and intelligence units, which gives them state identity cards, entry to protected buildings and warning of investigations. The clearest case came in 2003, when a commander of the interior ministry's special operations unit, which had fused with the Zemun clan, shot dead the elected prime minister, Zoran Đinđić. Since then prosecutors have charged a gang that carried state security identification and a businessman close to the ruling party whose cannabis farm, they say, was guarded by police and intelligence officers; both trials are still open.

The intelligence service has also been tied to Russia. In 2023 the US sanctioned the head of the Security Intelligence Agency (BIA) saying he helped Russia's activities in the region and supported a drug-trafficking network and illegal arms shipments; he resigned under Western pressure and became deputy prime minister the next year. The habit of armed insiders running the state from a private organisation is older: around the First World War, secret societies of army officers decided much of Serbian politics.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 8 out of 10, near the top of Europe, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 4.9. For people in Serbia that means the units meant to protect them have been used by gangs, once against the government they had voted for, and the agency that guards the country's secrets has been run by a man a foreign government accuses of helping Russia and drug traffickers.

Slovakia.d:
In Slovakia businessmen have reached into the police, the courts and the prime minister's office, and the public has mostly learned of it from journalists and leaked recordings before any court acted. A leaked secret-service wiretap file published in 2011 reportedly recorded executives of one of the country's largest investment groups discussing kickbacks on privatisations with ministers; the group called it fiction and no one was convicted, but the protests it set off shaped the next election. Businessmen from Calabria with suspected ties to the 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, set up farm companies in eastern Slovakia, where EU subsidies are paid, and one co-founded a company with the prime minister's chief adviser.

The clearest picture of how far it went came after journalist Ján Kuciak, who was finishing that story, and his fiancée were shot dead in 2018. Prime Minister Robert Fico resigned after mass protests, and messages on the phone of the businessman later charged with ordering the murder showed judges and a deputy justice minister working for him; in 2020 police detained 13 judges, among them the acting head of the Supreme Court, and several confessed. The same year prosecutors charged a former police president and the former heads of the national crime agency's top units with belonging to another businessman's criminal group and passing investigation details to people close to the ruling party; that trial continues.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 7 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 4.9. For Slovaks this has meant police chiefs who may have worked for a businessman rather than for them, court rulings that may have been bought, and a reporter killed for exposing these links before the state did.

South Africa.d:
South Africa's state has been run from inside by private networks twice in living memory, first a secret society and then a business family with foreign firms alongside it. Every prime minister and state president from 1948 to 1994 belonged to the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret all-male society that placed its members in top posts; by the late 1970s it held almost every cabinet seat as well as the heads of the army and the intelligence service.

After apartheid the reach came through money. Foreign arms makers paid large commissions to win the 1999 arms deal, and under Jacob Zuma's presidency the Zondo Commission, a judicial inquiry, found that ministers and the heads of Eskom, the state power company, and Transnet, the state rail and ports company, acted corruptly for the Gupta brothers, Indian-born businessmen who offered cabinet posts to officials willing to cooperate. Several of the world's largest consulting and engineering firms have admitted bribing officials at those companies.

Today the reach runs through the police, the prisons and local councils. Crime bosses have bought officers up to the national commissioner, who in 2010 was convicted of taking a trafficker's money while also heading Interpol. In Cape Town, gang leaders have paid a police brigadier to put his officers to work for them, got gun licences through staff of the police firearm registry, and bought weapons from police stores. Staff of a privately run state prison have been paid to help an inmate fake his death and escape.

For South Africans, the bribes paid to win power and rail contracts came out of the companies that supply their electricity and move their goods, and people who report gang crime cannot be sure whether the officer taking the statement, or the clerk issuing a gun licence, works for the gang.

St. Kitts and Nevis.d:
Nothing is documented yet for St Kitts and Nevis, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows an outside government, company, crime group or lodge paying Kittitian officials or placing people in office.

The Global Organized Crime Index, which scores every country on how far its officials work for criminal or outside interests, places St Kitts and Nevis near the middle of its scale, at 5 out of 10. It gives about 5.4 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. That describes officials under some pressure, with checks on them that are neither strong nor absent.

For people living there, this means no named official or company can be shown to be acting for an outside party. If outside money did reach in, it would most likely show up in who funds politicians, who wins public contracts and how licences are granted, and residents are best protected when those records are public.

Suriname.d:
In Suriname the cocaine trade did not need to buy officials from outside the government: for years it reached the presidency and the security services through the country's own leaders. Suriname lies on the Atlantic coast between Guyana and French Guiana, and the US Treasury says semi-submersible boats carry cocaine across the ocean from its ports and Guyana's.

Desi Bouterse, the former military ruler, was convicted in absentia in the Netherlands in 1999 of smuggling more than 450 kilograms of cocaine, never served the sentence because there was no extradition treaty, and was then elected president twice. While he held office his son Dino ran the country's counter-terrorism unit and used it to traffic cocaine; US agents arrested him in Panama, and he pleaded guilty in New York, including to offering a base in Suriname to people he believed were from Hezbollah, the Lebanese armed group.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 8.5 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 3.2. For the Surinamese, this meant that a counter-terrorism unit paid for by their taxes was used for drug trafficking, and that a court verdict against the man they twice elected president was never enforced.

Taiwan.d:
Taiwan faces the most sustained effort on the map to reach into a democracy from outside, by China through what it calls united front work: the Chinese Communist Party's system for winning over or recruiting people abroad. Money from Chinese provinces and city offices has funded small parties and local council candidates, paid for trips to China for elected village chiefs, where Chinese officials urged them how to vote. Chinese intelligence has placed people inside Taiwan's own security system for decades: since 2009 investigators have found its agents in the presidential office, the military intelligence bureau and the army's senior ranks, where a major general was jailed for life, and retired officers have been charged with recruiting serving ones.

Organised crime is the other channel, and it is older. In the 'black gold' years of the 1990s gangsters won public office, and a self-described gang leader co-chaired the legislature's committee overseeing the justice system. Today the Chinese Unification Promotion Party, which campaigns for union with China, was founded by a former leader of the Bamboo Union gang, and legislators alleged that Chinese official money reached it; the government has asked the Constitutional Court to dissolve it.

Taiwan's Anti-Infiltration Act, passed at the end of 2019, which bars taking money or instructions from China for political activity, is the basis for most recent cases, and many convictions can still be appealed. The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 4 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at 8. For Taiwanese voters this means a local candidate or village chief may have been paid or hosted by the government that claims their country, and the officers and aides meant to defend them against that government have, in case after case, been working for it.

Timor-Leste.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Timor-Leste, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows a foreign state, company, crime group or lodge paying officials or placing people inside its government.

Timor-Leste depends on oil and gas from the Timor Sea to fund its budget, and that kind of single, valuable source of public money is where outside interests often seek influence. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 4.5 out of 10 and the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs at about 3.9. That describes moderate pressure on officials with weak checks on them.

For people living there, this means no named official or company can be shown to be acting for an outside party. If a case exists, it would most likely surface through oil and gas deals, public contracts and policing, and those are the records residents would need to see.

Tunisia.d:
Little is documented for Tunisia, and the one case on record is disputed. Prosecutors accuse Ennahda, the Islamist party that led the government after 2011, of running a 'secret apparatus' that placed people inside state institutions, spied, and was involved in the 2013 assassinations of two leftist politicians. In June 2026 a Tunis court sentenced party leader Rached Ghannouchi to life and gave many others long terms; Ennahda calls the charges political, and rights groups called the trial part of a crackdown on opponents, so the court's finding cannot be taken as settled proof.

No case found so far shows a foreign state, company or crime group paying Tunisian officials. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 6.5 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at 4.3, which describes officials under real pressure and weak checks on them.

For people living there, if outside interests are paying or placing officials, it is most likely to show up in public contracts, customs and policing, and residents would pay through lost public revenue and weaker protection. The one infiltration charge that has reached court was brought by a government against its main opposition party, so Tunisians cannot easily tell a real network inside the state from an accusation used against rivals.

Uganda.d:
In Uganda outside influence reaches the state through foreign religious networks shaping its laws and through companies and brokers paying the men at the top for oil, arms and infrastructure deals.

The Fellowship, a US network that organises prayer breakfasts for politicians around the world, has a Ugandan chapter chaired by David Bahati, who first floated his 2009 bill proposing the death penalty for homosexuality at a Uganda prayer breakfast and has been a government minister since 2021. When Uganda passed the Anti-Homosexuality Act in 2023, a Ugandan activist named the president of an Arizona-based Christian lobbying group as one of those who had lobbied for it.

Money reaches the same level. A US jury convicted an agent of CEFC China Energy, a Chinese conglomerate, of arranging $500,000 for Uganda's foreign minister and urging a cash 'campaign donation' for President Yoweri Museveni so that both would steer business to the firm. The pattern is older: a judicial commission found that the president's brother took $800,000 from an arms broker over the purchase of helicopter gunships in poor condition, and MPs in 2011 tabled documents alleging an oil company paid the prime minister and two ministers for its concessions, which the company called defamatory and which were never tested in court. The ministers stayed in office and oversaw new oil contracts.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests here at 8 out of 10 and courts, police and watchdogs at 3.7. For gay Ugandans, the effect is a law that can send them to prison for life, backed by lobbyists from abroad. For everyone else, deals over the country's oil and its army's equipment have been shaped by payments that came to light only in commissions without consequences or in foreign courts.

United States.d:
In the United States the most common way outside interests get inside government is legal and open: they write the laws and staff the offices. Industry-funded groups led by the American Legislative Exchange Council, where companies and state legislators draft 'model bills' together, produced at least 10,000 bills introduced in state legislatures between 2010 and 2018, of which more than 2,100 became law. Think tanks and lawyers' networks staff whole administrations and the federal appeals courts, and executives from Wall Street banks and from coal, oil, drug and weapons companies have run the agencies that regulate or buy from their former employers.

Where the influence turns into bribery, it is often a utility or contractor buying a lawmaker; in Ohio, FirstEnergy paid about $60 million to a group around the House Speaker for a law rescuing its nuclear plants. Foreign governments work the same ground. Intelligence services have placed or recruited people inside the State Department, the CIA, the FBI and the armed forces since the Second World War, most recently China's, and North Korea has placed hundreds of its IT workers in remote jobs at US companies under stolen identities, earning money for its weapons programmes. Gulf and Caspian states hide the source of money they send to politicians: Azerbaijan's state oil company secretly paid for members of Congress to visit Baku, and in 2026 a company backed by the UAE's national security adviser was reported to have secretly bought nearly half of the Trump family's crypto business.

For Americans, the cost shows up in bills and rules: Ohio households pay electricity prices set by a law that was bought, many state laws were drafted by the industries they regulate, and voters cannot always tell which foreign government has paid the people they elect.

Vatican City.d:
The Vatican is both the centre of the Catholic Church and a sovereign state, with its own bank, the Institute for the Works of Religion (IOR), and its own courts that answer to the Pope. Outsiders have reached it in two ways: financiers tied to organised crime and secret lodges who were given control of its money, and Cold War intelligence services that placed informants among the clergy around the Pope.

The money route opened in 1969, when the Holy See made Michele Sindona, a Sicilian banker who laundered heroin money for Mafia families, its financial adviser, and large sums moved from his banks through the Vatican to Swiss accounts. Sindona belonged to P2, a secret Masonic lodge that had enrolled Italian intelligence chiefs and politicians, as did the chairman of Banco Ambrosiano, the Milan bank whose collapse in 1982 still shapes how the Vatican is seen. The IOR was Ambrosiano's main shareholder and was tied to the offshore companies that held the missing money; it paid creditors $224 million while denying liability, and when Milan magistrates sought to arrest its president in 1987, Italy's top court ruled that the Lateran Treaty shielded him, so he was never tried.

On the intelligence side, communist Poland's secret police had an informant among the priests who looked after Polish pilgrims close to John Paul II during the 1980s.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7 out of 10. For Catholics who give money to the Church, and for savers at the banks it deals with, this means losses caused through the IOR can fall outside the reach of ordinary courts, and any case against Vatican officials is heard by judges the Pope appoints.

Zambia.d:
Zambia's 1996 constitution declares it a Christian nation, and the pattern recorded here is organised religion moving into the machinery of government. Pentecostal and evangelical church networks, some of them founded abroad, are active in Zambian public life, and under President Edgar Lungu the state gave them a ministry of their own. In 2016 Lungu turned a religious-affairs desk into a full Ministry of National Guidance and Religious Affairs and appointed a cleric, Rev. Godfridah Sumaili, as a nominated MP so she could run it; she held the post for five years. After the 2021 election President Hakainde Hichilema folded the ministry into a department of the Vice-President's office.

The Global Organized Crime Index places Zambia in its Moderate band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 6.5 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at 4.7. No case is documented of a foreign state or company placing people inside the Zambian government.

For Zambians, the effect of the religious ministry was that one faith had a minister in the cabinet and a budget line to promote its values, while Zambians of other faiths, or none, had no equivalent voice in government. The ministry was created by the president, not through a public vote, and was dissolved the same way, so the place of religion in the state depends on who holds the presidency.

Andorra.d:
Andorra is a small mountain state between France and Spain whose economy has long relied on private banking for foreign clients. That makes its banks the obvious place for outside money to try to get in, and the documented pattern here is crime-group money handled by bank insiders rather than by politicians.

The case on the map is Banca Privada d'Andorra, whose senior managers, the US Treasury found in 2015, knowingly moved money for professional launderers working for transnational criminal organisations. Andorra took the bank over the next day and wound it up within a week. The US later withdrew its finding, but an Andorran court sentenced eighteen of the bank's executives in 2025; they are appealing, and shareholders argue the bank was closed on an administrative finding never tested in court.

Outside banking there is little on record. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Andorra 1 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests, the lowest possible score, and 8 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, the cost of the bank case fell on its ordinary clients, who had to prove their money was legitimate before they could get it back, some waiting years, while the country's standing as a banking centre, which much of its income depends on, was put in question.

Armenia.d:
Armenia's documented case of an outside power reaching inside the state comes from its neighbour and enemy, Azerbaijan. After the 2020 war in which Azerbaijan retook much of the territory around Nagorno-Karabakh, Armenia's National Security Service said in 2022 that Azerbaijani intelligence had recruited serving Armenian officers with access to state secrets. The method was personal: operatives posed as Armenian women on social media, built close relationships with officers and then offered money for information. The service said dozens of servicemen were involved and detained nineteen people, accused of passing on troop positions, equipment, the names of unit commanders and the layout of defences.

Outside the armed forces, no case of a foreign government, company, crime group or secret society placing people or money inside Armenia's ministries or companies remains on this map. The Global Organized Crime Index gives Armenia 3.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests, low by world standards, and about 5.6 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, around the middle of the range.

For Armenians, this means the documented danger has been inside the army, where officers selling the positions of their own units put the lives of soldiers and border villages at risk while the conflict was still live. Elsewhere the scores suggest institutions that work moderately well, and the places to watch for outside reach are who wins public contracts, who owns the companies running essential services and who funds political campaigns.

Bahamas.d:
The Bahamas lie on the sea and air routes between South America and Florida, and since the cocaine boom of the late 1970s traffickers moving drugs through the islands have paid the officials who police them. In the early 1980s Colombian smugglers used the Exumas as a base and paid ministers and police to let them through. A Royal Commission of Inquiry reported in 1984 wide corruption in the cabinet and the police; it found that Prime Minister Lynden Pindling had spent eight times his reported income and had received at least $57.3 million in cash, and while it did not find him guilty, five ministers resigned or were dismissed.

The pattern has returned. A US indictment filed in November 2024 says that since at least 2021 two high-ranking officers of the Royal Bahamas Police Force and a Bahamian military official helped cocaine arriving on charter flights from Colombia and Venezuela pass through Bahamian airports and onto boats for Florida, for bribes of $10,000 to $2 million, and that one officer demanded $2 million on behalf of an unnamed senior politician. The police commissioner, who was not accused, resigned the following week.

The Bahamas is also an offshore financial centre, where foreign banks and companies register to hold money. The Global Organized Crime Index gives it 3 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 5.6 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For Bahamians, this means that forty years apart, the officers responsible for guarding the islands' airports and coasts have been accused of selling that protection to traffickers, the case was brought by a foreign court rather than their own, and the politician named as wanting a share has not been identified to them.

Belarus.d:
No case of an outside party placing people or money inside Belarus's government or companies remains on this map after checking, so the picture here rests on how the country is rated rather than on documented incidents.

Belarus has been ruled by Alexander Lukashenko since 1994, and power is concentrated around the presidency and the security services. The Global Organized Crime Index, which scores every country on how far its officials work for criminal or outside interests, gives Belarus 9 out of 10 on that measure, among the highest in Europe. It gives about 3.1 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, which is among the lowest. Taken together, those scores describe a state in which officials are judged to act widely for interests other than the public's and in which no independent body is able to check them.

For people living in Belarus, this means that if an outside government, company or criminal group did get people inside a ministry or state firm, there would be no free press, independent court or opposition party able to expose it. The absence of a documented case here reflects how little can be investigated in the country as much as anything else, and residents have no independent channel to raise it themselves.

Bhutan.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Bhutan, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No foreign intelligence service, company, crime group, church or lodge has a documented presence in its government or companies, and none is listed as likely to be present.

Bhutan is a small Himalayan kingdom between India and China, which limits foreign investment and tourism, and it became a parliamentary democracy only in 2008. The Global Organized Crime Index, which scores every country on how far its officials work for criminal or outside interests, gives Bhutan 3 out of 10 on that measure, low by world standards, and about 4.7 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. The estimate rests on that index alone.

For people living there, this means no known cost from outside groups placing people in Bhutan's offices or firms, and the index rates this as a smaller problem than in most of the world. The middling resilience score means that if outside influence did arrive, through its large neighbours or through investment, the institutions that would have to catch it are not rated as especially strong. A documented case found later would replace this estimate.

Brazil.d:
Brazil has more documented cases of outsiders inside its institutions than almost any other country, and they come from three directions: organised crime, churches and companies.

Crime groups have bought their way into the police, courts and legislatures for decades: in Rio the bosses of the jogo do bicho, an illegal lottery, kept ledgers in the 1990s that implicated police, judges and congressmen. The PCC, a São Paulo prison gang that now runs much of the drug trade, has paid police to shield its members and, prosecutors say, owned city bus companies on public contracts, investment funds and more than a thousand petrol stations. Rio's militias, armed groups that began as off-duty police running protection rackets, and the Comando Vermelho drug faction have allies or alleged representatives in the state assembly and Congress.

Churches reach in through seats and appointments. Pastors of the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God founded the Republicanos party, the cross-party evangelical caucus lists 213 of the 513 federal deputies, and it has used seat deals to take committees such as the Chamber's human rights committee. In 2020 a former missionary from a US group known for converting isolated tribes was briefly put in charge of the federal unit that protects them, until a court annulled it. Companies reach in too: the farm caucus's agenda is drafted by an agribusiness-funded institute, and contractors and commodity traders have paid officials of the state oil company Petrobras.

For people living there, this means bus fares and petrol can feed a crime group, residents of militia areas pay protection to groups tied to their own representatives, the protection of isolated indigenous peoples was briefly put in a missionary's hands, and laws on pesticides, land and religion are often written by those with a direct stake in them.

Burundi.d:
In Burundi the documented reach comes from a foreign tobacco company working on the officials who write tobacco law. Leaked records from British American Tobacco (BAT), one of the world's largest cigarette makers, show payments to Burundian officials who handled tobacco control, part of a run of such payments in several East and Central African countries that researchers read as aimed at blocking laws modelled on the WHO tobacco treaty, which commits governments to restrict tobacco sales and marketing. A British fraud inquiry closed without charges and BAT denies the allegations, so these remain reports rather than findings.

If the payments worked as the records suggest, Burundians live under weaker tobacco rules than the treaty asks for: more advertising, cheaper and easier access, fewer health warnings, and over time more illness from smoking. No Burundian inquiry is recorded, so residents do not know which officials were paid or what they did in return.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Burundi among the countries where officials most often work for criminal interests, and its courts, police and watchdogs among the weakest. On those terms, an official who takes money from a foreign company is unlikely to be investigated at home, which is why the only account of these payments came from a British broadcaster and a British university.

Canada.d:
Most of what reaches inside Canadian government comes from foreign states, and it has done so since the Second World War.
