In 1945 a Soviet cipher clerk in Ottawa defected with documents showing a military-intelligence ring inside Canadian institutions that reached into Parliament itself. Russian military intelligence has since bought secrets from a navy analyst with access to the intelligence shared by the 'Five Eyes' countries, and Canada's intelligence service has said a scientist at its highest-security pathogen laboratory worked to benefit China's government.

Today China and India are the most active, working through diaspora communities and proxies. Canada's public inquiry into foreign interference found intelligence that India's proxy agents may have given illicit money to politicians to elect pro-India candidates, and a parliamentary intelligence committee reported that some MPs and senators had knowingly or half-knowingly helped foreign states, including by taking disguised money from foreign missions. The inquiry found no traitors in Parliament, but for voters it means a candidate on the ballot may have had a foreign government's help getting there.

Organised crime and companies reach in where public money changes hands. In Quebec, construction firms rigged bids for city public works and paid both the Mafia and the parties that ran city hall; mayors of Montreal and Laval fell over it. At the busiest land crossings into the United States, border officers have been convicted of waving smugglers through. Earlier, membership did the work: for the first half of the 20th century every mayor of Toronto belonged to the Orange Order, a Protestant fraternity. Canada's courts, police and watchdogs rank among the strongest measured by the Global Organized Crime Index, which is why most of this came to light through Canada's own inquiries.

China.d:
In China the reaching-in runs in two directions. The Communist Party places its own bodies inside companies, foreign ones included: the law requires any firm with three or more party members to set up a party organisation, nearly three-quarters of private companies had one by 2018 by the party's own count, and its United Front departments, which manage relations with groups outside the party, are told to 'guide' private firms.

In the other direction, businesses buy the officials who are meant to regulate them, and the record reaches the top: convictions for taking money from companies and smugglers have reached a Politburo member, the railway minister, a vice-minister of public security and the officials overseeing medicines and finance. The clearest case is the head of the national drug regulator, who approved more than 150,000 medicines over eight years, most from the firms that paid him, before he was executed in 2007. Foreign firms use the same routes, hiring officials' relatives to win business or, in one case, placing a Coca-Cola-founded science group inside the national disease control agency, where it steered obesity policy away from sugary drinks.

Lower down, gangs have bought deputy police chiefs and village party secretaries who shielded drug labs. The party answers with mass arrests and executions run by its own discipline bodies rather than independent courts. For people in China, this means medicines, trains and banks overseen by officials who may have been paid by the firms involved, and health advice shaped by food makers' money. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Chinese officials high for working with criminal interests.

Congo, Rep..d:
The Republic of Congo's state runs on oil, and the documented reach-in comes through the circle around President Denis Sassou-Nguesso, who has ruled for most of the period since 1979. Foreign oil traders have obtained the national oil company's crude by dealing with intermediaries close to his family. The clearest case is Gunvor, a Geneva oil trader, which between 2010 and 2012 lent the national oil company $750 million to be repaid in oil while paying nearly $30 million in commissions to two fixers close to the president's family; according to the case record the money was meant for his relatives, and a Swiss court convicted Gunvor in 2019.

The same circle is tied together by Freemasonry, a fraternal society whose members meet privately in lodges, swear oaths of mutual support and are often drawn from political and business elites. Press reports say Sassou-Nguesso is Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Congo-Brazzaville, which is linked to a French Masonic body, and that he sponsored the initiation of the Central African Republic's president. Lodge membership is lawful, and the reporting does not show any decision taken for a lodge, but it gives the president, his officials and foreign contacts a setting that voters, journalists and courts cannot see into.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates the country among those where officials most often work for criminal interests, with weak courts, police and watchdogs. For Congolese, this means oil that belongs to the state has been sold on terms set by foreign traders and the president's relatives, the case came to light in a Swiss court rather than their own, and little inside the country would check such ties.

Cuba.d:
Cuba is a one-party state whose own intelligence and security services control most of public life, and both documented cases of outside reach involve organised crime getting to the people at the top.

Before the 1959 revolution the American Mafia, through its financier Meyer Lansky, had an arrangement with Fulgencio Batista: Lansky's associates ran Havana's casinos and racetracks and Batista took kickbacks. After his 1952 coup Batista made Lansky an adviser on gambling reform, and the law was changed to let any hotel worth $1 million host a casino. The arrangement ended with the revolution, when the casinos were looted and then nationalised.

The second case ran through the revolutionary state itself. In 1989 General Arnaldo Ochoa, and an Interior Ministry colonel who ran the state's hard-currency businesses were convicted of letting the Medellín cartel move cocaine to Florida through Cuban waters and airspace, and both were executed by firing squad. It showed that a Colombian cartel could reach senior officers inside a state that tightly controls its own territory, and that they used state channels to help it. The trial was held by military courts that Cubans have no independent way to check, so the public record of how far the network reached is the one the government chose to give.

For Cubans, both episodes meant that decisions about their country, from who ran the hotels to what crossed their coastline, were sold by people in power to criminal outsiders. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Cuba's officials as relatively unlikely to work for criminal interests, with institutions of middling strength. No more recent case on the map shows outsiders inside the Cuban government, though the closed nature of the state means little would be reported if one did.

Djibouti.d:
Djibouti's documented case is a foreign company paying the state's own officials for a state contract. Ericsson, the Swedish telecoms equipment maker, admitted paying about €2.1 million to high-ranking Djibouti officials to win a contract with Djibouti Telecom, the state-owned telephone company, as part of a US settlement covering bribery in several countries. The payment went to the people inside the state who decide which foreign supplier builds a national network, so the contract was settled by the bribe rather than by price or quality.

For Djiboutians, the telephone network they pay for was built under a contract won by bribing their officials, and they learned of it from a US settlement rather than from any process at home. The officials who took the money were not named in public, and no case against them in Djibouti is recorded.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Djibouti in the middle range for officials working for criminal interests, with weak courts, police and watchdogs. The Ericsson payments are the only case on record.

Egypt.d:
In Egypt the outside forces that have reached the top of the state have mostly come through the army and through creditors. In 1952 the Free Officers, a secret network of junior officers recruited inside the army, seized power and ended the monarchy, and the body that succeeded their ruling council, the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces, still sits at the top of the Egyptian state. Since then the army has been the place where others try to get in: an armed Islamist group built a cell inside it that killed the president in 1981, and a member of two presidents' inner circles was a source for Israel's foreign intelligence service.

The other outside force that came close to the top is the Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt in 1928 that works to bring its members into power. In 2012 Mohamed Morsi won the presidency as the candidate of the Brotherhood's own party; the army removed him in 2013, most of the movement's leaders were jailed, and membership alone can now bring a prison sentence.

Creditors set the older pattern. After Egypt fell behind on its loans in 1876, its European lenders placed their own commissioners over its finances, and the debt fund they ran lasted until 1940; from 1883 to 1907 a British controller from the banking family that held Egyptian debt, effectively ruled the country. For Egyptians the result is a state run by officers who arrived through a secret network, which treats an organised religious movement as an enemy within, and where people who voted for the Brotherhood saw their president removed by the army. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 8.5 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at 3.75.

Estonia.d:
Estonia is a NATO and EU member on Russia's border, and the most serious documented reach into its state is Russian intelligence recruiting people inside the institutions meant to keep its secrets. Estonia has caught a series of Russian agents in its own defence and security bodies, paid by the SVR, Russia's foreign intelligence service, or the GRU, its military intelligence. The clearest case is Herman Simm, who headed the defence ministry's security department, the office that protected NATO and EU classified material, and passed those secrets to the SVR for thirteen years until his arrest in 2008. A serving army major later spied for the GRU for about a decade, and in 2021 Estonia convicted its first spy for China, a scientist with access to NATO research.

The second route runs through the banks. Because Tallinn's banks sit inside the European Union but next to Russia and the former Soviet states, money from those countries has used them as a gateway into Europe. In the Azerbaijani Laundromat, about $2.9 billion moved in 2012–2014 through shell companies with accounts at Danske Bank's Estonian branch, almost half of it from an account linked to Azerbaijan's ruling family, and part of it reached European politicians who defended Azerbaijan in the Council of Europe, Europe's main human rights body.

For Estonians this means that people trusted to decide who could see state secrets have themselves been working for the neighbouring power those secrets are guarded against, and that their banks were used to pay politicians elsewhere to speak for a foreign ruling family. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Estonian officials acting for criminal interests at 2 out of 10 and its courts and watchdogs above 8, among the strongest in the world, and the spy cases have ended in treason convictions.

Finland.d:
Finland today has one of the cleanest records on the map. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 1.5 out of 10 and the strength of its courts and watchdogs at over 8.4, among the highest in the world, and no current case shows a foreign state, company or criminal group paying Finnish officials.

During the Cold War it was different. The Soviet KGB assigned its officers in Helsinki, working under diplomatic cover at the Soviet embassy, to individual Finnish politicians and officials, so that many of them had a personal Soviet contact known as a 'kotiryssä', or 'home Russian'. The system reached President Urho Kekkonen, and a former Soviet diplomat later said the KGB general who ran it backed a candidate to succeed him. It is tied to what became known as Finlandization, the bending of Finnish policy to Moscow's wishes, and a leading Finnish newspaper reported in 2015 that the practice had almost ended.

What is documented now is the reach of a private elite network. The World Economic Forum, the Swiss foundation behind the annual Davos meeting, picks rising politicians under about 40 for its Young Global Leaders network, which brings them together with business executives over several years. President Alexander Stubb joined in 2009 and lists it on his official CV, and former prime minister Sanna Marin is also listed. Membership is lawful and public, and no finding says the network directed Finnish decisions.

For Finns, this means the foreign power that once had a contact for each senior politician has largely lost that access, and the open question now is whose views leaders hear in private meetings funded by large companies.

Georgia.d:
In Georgia, criminal and armed groups reached inside the state in the years after independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, and Russia has kept trying to recruit people inside its armed forces since. The clearest case of the first is the Mkhedrioni, a militia that helped overthrow the first elected president in 1991–92 and was then made the country's interior forces, and was accused of extortion and drug smuggling until it was outlawed in 1995.

Alongside it worked the 'thieves in law', a criminal fraternity born in Soviet prison camps whose members swear to live by its code and settle disputes for others. Through the 1990s Georgian governments treated them as part of the country's power structure, according to Georgian analysts and former officials. In 2005 Georgia made membership a crime in itself, but the fraternity has not disappeared: in late 2025 and early 2026 police arrested more than 100 people in a nationwide crackdown, while its leaders mostly direct things from abroad or from prison.

Russia's military intelligence, the GRU, has worked from inside Georgia's forces. Two years after the 2008 war between the countries, Georgia arrested air force pilots, a naval radio operator accused of passing secret codes and Russian citizens, accused of telling Russia how ready Georgia's forces were to fight; Russia called it spy mania.

For Georgians this means that for several years armed men accused of extortion were the state's own interior forces, a criminal network once tolerated by government is still active in their communities, and the army defending them against a neighbour that occupies part of their land has had that neighbour's informants in its ranks. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 4 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at 5.

Grenada.d:
Grenada has given ambassador titles to foreign businessmen, and the documented allegations here come from foreign investors dealing directly with the prime minister's office. In 2019 an Al Jazeera investigation reported that one foreign investor said he had paid about half a million dollars to Prime Minister Keith Mitchell, who said he received only $15,000 to cover travel. A US businessman said a partner had been offered a diplomatic post in return for kickbacks on state projects, which the government denies. No charge has been brought, and the claims rest on the investors' own statements.

For Grenadians, this means public contracts and diplomatic posts can be traded with foreign investors, and only the government's word stands between residents and that trade. If a kickback was asked for, it raised the cost of work done for the public. With no court test, residents are left with conflicting accounts. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 3.5 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at about 5.2, better than most of the region.

Guyana.d:
Guyana produces gold in its interior and has become a route for cocaine moving from South America by air and sea, and the people in both trades pay officials to keep their business moving. According to the US Treasury, the largest gold trading family in the country bribed customs officials to leave more than 10,000 kilograms of gold off customs declarations, paid officials for help in court matters and to win state contracts, and was helped by the top civil servant at the home affairs ministry, who took cash and gifts for contracts, gun permits and passports. The family denies wrongdoing.

Cocaine networks reach the police in the same way. In 2025 the Treasury sanctioned a serving police officer it says arranged safe passage for Mexican and Venezuelan traffickers, along with trafficking bosses and Colombians managing hidden jungle airstrips. None of these cases has been tried, and the US State Department calls corruption in Guyana a significant obstacle to stopping drugs.

Outside interests choosing who governs is older than the drug trade. Before independence the CIA secretly paid opposition parties to remove the elected premier Cheddi Jagan, and kept funding their leader Forbes Burnham, who became the first prime minister of independent Guyana in 1966.

For Guyanese, this means the customs officer, court official or ministry clerk they deal with for a permit or passport may have been paid by a large private business, and duty lost on undeclared gold, more than $50 million by the Treasury's count, was public money. People in the interior live near airstrips used for cocaine, policed by a force that traffickers have reached. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 8 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at about 4.3.

Iceland.d:
Iceland's economy has long rested on fishing, and the documented case of outside interests inside its government is the revolving door between the largest fishing companies and the ministry that regulates them. Kristján Þór Júlíusson, a former board chairman of Samherji, one of Iceland's biggest fishing firms, served as Minister of Fisheries and Agriculture from 2017 to 2021. In 2019 leaked documents showed Samherji paying bribes in Namibia for fishing quotas, and a whistleblower said that years earlier Samherji's chief had introduced Kristján, then health minister, to Namibians later accused of taking those bribes as 'his man' in government. Kristján said he had had no involvement with the company for about 19 years, and refused to resign when about 4,000 people protested in Reykjavík.

No case shows a foreign government or crime group placing people or money inside the state. The Global Organized Crime Index puts Iceland among the lowest anywhere for officials working for criminal interests and near the top for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. The Mont Pelerin Society, a private club of free-market economists and politicians, has members in the country, but membership is lawful and nothing on record shows it steering a decision.

For Icelanders, this means they are unlikely to meet an official quietly serving a foreign state or a crime group, but the fish stocks that belong to the nation have been regulated by a minister who came from the industry's leading company, a company later accused of bribing its way into another country's fisheries. Whether that tie shaped his decisions has not been tested by a court.

Iraq.d:
For most of the past century, who governs Iraq has been decided by groups organised outside its elected institutions and often backed from abroad. From the 1930s secret circles of army officers chose and removed governments, and in 1958 one of them, the Free Officers, ended the monarchy. After the 2003 invasion the United States put exiles it had funded for years at the head of the new state.

Iran's reach is now written into the state. Badr, a militia formed in Iran in 1982, held the Interior Ministry, which runs the police, across successive governments, and in 2006 the UN's human rights chief said hundreds of people had been tortured or executed under it. The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), about 67 mostly Shia militias almost all backed by Iran's Revolutionary Guards, were made a branch of the armed forces by a 2016 law, paid from the state budget, and their own chief of staff has said they take orders from Iran's supreme leader. Groups the US lists as terrorist staff numbered PMF brigades and hold seats in parliament, and the PMF's deputy chairman until 2020 was himself an adviser to Iran's Quds Force.

Money flows the same way. A fixer for foreign oil-service firms paid oil ministry officials more than $17 million for contracts after 2003, and in 2021–22 about $2.5 billion was taken from a tax account through fake refunds, with the director of the prime minister's office among those convicted.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Iraq 8.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 3 for its courts and watchdogs. For Iraqis this means their taxes pay militias whose leaders follow a foreign cleric, and oil and tax money can be taken by people working beside the head of government.

Jamaica.d:
In parts of Kingston, Jamaica's political parties and armed gangs have depended on each other for decades. In 'garrison' neighbourhoods, each loyal to one party, a local gang leader known as a 'don' delivers votes and keeps order, and in return receives public contracts and protection from the state. That is how a criminal organisation gets inside government in Jamaica: not by buying a single official, but by becoming part of how a constituency is run. The clearest case is Christopher Coke, leader of the Shower Posse, who ran Tivoli Gardens in the prime minister's own constituency; the government resisted his extradition to the United States for nine months, and the police and army operation that finally took him in 2010 killed at least 69 people.

Foreign companies have reached the parties through money as well. In 2006 the oil trader Trafigura, which held an agreement to lift oil for the Jamaican government, paid $31 million into an account linked to the governing party, which called it a donation and said it was returned; Trafigura called it a commercial payment, and Dutch prosecutors have taken the company to trial over possible bribery of Jamaican officials.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Jamaica 7.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and just over 5 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. For people in garrison neighbourhoods this means the person who controls their streets may be shielded by the party they are expected to vote for, and when the state does move against him, residents are caught in the fighting. For all Jamaicans, it means the parties that run the state have taken money from both gang leaders and a company doing business with the government, and the full account has come from foreign courts.

Kenya.d:
In Kenya, two groups have bought their way into the state: drug traffickers moving heroin through the port of Mombasa, and businessmen who win public money through deals arranged with ministers.

The traffickers have bought protection at every level they needed: police to look away, prosecutors and judges to stall cases, and politicians with a say over the port. The clearest proof came from the traffickers themselves: the Akasha brothers, who ran a Mombasa heroin business, admitted in a US court that they had paid Kenyan judges, prosecutors and police for two years to block their extradition, and none of those officials has been named or charged in Kenya. The suspicion reaches Parliament: Kenya's own security minister and the United States have named sitting MPs, including one who oversaw the Ports Authority as an assistant minister, as trafficking suspects; all denied it, and none has been convicted. A rights group has also accused army units fighting al-Shabaab in Somalia of sharing in a sugar and charcoal smuggling trade with the militants, which the military denies.

The business route works through the Treasury and ministries. In the early 1990s a company given a monopoly on gold exports, Goldenberg, drew public compensation for exports that barely existed, at a cost estimated at more than a tenth of Kenya's annual output, with the finance minister's approval; a decade later phantom firms won security contracts that were never delivered. Inquiries named senior officials and none was convicted.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Kenya 8 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests. For Kenyans this means public money has gone to firms that delivered nothing, and the officials and lawmakers named as protecting traffickers have still not faced a court at home.

Kosovo.d:
In Kosovo, the documented concern is that the state's own founding generation has been accused of running criminal trades from inside government. A 2010 Council of Europe report said a group of former Kosovo Liberation Army commanders, led by the then prime minister Hashim Thaçi, controlled trades including heroin; Thaçi denied it, and while he is now on trial for war crimes, the organised-crime claims have never been tested in court.

The Global Organized Crime Index does not score Kosovo separately; North Macedonia's figures, 6.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and just over 5 for courts and watchdogs, stand in for it here. For people in Kosovo this means the claim that a former prime minister's circle profited from heroin is still unanswered by any court.

Latvia.d:
Latvia has been reached from outside in two ways: Russia's security services working through the parties that speak for the country's large Russian-speaking minority, and private bank owners paying the official who supervised them. Those parties give Moscow a natural route into Latvian and European politics. Leaked emails published in 2024 show Tatjana Ždanoka, who represented Latvia in the European Parliament for twenty years and co-led the Latvian Russian Union party, reporting to officers of the FSB, Russia's main security service, from at least 2004. Latvia's security service has opened a criminal case and the European Parliament penalised her, but she has not been convicted.

Bank owners have reached the top of the regulator. In 2023 a court jailed the former governor of the Bank of Latvia, who also sat on the European Central Bank's governing council, for six years for taking a bribe from a Riga bank's shareholders in return for help with the financial regulator.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Latvia 2.5 out of 10 for officials working for outside interests and above 7.5 for its courts and watchdogs. For people in Latvia, this means one of the people they sent to make European law was, on her own emails, reporting to a foreign intelligence service, and the official meant to keep banks honest with their money was for sale to a bank's owners. Courts and investigators here have caught both, years after the fact.

Libya.d:
Libya is split between a government in Tripoli and the forces of Khalifa Haftar in the east, and on both sides armed groups have taken over the state bodies that are meant to police them. Smuggling networks have their own people in coast guard units, ports and the fuel distribution system, so that the officials who should stop fuel, migrants and drugs leaving the country are the ones moving them. In Zawiya the UN sanctioned the serving coast guard commander in 2018 for fuel smuggling and migrant trafficking. The Sentry, an investigative group, estimates that about $20 billion of subsidised fuel was diverted in 2022–24.

Religious movements and foreign backers reach in alongside the armed groups. The Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement, reached the top of the Tripoli government through its political arm, whose member chaired the High Council of State from 2018 to 2023. Followers of a Saudi cleric whose Salafi teaching demands obedience to rulers, known as Madkhalis, hold strong positions in a Tripoli security force and in units of Haftar's army, and run the eastern mosques authority. Foreign states backing one side have even reached the UN's mediator: in 2015 the UN envoy leading the peace talks was found negotiating a well-paid job with the UAE, which backed one camp, while assuring it he could 'control the process'.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Libya 9.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 2 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. For Libyans this means they pay for a fuel subsidy that is resold abroad, the police and preachers in their area may answer to one movement, and migrants picked up at sea can find themselves in the hands of a coast guard run by the people trafficking them.

Madagascar.d:
Madagascar's documented outside reach comes through elections, from a foreign network that courts several candidates at once. In the 2018 presidential race, political strategists tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, the businessman behind the Russian private military company Wagner, worked with as many as eight candidates, offering cash or promises of money, according to the Russian outlet Proekt and the BBC; the winner denied being Russia's candidate and no evidence showed he took Russian money.

This is the approach Prigozhin's network used across much of Africa: back several contenders, so that whoever wins may owe something. In Madagascar it met a state that the Global Organized Crime Index rates as highly exposed, with officials often serving criminal or outside interests and weak courts, police and watchdogs to check them.

That weakness is why no Malagasy court or official inquiry has set out who took money or what was promised in return. For Malagasy voters it means they chose a president in a race where a foreign network was paying or courting candidates, and they have no official record of which of the people they elected, if any, owe that network anything.

Mali.d:
In Mali, the outside forces that reach into the state are mostly cocaine traffickers crossing the Sahara and the Sahel, the dry belt south of it, together with the armed groups and officials who protect them. South American cocaine moves through the region on its way to Europe. Where the routes cross desert airstrips and border posts, traffickers pay local officials and armed groups to let the cargo through, and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime has found that the traffickers include members of the political elite and armed-group leaders, and that the profits go into gold and property. The clearest single example is the 2009 'Air Cocaine' flight, when a Boeing 727 from Venezuela unloaded at a desert strip in the north and was burned, under protection that investigators traced to local officials and armed groups; no senior figure was ever convicted.

There is also an older report, from the magazine Jeune Afrique in 2012, that the president of the time oversaw Mali's national body of Freemasonry, a fraternal society whose members meet privately. It does not show any decision taken for the lodge.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Mali's courts, police and watchdogs among the weakest in the world and finds officials widely serving criminal interests. For people in Mali this means that traffickers and the officials who shelter them are rarely brought to court, and that drug money pays armed groups fighting in the areas where they live.

Mauritius.d:
Outsiders have reached into Mauritius in two ways on the record: foreign builders paying officials for public contracts, and a foreign financier getting close to the head of state while seeking a licence from the state.

The contract route runs through middlemen. The money passes through agents or consultants, so the official who decides the contract never appears on the company's books. The African Development Bank, which lends for infrastructure, found that a Danish power-plant builder had more likely than not paid members of the Mauritian administration in this way during the tenders for the state electricity company's Saint-Louis power station, and barred it from its projects for nearly two years. That is a lender's decision, not a court verdict, and it names no Mauritian official.

The second case reached the presidency. President Ameenah Gurib-Fakim was vice-chair of a charity run by an Angolan banker, Álvaro Sobrinho, and used its credit card for private spending while he was seeking a banking licence from the Mauritian financial regulator, which she asked to issue it. After a newspaper published her card statements in 2018 she repaid the money and resigned, and the government set up a commission of inquiry into her conduct.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds a moderate level of officials serving outside interests in Mauritius and rates its institutions in the middle range. For Mauritians this means part of the electricity they pay for comes from a station whose builder was found to have paid officials, and their head of state was spending a licence-seeker's money while pressing the regulator on his behalf. No official has been named in the power case, so people do not know whether those involved are still in the public service.

Monaco.d:
The cases that touch Monaco come from the international bodies and wealthy foreign residents who base themselves there. The principality hosts sports federations and some of the world's richest people, and the documented problems arise where their money meets the decisions made in Monaco.

The clearest case is World Athletics, the governing body of track and field, which has its headquarters in Monaco. Its former president, Lamine Diack, was convicted in France of taking money from Russian sports officials to delay doping cases against Russian athletes, so that suspected dopers could compete at the 2012 London Olympics. In the second case, Dmitry Rybolovlev, a Russian billionaire who owns the AS Monaco football club, was suspected of courting Monaco officials, including a former public prosecutor; the case was closed after the courts ruled that the phone messages it rested on had been obtained unlawfully, so no court has decided whether officials were influenced.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds a fairly low level of officials serving outside interests in Monaco. For people there, the athletics case shows a body run from their city selling decisions to a foreign state, at the expense of athletes everywhere who competed clean. The Rybolovlev case leaves residents with no finding either way on whether a wealthy resident could buy favour from their prosecutors.

Mozambique.d:
Mozambique has been reached from outside by foreign lenders and contractors who paid its officials, and by drug traffickers who have worked alongside the ruling party for decades.

The clearest case is the 'hidden debts'. Foreign banks, including Credit Suisse and Russia's VTB, lent about 2 billion dollars to three state companies for fishing and maritime security projects with Privinvest, an Emirati-Lebanese shipbuilder, under state guarantees kept from parliament and the International Monetary Fund. US prosecutors said hundreds of millions went in bribes and kickbacks to bankers and Mozambican officials, the former finance minister was convicted in the United States, and Mozambique's own constitutional council declared the loans void. The arrangement depended on a few officials signing guarantees in the state's name without telling the bodies meant to approve them.

Traffickers have used the country as a heroin route for about thirty years. Research for the Global Initiative against Transnational Organized Crime in 2018 described what its authors called tight integration between traffickers and ruling-party figures, pointing to almost no heroin seizures in all that time, and a businessman designated as a trafficker abroad has remained prominent at home without charge.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials in Mozambique serving criminal interests to one of the highest degrees anywhere. For Mozambicans the hidden loans meant debt their parliament never approved. When the loans came to light in 2016, the IMF and World Bank froze support, and one study estimated that two million people were pushed into poverty.

Nepal.d:
Nepal lies between China and India, and both have long tried to influence which leaders and parties govern in Kathmandu. The documented outside reach into Nepal's politics comes from two directions: a foreign state working through the ruling party, and an Indian crime syndicate working through a member of parliament.

When members of the governing Nepal Communist Party revolted against their own leader, Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli, in 2020, China's ambassador held a series of meetings with Oli, the president and senior party leaders, and Nepali media reported that she urged them to keep the party united. Later that year Beijing sent a delegation from the Chinese Communist Party's International Department, the office that manages its ties with foreign parties, to meet the same leaders. Former ministers and diplomats called this interference; the Chinese embassy said it only wished to see the party united.

Earlier, in the 1990s, an MP who held ministerial posts in two governments was reported to work with D-Company, the Indian crime syndicate of Dawood Ibrahim, and with Pakistan's intelligence agency, in gun-running, drug trafficking and sheltering fugitives; he was shot dead in Kathmandu in 1998 and the reports were never tested in court.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials in Nepal widely serving criminal or outside interests and rates its institutions as weak. For Nepali voters this means a split inside the party they elected was discussed with a foreign ambassador while the public was still learning of it, and that a seat in parliament has been held by someone reported to serve a foreign crime network.

Niger.d:
Niger lies on a Sahel route that the UN drugs office describes as a natural stopover for South American cocaine heading to Europe. Where a trafficking route crosses a thinly policed country, traffickers make use of local officials, whose vehicles and offices are less likely to be searched; the clearest example is a mayor caught in early 2022 with more than 200 kilograms of cocaine in his vehicle, with no outcome recorded since. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Niger high for officials working for criminal interests and low for the strength of its courts and police, so residents have little reason to expect a trial that shows who else was involved.

An older thread runs through the presidency. Press reports have named a former president, like several heads of state in former French West and Central Africa, as a Freemason, a member of a fraternity whose members swear mutual support, though no official finding confirms it.

Oman.d:
The clearest documented reach into Oman's state came from Britain, and its effect is still felt: the sultan whom British officers helped put in power in 1970, Qaboos, ruled for half a century. At the time Oman's armed forces were under de facto British command. On 23 July 1970 the British commander briefed the Omani officers who carried out a palace coup in Salalah that removed Sultan Said bin Taimur and installed his son, who was then under house arrest and had been sent the plan on cassette tapes by British officials. Accounts based on British records say MI6, the Foreign Office and the Ministry of Defence planned it and the prime minister approved it; Britain denied involvement for forty years, saying its officers had acted on their own.

Nothing documented since then shows a foreign state, company, crime group or secret society with people or money inside Omani offices or firms. The Global Organized Crime Index places Oman in its moderate band, scoring it in the middle range both for officials working for criminal or outside interests and for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. Read together, those scores suggest that outside interests have some room to reach officials and that the bodies which would expose them are of middling strength.

For Omanis, this means the ruling line they have lived under for most of the past five decades began with a decision made largely in London, by officers commanding their own army. Today they cannot see whether contracts go to favoured firms or whether crimes linked to officials go unpunished; published court records, audits and lists of who owns the companies doing business with the state would be the first places such a pattern would show.

Papua New Guinea.d:
In Papua New Guinea, outsiders have reached officials through contracts paid for by Australia and through police who let drug flights land.

Australia's offshore asylum centre on Manus Island brought large contracts paid in Australian dollars into a country where officials decide on visas, land and permits, and a former contractor executive has alleged that some of that money reached a businessman close to senior officials, an allegation that is denied and untested. Drug traffickers using PNG as a route to Australia have relied on police help: after a plane carrying 548 kilograms of cocaine crashed near Port Moresby in 2020, the police commissioner said there are criminals in uniform in the constabulary, yet the officers alleged to have helped were not charged.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores PNG among the highest in the world for officials working for criminal interests and low for the strength of its courts and police, so residents have little reason to trust the force to police itself.

Poland.d:
In Poland, the clearest case of an outside body placing its people inside the state comes from a domestic religious-legal movement rather than a foreign power. Ordo Iuris, a conservative Catholic legal institute that drafts laws and campaigns to change policy, saw its co-founder, Aleksander Stępkowski, made deputy foreign minister by the Law and Justice government in 2015 and then appointed to the Supreme Court with no prior experience as a judge, through an appointments council whose overhaul was contested, before he was made acting head of the court in 2020.

For Poles, this meant that the court of final appeal was led for a time by the founder of an organisation that writes the laws it then wants upheld, and that the near-total abortion ban put before parliament in 2016 came from the same institute.

The foreign reach documented in Poland is aimed at the systems that hold state secrets and public data, and it comes from Russia's camp and from China. Prosecutors say Chinese intelligence worked through a senior Huawei employee and a former officer of Poland's own security service to win contracts giving insight into state and local government data systems; both deny it, and the trial has been held behind closed doors. In 2024 a Warsaw judge who sat in the department ruling on whether military and intelligence officers could see classified information fled to Belarus, Russia's close ally, and asked for asylum there; Polish officials say he worked for Russia, which has not been proven. Poles cannot easily follow what either case shows about who had access to their state's secrets and records.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Poland in the middle range for officials working for criminal interests.

Russia.d:
In Russia the reach has run in two directions since the Soviet Union ended. In the 1990s, private money and crime groups reached into a weak state; since then, the state's own security services have reached into business, sport and local government.

In 1995 a group of bankers lent money to Boris Yeltsin's cash-short government in return for shares in the country's largest state companies, in rigged auctions run by insiders, and some then paid for his 1996 re-election and took government posts: the banker who proposed the scheme became first deputy prime minister, and another tycoon joined the Security Council. Crime groups took over enterprises in the same years, including St Petersburg's main fuel company and the Lada carmaker's sales network.

Today the FSB, Russia's security service, and the officials around the president use arrests, decrees and friendly banks to move companies into the hands of people they trust. The same services reach into bodies meant to be independent: reports for the World Anti-Doping Agency found that the sports ministry and the FSB ran a state system through the Moscow testing laboratory that hid doped athletes, protecting more than 1,000 Russian competitors between 2011 and 2015. In the regions, criminal gangs have operated for years under the protection of local police and officials.

For Russians, the largest companies they work for were handed out in the 1990s to the people who financed the president, and a business can now be lost through an arrest rather than a court case the owner could win. The Global Organized Crime Index gives Russia one of the highest scores in the world for officials working for criminal interests and low marks for its courts and watchdogs.

Sao Tome and Principe.d:
São Tomé and Príncipe is a small island state in the Gulf of Guinea that shares an offshore oil zone with Nigeria, and its one recorded case of outsiders reaching in comes from the race for those oil rights. ERHC, a small Houston oil company controlled from 2001 by a Nigerian businessman who was a major donor to Nigeria's ruling party, obtained unusually favourable terms, including the right to pick the best blocks without the usual fee. In 2005 São Tomé's attorney general reported that bidding in the shared zone showed serious procedural deficiencies and political manipulation and that ERHC may have made improper payments to government officials. The FBI raided ERHC's Houston offices in 2006, the company denied wrongdoing, and no charges were reported.

The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic relations with many states, is also present; that is lawful and not evidence of wrongdoing. The Global Organized Crime Index scores the country low for officials working for criminal or outside interests, though its courts, police and watchdogs are also rated below the middle of the scale, which means fewer bodies able to find outside pressure if it were there.

For people in São Tomé and Príncipe, this means the oil under their waters, potentially the country's largest source of income, was parcelled out in a process their own attorney general found manipulated, and no court has said who was paid. They are best protected when they can see who wins resource rights and public contracts and who owns the companies that hold them.

Seychelles.d:
Little has been proven about outsiders reaching into the Seychelles state, and what has been reported centres on the heroin that moves through the islands of the western Indian Ocean. People who use drugs, prison staff and former anti-narcotics officers interviewed for research published in 2021 described police who release dealers after a payment, resell seized drugs and protect some traffickers while pursuing their rivals, and they said corruption in the anti-narcotics bureau reaches high. A parliamentary committee separately found irregular payments of about US$6 million, involving the drug-enforcement agency and the financial intelligence unit, sent to offshore companies in Mauritius.

None of this has been tested in court: as of 2021 the Anti-Corruption Commission had no active case of drug-related corruption. The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 4 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 5.4, both near the middle of the scale.

For residents this means the agencies they are told are fighting the drug trade are described as compromised by the people who work closest to them, while no court has yet said who was paid or by whom. In a 2017 survey by the Anti-Corruption Commission, more than four in five of the roughly 15,000 people who answered said corruption was very high.

Slovenia.d:
The documented attempt from outside to buy decisions in Slovenia came through arms buying, the part of government where a single contract is large and the details are kept from the public. In 2006 Patria, a Finnish state-owned arms maker, won a deal worth 278 million euros to supply 135 armoured vehicles, and the Finnish broadcaster YLE later alleged that bribes were paid partly aimed at Prime Minister Janez Janša.

Courts in three countries reached different conclusions. A Slovenian conviction of Janša was annulled by the Constitutional Court and the case lapsed without a new ruling; defendants in Finland were acquitted, and one middleman was convicted in Austria. No court has a standing finding that Janša took money, and he denies it.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 6.5 out of 10, higher than most of its EU neighbours, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 6.2.

For Slovenians, the Patria case shows what that gap looks like in practice. Taxpayers paid for the country's largest arms purchase while a foreign broadcaster said it had been won with bribes, and voters have had to judge the prime minister at several elections since without a final answer from any court.

South Sudan.d:
South Sudan's government has let outsiders into its core through businessmen who live off state contracts and then move into high office. Benjamin Bol Mel, whose construction company received road contracts worth tens of millions of dollars without competitive bidding while he was the president's financial adviser, was sanctioned by the United States for corruption in 2017 and still became a vice president and deputy head of the ruling party in 2025, until a decree removed him nine months later.

Oil is the state's main income, and foreign commodity traders have bought access to it through officials. Glencore admitted in a UK court in 2022 to paying bribes for oil business in five African countries, South Sudan among them.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 9 out of 10 and courts, police and watchdogs at about 2, among the worst in the world. For South Sudanese this means oil revenue that belongs to the public is traded through officials for private payments, and contracts go to people close to the president without a tender.

St. Lucia.d:
Nothing is documented here, so this is an estimate. No case has been found of foreign governments, companies or criminal groups paying or placing officials in St Lucia.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 3 out of 10, which is low, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 5.5, near the middle of the scale. The main risk in the eastern Caribbean is the cocaine route north from South America, which passes through these islands.

For residents, the absence of a documented case means there is no known instance of officials here being paid or placed from outside. It also means the estimate rests on the index's own assessment rather than on any investigation or court case in St Lucia, and it would change if a case came to light, most likely through the drug route.

Sweden.d:
In Sweden the reach into the state comes from two directions: criminal networks working through ordinary public administration, and foreign intelligence services recruiting people inside Sweden's own security agencies.

The criminal route is the larger one today. A 2023 research review for the SNS think tank found that criminal networks have people inside government agencies, run companies in the welfare sector, such as home care, schools and assistance services, and draw on social insurance; wrong welfare payments are estimated at 13 to 16 billion kronor a year. Municipalities are most exposed, because they spend much of the money with less oversight. Courts have convicted police employees of passing data from police registers to these networks, and police reporting calls insider access a systematic weakness.

Russian military intelligence, the GRU, has placed agents inside the Swedish state in two separate generations. During the Cold War an air force colonel in the defence minister's office passed it about 20,000 pages including Sweden's air defence plans, and from 2011 to 2021 a man who had worked for both the Security Service and military intelligence passed it information for money, for which he was jailed for life in 2023.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 2 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 7.4. For Swedes this shows where the problem lies: their taxes fund welfare companies that criminal groups run, the losses fall on municipal budgets for care and schools, people who report crimes can be identified to the groups they reported from inside the police, and the agencies meant to catch foreign spies have themselves been penetrated.

Tajikistan.d:
Tajikistan's long border with Afghanistan is one of the main routes for Afghan heroin and hashish heading north to Russia and Europe, and the drug trade reaches into the officials who are meant to stop it: border guards, police, diplomats and, by some accounts, the head of the agency created to fight it. Analysts and diplomats cited by EurasiaNet in 2012 said some estimate drug money at the equivalent of 30% of the economy, and that major traffickers enjoy high-level protection.

The record shows how far up it can go. In 2000 Kazakh security officers seized about 62 kilograms of heroin near Almaty from two cars, one of them the Tajik ambassador's, and arrested him. In 2004 the head of the national Drug Control Agency, a former commander of the presidential guard, was jailed for life on charges that included drug trafficking; many saw the arrest as political, though critics who accepted that it was also said he had links to the trade. Lower down, in 2012 a military court jailed five officers of a border unit on the Afghan frontier after the checkpoint chief was caught with 20 kilograms of hashish.

Apart from that one disputed case, convictions stop at the level of local officers, and most seizures are of small dealers. The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 9 out of 10, among the highest in the world, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 2.5.

For people in Tajikistan this means the border is a route rather than a barrier, police and prison guards are reported to control street and prison sales, and if drug money makes up a large share of the economy, many families depend on it for work while officials who refuse to go along are at risk.

Togo.d:
Togo's one documented case of outsiders reaching into its government comes from a foreign conglomerate and the country's main economic asset, the deep-water port of Lomé. French investigators allege that subsidiaries of the Bolloré Group, the conglomerate of the French billionaire Vincent Bolloré, provided President Faure Gnassingbé's 2010 election campaign with communications work at below its real price through its advertising agency, and that the group then secured control of the port. Bolloré admitted the facts in 2021 under a guilty-plea procedure, but a Paris court refused the deal, and in 2026 he was ordered to stand trial in Paris. A similar arrangement is alleged in Guinea. The group sold its African ports business in 2022.

The Global Organized Crime Index puts Togo in its high band, scoring it 7.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 4.4 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, below the middle of the range. Read together, those scores suggest outside interests have room to reach officials and the bodies that would expose them are weak.

For Togolese, this means the concession to run the port through which much of their trade passes is alleged to have been handed to a company that helped the president win re-election, a family that has held the presidency since 1967. The case is being tried in France, and no Togolese court has examined it, so residents depend on a foreign trial to learn how the deal was made.

Turkiye.d:
In Turkey, secret networks inside the army, police and courts have shaped the state for more than a century. An oath-bound society of army officers seized the Ottoman government in 1913. In recent decades the Gülen movement, a religious network led by the preacher Fethullah Gülen, placed its followers as judges, prosecutors, police and military officers, at first in alliance with the government. Courts and official bodies have found that its followers obtained leaked questions for the civil-service, police and judges' entrance exams so that members would be hired, and used police and prosecutors' posts to go after the intelligence chief; a former deputy head of the board that appoints judges testified that, after followers won seats on it in 2010, about a hundred of them were placed on the appeals court.

The government blames those followers for the failed coup of July 2016 and dismissed about 150,000 people from public jobs, including about a third of the country's judges in a single day, without a court ruling on each person. Courts have convicted hundreds of officers over the coup, but for most of those dismissed the evidence of membership was never tested, and journalists report that another religious order, the Menzil Sufis, has since filled many of the emptied police posts, which the government denies.

A second pattern links police and ministers to the Grey Wolves, the ultranationalist youth wing of the MHP, now President Erdoğan's partner in government. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 9 out of 10. For people in Turkey this means the state jobs and courtrooms they deal with have been staffed by whichever religious network held the hiring, and a public servant can lose a career on an accusation of hidden loyalty.

Ukraine.d:
Ukraine is fighting a war against Russia while still dealing with networks that reach into its parliament, security services, state companies and border posts from inside. The deepest reach has been Russia's own. Before and after the 2022 invasion, Russian services recruited officers inside the SBU, Ukraine's main security service, and the prosecution service: by mid-2022 the president said 651 treason and collaboration cases had been opened against law-enforcement officials, and the SBU's own head for Crimea was detained as a suspected agent. Ukrainian investigators say Russian military intelligence built a network of MPs in parliament, and the leader of the main pro-Kremlin opposition party, a personal friend of Vladimir Putin, was charged with treason and later handed to Russia in a prisoner exchange.

The other lasting pattern is business circles close to those in power taking a cut from state firms. In the 2000s the company that supplied all of Ukraine's imported gas was suspected by Ukrainian politicians and US diplomats of being controlled by a Russian crime boss. In 2025 Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau said a group led by a businessman and friend of President Zelensky took about $100 million in kickbacks from contractors of Energoatom, the state nuclear power company. At the western border, customs and border officers have been charged with running smuggling channels into the European Union.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in Ukraine at 8 out of 10, and its courts, police and watchdogs at 4.5. For Ukrainians, this means the security officers meant to protect them may have been passing information to the army invading them, and kickbacks at the nuclear company raise the cost of keeping electricity on while Russia bombs the grid.

Uruguay.d:
Uruguay has strong courts and watchdogs by world standards, and no current case shows outside groups with people inside its government. The Global Organized Crime Index puts it in the Low band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 3.5 out of 10 and the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs at 7.5.

The documented case of outside reach comes from the years of military rule, when a foreign religious movement bought its way into the financial system. In 1981 the Unification Church, the Korean-founded movement of Sun Myung Moon, bought 49% of Banco de Crédito, one of the country's oldest banks, and started a daily newspaper that declared itself 'fully identified' with the military government. A later parliamentary commission found that the bank had lent about US$100 million, about a sixth of all its loans, to companies linked to Moon's movement before it closed in 2002.

The effect is still felt by Uruguayans who kept their savings in that bank or depended on its stability: a foreign group that owned almost half of it used depositors' money to fund its own companies, under a government that faced no free press or opposition able to ask questions. That case is the reason the risk is not zero, but in present-day Uruguay the courts, parliament and press are able to investigate such an arrangement if it happened again.

Venezuela.d:
In Venezuela the state itself has been accused of becoming a channel for drug trafficking, run by the same military circle that took power with Hugo Chávez. Chávez built a secret movement inside the army from 1982, tried to seize power with more than 2,000 troops in 1992, and after his election in 1998 put fellow plotters in charge of intelligence and regional governments. Since 2008 the United States has named officers from that circle, including heads of military intelligence and the main intelligence service, as working for the FARC, the Colombian guerrilla army that financed itself through cocaine. US prosecutors call the network 'Cartel de los Soles'; analysts dispute that it is an organised cartel. A head of military intelligence and a retired general have pleaded guilty in US courts, while a head of the anti-drug office charged in New York was promoted to interior minister. Nicolás Maduro, seized by US forces in January 2026, has pleaded not guilty and has not yet been tried.

A second route ran through Cuba. Under secret agreements signed in 2008, Cuban officers oversaw the rebuilding of Venezuela's military intelligence service, which then turned to watching Venezuela's own soldiers. Foreign contractors have also been accused of buying access through campaign payments in return for priority on public works, claims no Venezuelan court has examined.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in Venezuela at 9 out of 10 and its courts, police and watchdogs at 1.9, among the lowest in the world. For Venezuelans this has meant police and anti-drug agencies led by men accused of working for traffickers, soldiers who disagreed with the government watched under foreign supervision, and public works contracts awarded without open scrutiny, with no domestic court able to examine any of it.

Zimbabwe.d:
In Zimbabwe the line between the ruling party and the businesses that profit from the state has largely disappeared. The pattern is for a small circle of business people close to President Mnangagwa and the ZANU-PF party to win state contracts paid with public money, and then to move into the party and the government themselves. The clearest example is Kudakwashe Tagwirei, whose company Sakunda grew through fuel trading and a $3 billion state farming contract paid in Treasury bills; the United States and Britain sanctioned him for misappropriating public funds, which he denies, and in October 2026 he was made a cabinet minister in charge of investment.

The same overlap runs through the gold trade, Zimbabwe's main source of hard currency. In 2023 undercover reporters recorded brokers, among them a preacher whom the president had appointed ambassador-at-large and presidential envoy, apparently offering to use their positions to bring illicit cash into the country, swap it for gold and sell the gold abroad as clean money. The government's financial intelligence unit said it found no evidence for the claims, and a commission was appointed.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in Zimbabwe at 8 out of 10 and its courts, police and watchdogs at 3. For Zimbabweans this means that money meant for fuel, seed and fertiliser passes through firms owned by people who now sit in the cabinet, and gold dug from their land can be used to clean criminal money abroad, with the president's own envoy filmed offering the service. Investment policy is now run by a man two Western governments accuse of taking public funds.
